answer_a:
● think_tool(This is a Table 3 ablation for the Ev…)

Cross-Lingual Lexical Bootstrapping for Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation
via Cognate-Guided Code-Switching### ProblemNeural machine translation (NMT)
systems require large parallel corpora to achieve acceptable quality. For the
vast majority of the world's languages — those with fewer than1 million speakers
and minimal digitized text — parallel data is scarce or nonexistent. Existing
low-resource approaches fall into three categories: transfer learning from a
high-resource parent language, unsupervised methods that rely on monolingual
corpora and back-translation, and data augmentation using lexical substitution.
Each has a known ceiling: transfer learning degrades sharply when the parent and
target are typologically distant; unsupervised methods produce fluent but
semantically brittle output; and lexical augmentation methods are limited by the
coverage of existing bilingual lexicons. No current method systematically
exploits the phonological and orthographic signal shared between related
languages — cognates — to generate synthetic parallel data at the sentence
level, then uses that data to train a joint encoder that generalizes beyond the
lexical overlap.

HypothesisH1. Incorporating cognate-guided code-switching as a data augmentation
strategy injects sufficient parallel signal into low-resource MT training to
improve BLEU by ≥3 points over back-translation-only baselines at
the10k-sentence parallel data regime.

H2. A shared bilingual encoder pretrained on a cognate-detection objective
learns cross-lingual representations that transfer better to the translation
task than standard cross-lingual language model pretraining (e.g., XLM-R)
because the objective forces alignment at the subword level rather than the
sentence level.

H3. The gains are largest for language pairs with moderate cognate density
(15–35% lexical overlap) and diminish at both very high overlap (where standard
transfer already works) and very low overlap (where the signal from cognates is
too sparse). This produces an identifiable U-shaped utility curve, which can be
used to decide a priori whether cognate bootstrapping will help a given language
pair.

MethodThe proposed method, CognateBoot, proceeds in four stages:

Stage1: Cognate Detection and Lexicon Induction. Given a source language L_s and
target language L_t with a small seed parallel lexicon (500–2000 entries), train
a cognate classifier that operates on subword sequences. The classifier uses
edit distance over phonemized forms (via the Epitran grapheme-to-phoneme
library) combined with a learned alignment score from a2-layer Transformer over
character n-grams. This detects cognates even when orthographic divergence is
high (e.g., Spanish noche → Italian notte). Output: a bilingual cognate lexicon
of size k (target:5,000–20,000 pairs, depending on language pair).

Stage2: Cognate-Guided Code-Switching Augmentation. For each sentence in the
target-side monolingual corpus (which is assumed to be larger than the parallel
data, e.g.,100k–500k sentences), identify content words that have a known
cognate in L_s via the induced lexicon. Replace each such word with its cognate
equivalent with probability p =0.3 (tuned on a held-out development set). Apply
a syntactic constraint: only replace nouns, verbs, and adjectives; function
words and inflected forms are skipped unless the cognate match is exact in lemma
form. The result is a code-switched sentence that mixes L_t content with L_s
lexical insertions, creating a synthetic parallel-like signal without requiring
a full translation model.

Stage3: Joint Encoder Pretraining on Cognate Detection. Pretrain a6-layer
Transformer encoder on a binary classification task: given a pair of sentences
(s_i, t_j) — one from L_s, one from L_t — predict whether they are translations.
The positive pairs come from (a) the seed parallel corpus, (b) synthetic
translation pairs where t_j is the code-switched version of s_i, and (c)
back-translated pairs from a preliminary unsupervised NMT model. Negative pairs
are sampled from mismatched corpora. This is a scaled-down version of the XLM
translation-pair pretraining objective, but with two key differences: (i) the
training set is heavily weighted toward cognate-rich sentences (oversampled3×),
and (ii) the encoder is shallow (6 layers vs.12–24 in XLM-R) to match
low-resource compute budgets.

Stage4: Finetuning with Downsampling Curriculum. Finetune the pretrained
encoder–decoder on the seed parallel corpus (10k sentences) using a curriculum
that sorts training examples by cognate density from high to low. The intuition:
early training on cognate-dense examples anchors the cross-lingual mappings, and
later examples with fewer cognates force generalization beyond lexical overlap.
Decoding uses beam search with length penalty α =0.6. All experiments use
fairseq with a single GPU (12 GB VRAM).

Dataset and BenchmarkExperiments target three language pairs spanning the
cognate-density spectrum:


                 Cognate Density                  Monolingual
 Language Pair   (est.)           Seed Parallel   (target)         Family
 Spanish →       ~35%             10k (FLoRes     200k (OSCAR)     Romance
 Catalan                          dev)
 Indonesian →    ~25%             10k (FLoRes     200k (OSCAR)     Austronesian
 Malay                            dev)
 Hindi →         ~15%             10k             200k (OSCAR)     Indo-Aryan
 Bengali                          (Samanantar
                                  sample)


All evaluation uses the FLoRes-101 test sets (101-way translation). Development
sets are held out from the training data (1k sentences per pair).

Justification. These pairs cover moderate to high cognate density within a
single family branch. Spanish–Catalan tests near the upper bound of expected
utility; Hindi–Bengali tests the middle region where the method should produce
maximum relative gain; Indonesian–Malay tests a pair with high lexical overlap
but low orthographic convergence (both use Latin script, but phoneme-to-grapheme
mappings differ). An additional low-density pair (Swahili → Zulu, ~8% detectable
cognate rate) is included to test the lower bound of the U-shaped hypothesis.

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: BLEU (sacrébleu, signature:
nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp)

 • Secondary: chrF2++ (character-level metric robust to cognate surface forms);
   COMET (crosslingual embedding-based metric, wmt20-comet-da model)
 • Ablation diagnostics: cognate-BLEU (BLEU computed only on sentences with ≥3
   detected cognates), non-cognate-BLEU (sentences with ≤1 cognate) — to
   localize where gains come from- Statistical rigor: each condition run with3
   different random seeds;95% bootstrap confidence intervals reported for all
   main comparisons### Baselines1. Back-translation only (Edunov et al.,2018):
   unsupervised NMT baseline using target-side monolingual data with no
   code-switching or cognate signal.

 2 XLM-R + finetune (Conneau et al.,2020): initialize encoder with XLM-R-base,
   finetune on the10k seed parallel data (no cognate augmentation).
 3 Lexical substitution baseline (Lample et al.,2018): replace random target
   words with source-word translations from a bilingual dictionary (MUSE induced
   lexicon) at rate p =0.3, without cognate filtering.
 4 Full-data upper bound (Transformer-base,100k parallel sentences from OPUS, no
   augmentation): establishes the performance ceiling for each pair given
   abundant data.

Ablations| Ablation | Component Removed | Expected Impact |

|---|---|---| | A1 | Cognate detection (use MUSE lexicon instead) | BLEU drops
~1–2 pts; MUSE covers fewer cognates and includes false positives | | A2 |
Code-switching (use back-translation only in Stage3 pretraining) | BLEU drops
~2–3 pts; confirms cognate augmentation is the key signal | | A3 | No syntactic
constraints in code-switching (replace all words, including function words) |
BLEU gains diminish; function-word replacement increases noise | | A4 | Flat
training (no curriculum; shuffle all training data) | BLEU drops ~0.5–1 pt;
curriculum matters at the margin but is not the core driver | | A5 | Pretrain
without cognate weighting (uniform oversampling) | BLEU drops ~1 pt;
cognate-rich pretraining provides a measurable boost |

Expected Failure Modes1. Cognate detection error propagates. If the induced
cognate lexicon has high precision but low recall (the expected failure mode of
edit-distance-based detection), the augmentation signal will be sparse. A recall
<10% would make Stage2 indistinguishable from random lexical substitution.
Mitigation: if Stage1 recall is below15% on a held-out cognate gold set, fall
back to a dictionary-based method (A1 configuration) and flag the result as a
non-cognate-driven outcome.

 2 Code-switching degrades target-language fluency. Replacing content words with
   source-language cognates may produce sentences that are locally
   understandable but whose global syntactic structure is corrupted (e.g.,
   verb-argument order mismatches between L_s and L_t in the Hindi–Bengali pair,
   where word order is more flexible). Mitigation: the syntactic constraint
   (Stage2) blocks function-word replacement; if LM perplexity on augmented
   sentences exceeds1.5× the perplexity on natural text, reduce p from0.3
   to0.15.
 3 Pretrained encoder overfits to cognate-detection proxy. The Stage3 binary
   classification task may produce an encoder that learns shallow orthographic
   cues (e.g., "if both sentences share the character sequence 'tion', predict
   positive") rather than deeper cross-lingual alignment. Mitigation: evaluate
   the pretrained encoder on the XL-Speech sentence retrieval task after Stage3;
   if recall@1 <20%, add a masked language modeling objective (λ =0.3) as
   regularization.
 4 Curriculum training causes catastrophic forgetting. If early
   high-cognate-density examples over-represent one domain (e.g., news text),
   the model may forget later low-cognate examples from other domains.
   Mitigation: monitor per-domain BLEU during finetuning; if a domain regresses
   by ≥2 BLEU relative to its starting point, revert to uniform shuffling.
 5 U-shaped curve is not observed — cognate density does not predict gain
   magnitude. This would falsify H3 and suggest that typological similarity
   (rather than lexical overlap per se) drives the improvement. If H3 fails, the
   paper will report the negative result and argue for a broader typological
   feature analysis instead.

Limitations1. Gold cognate lexicons are unavailable for most language pairs. The
evaluation relies on automatic cognate detection, which is itself an open
research problem for distantly related languages. Results on Spanish→Catalan may
overestimate performance on pairs with no standardized orthography.

 2 Monolingual corpus size is assumed (200k sentences). For languages with truly
   minimal digitization (e.g., <50k sentences total), the code-switching stage
   produces too few augmented sentences to affect training. The method is
   designed for languages with moderate digital presence (Wikipedia-sized or
   larger) rather than "extreme" low-resource languages (<10k sentences).
 3 No morphological handling. CognateBoot treats each word as an atomic unit. In
   morphologically rich languages (e.g., Bengali, Swahili), a single lemma may
   have dozens of surface forms, many of which will not be recognized by the
   edit-distance-based cognate detector. This systematically underestimates the
   true cognate density for inflected forms. A future extension would
   incorporate morphological segmentation (e.g., BPE over morphemes).
 4 Single GPU constraint limits encoder depth. The6-layer encoder may be too
   shallow to capture the cross-lingual abstraction that cognate-rich
   pretraining should provide, particularly for the Hindi→Bengali pair where
   script divergence adds visual noise. Results with a deeper encoder (12
   layers) on a subset of the data are reported as a secondary analysis but are
   not the primary claim.
 5 Evaluation languages are all from the same macro-family (Indo-European +
   Austronesian). The typological range is limited. Claims about
   generalizability to unrelated language families (Niger-Congo, Sino-Tibetan,
   Pama-Nyungan) are speculative until tested.
 6 Negative result risk on Swahili→Zulu. If the low cognate density (~8%)
   produces no measurable gain over back-translation, the U-shaped hypothesis is
   not fully tested (it requires a point near zero gain, not negative gain). A
   zero-result on this pair would be inconclusive rather than confirming the
   lower bound.

Research Proposal: Cross-Lingual Contrastive Retrieval for Low-Resource Neural
Machine Translation## Title
CREST-MT: Cross-Lingual Contrastive
Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Machine Translation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Neural machine translation (NMT) for low-resource language pairs suffers
from data sparsity. While massively multilingual pretrained models (e.g., mBART,
NLLB) provide a strong foundation, they are expensive to deploy and fine-tune,
and their coverage of truly low-resource languages remains uneven. Current
approaches either rely on large-scale back-translation (which introduces noise)
or on pivoting through a high-resource language (which compounds errors). There
is no established method that efficiently selects high-quality synthetic
training data from monolingual corpora without requiring a seed translation
system or a large teacher model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Cross-lingual sentence embeddings, learned via a lightweight
contrastive objective on a small bilingual dictionary (≤5k entries), can
retrieve high-quality parallel sentence pairs from monolingual corpora to
augment a small seed parallel corpus. An NMT model fine-tuned on this augmented
data will outperform: (1) training on the seed corpus alone, (2) standard
back-translation augmentation, and (3) using generic multilingual sentence
encoders (e.g., LaBSE) for retrieval, particularly when the total compute budget
is ≤1 GPU-day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Retriever1. Input:5,000 word-level
translation pairs from a bilingual dictionary (or automatically induced via
unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction). Two large monolingual corpora (source
side: ~5M sentences, target side: ~5M sentences).

2 Encoder: A small dual-encoder Transformer (2 layers,256-dim hidden,4 heads —
≈6M parameters) initialized independently on source and target monolingual
data via masked language modeling (1 epoch each).
3 Contrastive alignment: For each dictionary entry, sample an equal number of
unrelated source/target words as negatives. Optimize with InfoNCE loss + a
margin of0.3. No back-translation or parallel data is needed.
4 Retrieval: Encode all sentences from both monolingual corpora with the
aligned encoder. For each source sentence, retrieve the top-5 target
sentences by cosine similarity. Apply a confidence threshold (≥0.7) to retain
only high-confidence pairs.

Stage2: NMT Fine-Tuning1. Seed parallel corpus:20k sentence pairs.

2 Augmented corpus: Seed + high-confidence retrieved pairs (expected
yield:50k–150k depending on language pair — accept50k as minimum).
3 Model:6-layer Transformer (512-dim,8-head encoder-decoder) — intentionally
kept small.
4 Training: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy (label smoothing ε=0.1), Adam
(β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98), inverse sqrt learning rate scheduler (warmup4000 steps).
Batch size4096 tokens. Early stopping based on dev perplexity (patience5).1
GPU-day budget on a single A100.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Size | Source |

|---|---|---| | Bilingual dictionary |5,000 pairs | Wiktionary / PanLex /
automatic induction | | Seed parallel (train) |20k pairs | JW300 or Tatoeba | |
Monolingual (source) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | |
Monolingual (target) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | | Dev |2k
pairs | FLORES-200 dev split | | Test |2k pairs | FLORES-200 devtest split |

Language pair: Gujarati → English (gu-en), a genuinely low-resource pair with
under100k publicly available parallel sentences. The same pipeline should also
be evaluated on a second pair (e.g., Kazakh → English) to ensure results are not
language-specific.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- BLEU (sacrébleu signature:
nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp) — primary metric- chrF++
(character-level) — secondary, captures morphologically faithful translations-
COMET (wmt22-comet-da) — neural metric for semantic adequacy- Retrieval
precision@1 on held-out bilingual dictionary entries (to validate the retriever
quality in Stage1)

• Effective augmentation yield: number of retrieved pairs above the confidence
thresholdAll NMT models are run with 3 random seeds. We report means with95%
bootstrap confidence intervals.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| # | Method | Key Difference from CREST-MT |

|---|---|---| | B1 | Seed-only fine-tuning | No data augmentation | | B2 | Seed
+ standard back-translation | Uses a target→source model to back-translate
target monolingual data | | B3 | Seed + LaBSE-based retrieval (Feng et al.,2022)
| Replaces our contrastive retriever with the publicly available LaBSE encoder |
| B4 | mBART-50 fine-tuned on seed (4 layers unfrozen) | Multilingual pretrained
baseline,4× parameter cost | | B5 | Random retrieval: seed + randomly paired
monolingual sentences | Upper bound on noise; controls for data quantity alone |
| B6 | Bilingual dictionary induction baseline: replaces the dictionary with an
automatically induced one (unsupervised) | Tests sensitivity to dictionary
quality |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Retriever size: Remove contrastive alignment entirely (train on
word-level MLM only, no bilingual signal).

2 Confidence threshold: Vary the threshold (0.5,0.7,0.85,0.95) to measure
precision–recall trade-off on retrieved pairs.
3 Dictionary size: Reduce dictionary from5k →1k →200 entries to measure how
much bilingual signal the retriever needs.
4 Negative sampling strategy: Compare random negatives vs. in-batch negatives
vs. hard negative mining via TF-IDF similarity.
5 Monolingual data quantity: Subset source/target monolingual data from5M →500k
→50k sentences.
6 NMT model scale: Increase NMT to12-layer/1024-dim to test whether gains
persist in larger models.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|---|---|---| | Retriever yields no high-confidence pairs (<50k) | Medium —
depends on how well dictionary covers the monolingual data | Fall back to a
weaker threshold (0.5) and filter by round-trip consistency instead; if still
<50k, report ablation (A2) to characterize the threshold boundary | | Augmented
data is too noisy and degrades BLEU | Low–Medium — random retrieval baseline
(B5) bounds noise, and contrastive retrieval should be better than random |
Measure per-pair confidence and stratify test-set BLEU by retrieval confidence
quartiles; if low-confidence pairs actively hurt, use confidence-weighted
training loss | | Dictionary quality is poor (many incorrect entries) | Low for
Wiktionary; Medium for automatically induced dictionaries | B6 ablation tests
this explicitly; if Wiktionary exists for the language pair, use it; if not,
report the induction baseline separately | | Gains appear only on small NMT
model, vanish at scale | Medium — larger models have stronger language priors
and may not benefit from extra data | Ablation A6 tests this directly; if gains
vanish, reframe contribution as "efficient retrieval for small models" | |
Computational budget (1 GPU-day) is insufficient | Low — the small encoder and
modest NMT are designed to fit this budget | Profile training step time; if
close to the limit, reduce monolingual data to2M sentences and cap NMT epochs
at30 | | Results are language-pair specific | Medium — gu-en may be easy due to
shared script in some domains, or hard due to limited data quality | Replicate
on a second language pair (kk-en) with distinct script and different data
sources; report both in the main paper |

Research Proposal: Self-Improving AI Agents for Software Engineering via
 Iterative Execution Feedback## TitleEvoForge: A Self-Evolving Code-Generation
   Agent that Learns from Execution Traces Without Explicit Validation Memory

ProblemLarge language models (LLMs) applied to software engineering tasks — bug
repair, feature implementation, test generation — currently rely on either a
single prompt or a fixed retrieval corpus. When an agent produces a flawed
patch, standard approaches either re-sample from the same prior (wasting samples
on the same failure modes) or retrieve external examples that may not match the
local code context. The core problem is how to enable an agent to improve its
own code-generation policy across repeated attempts on the same task without
maintaining an explicit store of past errors and rejection rules. If
validation-driven memory is removed, does the agent collapse to random
resampling, or can it extract useful signal from execution traces alone?

HypothesisA code-generation agent that conditions each subsequent attempt on the
full execution trace (stdout, stderr, exit code, runtime exception type) of its
previous attempt — but not on an explicit memory of which past ideas were
rejected or why — can still improve monotonically across iterations. The
execution trace itself carries implicit validation signal: a timeout suggests an
infinite loop, a specific exception type narrows the space of viable next moves,
and a partial output with a low exit code hints at a near-miss. We hypothesize
that this implicit signal is sufficient to achieve comparable final accuracy to
a system that maintains an explicit validation-evolution memory, at the cost of
more iterations on average.

MethodEvoForge operates as a loop over a single task-instance:

 1 Initial prompt — A task description (e.g., "fix the bug in sort_utils.py")
   plus the full codebase context is fed to an LLM, which generates a candidate
   patch.
 2 Sandbox execution — The patch is applied and the test suite (or a safe
   subset) is run. Stdout, stderr, exit code, and any exception traceback are
   captured.
 3 Contextualized re-prompt — The entire interaction history for this task
   (previous patches + their execution traces) is appended to the prompt.
   Importantly, the prompt contains only the raw traces; no external
   validation-evolution memory (e.g., a "failed_directions.json" or a learned
   rejection classifier) is consulted or injected.
 4 Repeat — Steps2–3 run for up to K iterations or until all tests pass.

Key design choices:

 • No cross-task memory. Each task is independent; learning does not accumulate
   across tasks. This isolates the -IVE ablation.
 • Trace-only signal. The agent never sees a binary "pass/fail" label in a
   structured format; it must infer success/failure from the raw trace output.
 • Same LLM checkpoint throughout. No online fine-tuning; all improvement comes
   from in-context adaptation.

Dataset / BenchmarkSWE-bench Verified (the curated subset of SWE-bench with500
task-instances from real Python repositories, each with a bug report, a codebase
snapshot, and a test suite). We use the lite split (300 instances) to keep
compute feasible:

 • Validation split:100 instances for prompt tuning and iteration-budget
   selection.
 • Test split:200 instances for final evaluation.

Each instance requires generating a patch that passes the held-out tests.

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary? |

|--------|-----------|----------| | % Resolved (pass@k) | Fraction of instances
where any of k iterations produces a passing patch | Primary | | Mean iterations
to resolve | Average number of iterations among resolved instances | Secondary |
| Trace utilization | Fraction of iterations where the new patch is different
from the previous one (measures whether the trace is being used vs. ignored) |
Process metric | | Pass saturation curve | % resolved after1,2,3, … K iterations
| Diagnostic |

All metrics are reported with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across3 seeds
(varying the LLM sampling temperature at iteration1 only).

Baselines1. Static single-prompt (pass@1) — The same LLM asked once with the
task description and codebase; no iteration. (Lower bound.)

 2 Resampling without trace — K independent i.i.d. samples from the same prompt;
   the best patch (by test pass rate or by an oracle) is selected. (Controls for
   the benefit of more samples alone.)
 3 Best-of-N with execution reranking — Generate N independent patches; run all
   in the sandbox; pick the one with the highest pass rate on a held-out
   validation test split. (Stronger baseline — uses the same sandbox but no
   sequential conditioning.)
 4 Full EvoScientist (with -IVE enabled) — The same sequential loop but with an
   explicit validation-evolution memory (stores failed directions, rejection
   criteria, and execution failure patterns). (Upper bound.)

Ablations (Internal)

 • Trace verbosity ablation. Feed only the exception type + error message (no
   stdout) vs. the full trace, to measure how much signal resides in structured
   error types vs. unstructured output.
 • Iteration budget K. Sweep K ∈

Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

Research Proposal: Addressing Accuracy Issues in Automated LLM Evaluation---

Title
Calibrated Ensemble Evaluation (CEE): Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Accuracy
through Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Model Deliberation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based automated evaluators ("LLM-as-a-judge") are the dominant method
for evaluating open-ended text generation at scale, but suffer from four
well-documented accuracy issues:

1 Systematic biases — position bias (preferring first or second response),
verbosity bias (preferring longer outputs), and self-enhancement bias
(preferring outputs from models similar to the judge).
2 No uncertainty quantification — standard practice returns a point estimate
(score or preference) with no confidence, making it impossible to know when
the judge is uncertain vs confident.
3 Low inter-rater reliability — agreement between LLM judges and human raters
varies wildly across domains (Spearman ρ ranges from0.3 on creative writing
to0.7 on factual QA).
4 Rubric brittleness — even with detailed rubrics, LLM judges often fail to
follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

The core unmet need is an evaluation framework that produces trustworthy scores
— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing evaluation into atomic quality criteria, aggregating
judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated
set will significantly improve accuracy — defined as Spearman rank correlation
with held-out human judgments — over the standard single-model, single-pass,
holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method (3-stage pipeline)

Stage1: Atomic Criterion DecompositionInstead of asking a judge for a single
"overall quality" score (which collapses heterogeneous dimensions), decompose
evaluation into6 atomic rubrics:

#  Criterion              Definition
1  Relevance              Does the response address the prompt directly?
2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)
3  Coherence              Is the response logically structured and internally
consistent?
4  Completeness           Does the response cover the scope requested?
5  Conciseness            Is the response free of unnecessary verbosity?
6  Instruction Following  Does the response obey format, length, and style
constraints?

Each criterion is scored on a1–5 Likert scale by each evaluator model, using a
criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and
the response. This prevents any single criterion from dominating.

Stage2: Multi-Model Panel with UncertaintyQuery a panel of K =3 to5 diverse LLM
evaluators (from different model families, e.g., GPT-4o, Claude3.5 Sonnet,
Llama370B, Gemini2.0 Flash, Mistral Large). Each model scores each response on
all6 criteria.

For each (model, criterion, response) triple, also extract the log-probability
of the score token(s) as a proxy for the model's confidence in that judgment.
This gives a per-criterion confidence weight.

Stage3: Calibration LayerUsing a held-out calibration set of N =500–1,000
examples with human ratings on the same6 criteria (collected from3 annotators
per example):

1 Score Aggregation: Per criterion, compute a confidence-weighted average
across models: s_c = Σ_i w_i_c * score_i_c / Σ_i w_i_c where w_i_c =
exp(logprob_i_c) is model i's confidence on criterion c.
2 Bias Correction: Fit a small logistic regression or isotonic regression per
criterion to map the aggregated score s_c to a calibrated score ŝ_c that
minimizes expected calibration error against human ratings.
3 Uncertainty Output: For each response, output both the calibrated score
vector ŝ ∈ [1,5]^6 and a per-criterion uncertainty interval derived from the
weighted variance across the panel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Dataset | Use | Size | Human Annotations |

|---------|-----|------|-------------------| | MT-Bench | Primary evaluation |80
multi-turn questions,3,360 model outputs | Human preference + pairwise ratings
(published) | | Chatbot Arena (subset) | Primary evaluation |10K randomly
sampled comparisons | Human preference votes (public) | | FLASK | Fine-grained
evaluation | ~1,700 model outputs | Human ratings on12 fine-grained dimensions |
| ShareGPT + rubric annotation | Calibration set |500 examples,3 annotators/ex |
Collected fresh (6 atomic criteria + overall) | | AlpacaEval2.0 | OOD test |805
examples | Length-controlled win rates (indirect human signal) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What it measures | Target |

|--------|-----------------|--------| | Spearman ρ (with human scores) | Rank
correlation — primary metric | >0.65 (vs ~0.50–0.55 for GPT-4 baseline on
creative/ open-ended tasks) | | Exact + Adjacent Agreement | Score-level match
with humans | >60% exact +85% adjacent | | Position Bias Rate | % of trials
where swapping A/B order flips the preference | <5% (vs ~15–20% for single-model
judges) | | Verbosity Correlation | Pearson r between predicted score and
response length (log tokens) | |r| <0.10 (vs ~0.35 for rubric-free judges) | |
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) | Binned calibration of confidence vs accuracy
| <0.08 | | Test-Retest Consistency | Variance across3 independent runs on same
input | σ² <0.02 per criterion | | Cost per Evaluation | API cost per evaluation
@ inference time | Report in USD for transparency |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why chosen |

|----------|-------------|------------| | GPT-4-as-a-judge (holistic) | Single
GPT-4 call scoring "overall quality"1–5 | De facto standard in most LLM
evaluation pipelines | | GPT-4-as-a-judge (with rubric) | Same model, but with
the6 atomic criteria in prompt | Controls for rubric decomposition effect alone
| | PairRM | Trained pairwise reward model (based on Llama) | Representative of
trained, task-specific evaluators | | JudgeLM | Fine-tuned evaluator on100K
human judgments | Strongest published fine-tuned baseline | | Majority Vote (3x)
| Same model (GPT-4) called3 times, majority vote | Controls for the effect of
repeated sampling alone | | Humans (held out) | Human judgment on held-out test
set | Upper-bound oracle (no automated evaluation is expected to match this, but
it anchors the comparison) |

everything else fixed, tested on the MT-Bench test set:

Ablation                 Variation                  What it isolates

single holistic "overall"  structure
judgment

confidence-weighted        confidence signal

raw aggregated scores)     calibration

×3) vs cross-family        diversity vs repeated

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

|-------------|-----------|------------| | Calibration overfitting — the
calibration layer overfits to the small (500-example) human set and degrades on
OOD distributions like AlpacaEval | Medium | Use regularization (isotonic
regression with smoothing); report OOD performance separately; scale calibration
set to1,000 if budget permits | | Model collinearity — diverse models produce
correlated errors on the same failure cases (e.g., all miss subtle factual
errors in stylized text) | Medium-High | Analyze error correlation matrix across
models; if collinearity is high (>0.8 across all pairs), consider subsampling to
the two most independent models | | Criterion decomposition misses holistic
qualities — atomic rubrics fail to capture emergent dimensions (interestingness,
novelty, tone) that drive human preferences | Medium | Add a7th "overall
gestalt" criterion alongside atomic ones; check whether the holistic dimension
is needed for high human correlation via ablation | | Computational cost — K ×6
API calls per evaluation (e.g.,5 ×6 =30 calls) is15–30× more expensive than a
single-judge baseline, limiting practical adoption | High | Accept cost as a
trade-off for research-phase accuracy; report cost per evaluation; investigate
whether pruning to the top-2 criteria after a pilot study can reduce calls3×
with minimal accuracy loss | | Rubric leakage — models exhibit new
criterion-specific biases (e.g., always giving "conciseness" low scores to long
but good answers) | Medium | Exploratory analysis of per-criterion score
distributions; adjust rubric wording in a small pilot (N=50) before finalizing |
| Human annotation bottleneck — collecting500 ×6 ×3 ≈9,000 reliable
atomic-criterion annotations is expensive and slow | High | Use existing FLASK
dataset (already has fine-grained annotations) to bootstrap; only collect ~200
fresh annotations for the calibration held-out set | | Log-prob confidence is
poorly calibrated — score-token log-probs may not reflect true judgment

to0 for evaluation calls; if log-probs still unreliable, replace with

as an alternative confidence signal |

 AI Agentic Workflow for Clinical Decision Support: A Multi-Agent Framework for
Differential Diagnosis and Treatment Planning## ProblemClinical decision-making
  in complex, multi-morbidity cases remains a high-error domain. Single large
language models used as standalone decision aids exhibit well-documented issues:
hallucination in diagnostic reasoning, sensitivity to prompt phrasing, inability
  to self-correct, and poor calibration of uncertainty. While LLM-as-judge and
chain-of-thought prompting improve structured reasoning, they do not provide the
 iterative verification, role specialization, or consensus-building mechanisms
 that characterize high-reliability human clinical teams. Existing multi-agent
healthcare frameworks either hardcode agent roles (preventing adaptation to case
complexity) or lack rigorous mechanisms for resolving inter-agent disagreement.
 No current system combines (a) role-specialized agents with distinct epistemic
 perspectives, (b) a structured deliberation protocol for conflict resolution,
 and (c) grounding in external clinical knowledge bases — all within a single,
                       reproducible evaluation pipeline.

HypothesisA multi-agent framework composed of specialized clinical reasoning
agents — each assigned a distinct epistemic role (diagnostician, evidence
reviewer, treatment planner, skeptic) — communicating via a structured
deliberation protocol will produce differential diagnoses and treatment plans
that are more accurate, more complete, and better calibrated than (1) a single
LLM with chain-of-thought prompting, (2) an ensemble of LLMs with majority
voting, and (3) a single LLM augmented with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
from clinical literature. Specifically, we hypothesize that the skeptic agent —
tasked explicitly with identifying evidential gaps and alternative explanations
— will provide the largest marginal contribution to diagnostic accuracy among
all roles.

MethodArchitecture. A four-agent system operating over a shared case context:

 1 Diagnostician Agent — Proposes a differential diagnosis ranked by likelihood,
   with reasoning chains. Prompted to simulate inductive clinical reasoning from
   presented symptoms, history, and lab values.
 2 Evidence Reviewer Agent — Retrieves and summarizes relevant literature (via a
   frozen RAG pipeline over PubMed abstracts and clinical guidelines). Assesses
   each proposed diagnosis against available evidence.
 3 Treatment Planner Agent — Given a provisional diagnosis, proposes treatment
   options with rationale, contraindications, and monitoring recommendations.
 4 Skeptic Agent — Reviews the Diagnostician's differential and the Evidence
   Reviewer's assessment, identifies missing information, alternative
   explanations, cognitive biases, and requests specific clarifications or
   additional tests.

Deliberation Protocol (modified Delphi). All agents read the case independently.
The Diagnostician produces an initial differential. The Evidence Reviewer
annotates each candidate. The Skeptic issues critiques and queries. The
Diagnostician may revise. After up to three rounds, a final differential and
treatment plan are produced. Agreement is measured via inter-agent rank
correlation across rounds; persistent disagreement triggers an explicit
uncertainty flag in the output.

Grounding. The Evidence Reviewer uses a frozen RAG pipeline (BM25 +
Sentence-BERT retriever over MedQA-relevant PubMed abstracts,2020–2025). No
online search. No training or fine-tuning of the underlying LLM.

LLM Backend. GPT-4o for all agents (temperature0.3 for consistency;
temperature0.7 for the Skeptic to encourage divergent thinking).

Dataset / BenchmarkMEDQA (USMLE Step2 &3 subset) —1,273 multiple-choice
questions with clinical vignettes. We use the open-ended answer variant (no
options provided to the system; system generates a free-text diagnosis and we
match against gold-standard answers via semantic equivalence judged by an
independent LLM). This avoids the gaming of multiple-choice options.

MIMIC-IV (subsample) —200 de-identified emergency department cases with
confirmed discharge diagnoses. Used for open-ended differential diagnosis
generation. Cases are selected to include at least one co-morbidity and one
diagnostic uncertainty signal (e.g., equivocal lab values, overlapping symptom
profiles).

Primary metric per case: Top-1 diagnostic accuracy, Top-3 recall (whether the
correct diagnosis appears in the top three of the differential), and
completeness (proportion of the gold-standard workup steps mentioned in the
treatment plan).

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Definition |

|---|---|---| | Diagnostic accuracy | Top-1 Accuracy | Correct diagnosis ranked
first | | Diagnostic accuracy | Top-3 Recall | Correct diagnosis in top three |
| Reasoning quality | Completeness Score | Fraction of gold-standard workup
steps mentioned | | Calibration | Uncertainty Flag Rate | Fraction of cases
where system flags persistent disagreement | | Robustness | Perturbation
Stability | Agreement across3 rephrasings of the same vignette | | Ablation
contribution | Marginal (\Delta) Accuracy | Per-agent removal effect on Top-1
Accuracy |

Uncertainty is reported as95% bootstrap confidence intervals over1,000
resamples. Statistical significance tested via paired bootstrap test ((\alpha
=0.05), Bonferroni correction across6 pairwise comparisons).

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Rationale |

|---|---|---| | Single LLM (CoT) | GPT-4o with chain-of-thought prompt; single
best diagnosis | Measures benefit of multi-agent deliberation over a strong
single model | | Ensemble (Majority Vote) |4 independent GPT-4o CoT runs;
majority vote on top diagnosis | Isolates effect of role specialization from
simple aggregation | | Single LLM + RAG | GPT-4o CoT with same RAG pipeline used
by Evidence Reviewer | Isolates effect of multi-agent deliberation from
retrieval augmentation alone | | Full Multi-Agent (proposed) | All four agents +
deliberation | Target system |

Ablations| Ablation | Change | Target Question |

|---|---|---| | -Skeptic | Remove Skeptic agent; Diagnostician + Evidence
Reviewer + Treatment Planner only | Is the skeptic the highest-contribution
role? | | -Evidence | Remove Evidence Reviewer; Diagnostician + Skeptic +
Treatment Planner, no RAG grounding | How much does evidence retrieval matter
vs. internal knowledge? | | -Deliberation | Agents produce independent outputs;
final output is simple majority vote of Diagnostician and Skeptic (no iterative
rounds) | Does iterative refinement add value beyond one-shot ensemble? | |
-Treatment | Remove Treatment Planner; Diagnostician + Evidence Reviewer +
Skeptic only; no treatment plan output | Does treatment planning distract from
or inform diagnostic accuracy? | | Single Round | Deliberation limited to one
exchange (no revision) | Is multi-round convergence necessary? |

Expected Failure Modes1. Agent homogenization. Despite distinct role prompts,
all four agents may converge to similar reasoning patterns because they share
the same base LLM. If inter-agent disagreement is low across most cases, the
deliberation protocol provides no benefit over a single model, and the skeptic
role is effectively vacuous. Detection: compute average pairwise rank
correlation of differentials across agents. Correlation >0.85 across all case
types would indicate homogenization.

 2 Skeptic over-rejection. The skeptic agent, prompted to be critical, may
   reject valid diagnoses too aggressively, reducing Top-3 recall even when the
   Diagnostician was initially correct. Detection: compare the skeptic's
   false-negative rate on cases where the Diagnostician's top candidate was
   correct.
 3 RAG retrieval brittleness. The frozen RAG pipeline may fail on cases
   requiring reasoning about rare diseases, very recent findings (post-2025), or
   non-textual data (imaging, lab trends over time). This would limit the
   Evidence Reviewer's utility to the most common conditions, systematically
   under-serving the cases where decision support is most needed. Detection:
   stratify Top-1 accuracy by case rarity (frequency in training corpus).
 4 Deliberation divergence. Rather than converging, agents may oscillate or
   drift across rounds, especially on ambiguous cases. The fixed three-round
   limit may cut off convergence prematurely or force convergence to a
   lower-quality consensus. Detection: measure cross-round change in
   differential rankings; flag cases where rank correlation between round2 and
   round3 is <0.7.
 5 Perturbation instability. Small rephrasings of the vignette may produce
   substantially different differentials. This is a known failure of LLM-based
   clinical reasoning and may be amplified rather than mitigated by multi-agent
   interaction if all agents share the same sensitivity pattern. Detection: the
   Perturbation Stability metric directly measures this; if <0.6 across the
   MIMIC subset, the system is not robust enough for deployment.

Limitations1. No image modalities. The system processes only text vignettes.
Real clinical decision support must integrate imaging, pathology, and waveform
data. Extending to multimodal inputs is left to future work.

 2 No online updating. The RAG corpus is static (2020–2025). Rapidly evolving
   areas (emerging pathogens, new drug approvals) are not reflected. A
   production system would require continuous index updates.
 3 Single LLM backend. All agents use GPT-4o. Results may not generalize to
   other base models (e.g., Claude, Gemini, open-weight models). The relative
   contributions of role specialization vs. base model capability cannot be
   disentangled without cross-model replication.
 4 Benchmark scope. MEDQA and MIMIC-IV cover US-based clinical practice.
   Diagnostic reasoning patterns, treatment guidelines, and prevalent conditions
   vary significantly across healthcare systems. Generalizability to non-US,
   low-resource, or primary-care settings is unvalidated.
 5 No safety-critical evaluation. Diagnostic accuracy on benchmarks is a proxy
   measure. Real-world deployment requires prospective clinical validation,
   assessment of workflow integration, and measurement of downstream patient
   outcomes. This proposal addresses only the algorithmic foundation.
 6 Evaluation via LLM judge. Using an LLM to judge semantic equivalence for
   open-ended diagnosis introduces circularity concerns. A secondary human
   evaluation on a100-case subset (with two board-certified physicians) is
   planned but not yet funded or IRB-approved.
 7 Calibration is measured, not controlled. The uncertainty flag rate is
   descriptive; the system cannot dynamically adjust its decision threshold or
   defer to human review based on estimated confidence. A calibrated deferral
   mechanism is a natural extension but is not implemented here.

Research Proposal: Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Clinical Trial Eligibility
Screening## Title
TrialMatch: A Structured Multi-Agent Debate Framework for
Zero-Shot Clinical Trial Eligibility Screening

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Clinical trial enrollment is the bottleneck of medical research.
Eligibility screening — determining whether a patient's unstructured EHR notes
satisfy a trial's inclusion/exclusion criteria — is currently performed manually
by coordinators. This is slow, error-prone, and does not scale to the ~400,000
trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Single-pass LLM prompting achieves ~70–75% F1 on eligibility classification
(TrialGPT,2024), but suffers from two issues: (a) it hallucinates criterion
matches for ambiguous or missing data, and (b) it does not handle contradictory
criteria across multiple trials for the same patient.

Open question: Can a multi-agent debate architecture, where specialized agents
argue for and against each criterion, outperform a single monolithic LLM on this
task?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-agent debate system — where one agent argues for criterion
satisfaction (citing specific evidence), a second argues against, and a judge
agent synthesizes the final decision — will improve F1 by ≥5 points over a
single-pass LLM with equal total inference cost, because forced adversarial
reasoning reduces hallucination on borderline criteria.

Null hypothesis: Multi-agent debate does not significantly outperform
single-pass prompting when both use the same backbone LLM and comparable token
budgets.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Architecture: TrialMatchThe system operates in three stages per
patient-trial pair:

1 Evidence Extraction: An extractor agent reads the patient note + trial
criteria and produces a structured table mapping each criterion to the spans
of text that are relevant (or marks the criterion as "no evidence in note").
2 Adversarial Debate (per criterion):

• Pro Agent — given the criterion and extracted evidence, argues why the
patient meets this criterion.
• Con Agent — given the same evidence, argues why the patient does not meet it.
• Each agent is temperature-decayed (T=0.7 →0.3) over3 rounds; they see each
other's arguments.

3 Aggregation & Prediction:

• Judge Agent — reads the debate transcripts for all criteria and produces:
• A binary eligibility decision (eligible / ineligible)
• A confidence score - Citations to specific spans in the original
noteBackbone: Llama-3.1-70B (or a similarly capable open model), quantized to
allow multi-agent rollouts on a single A100.

Prompt structure: Each agent is prompted with a role persona (e.g., "You are a
conservative clinical reviewer who requires explicit documentation before
approving") to ensure separation of perspectives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary: TrialGPT benchmark (Jin et al.,2024) —183 patient
summaries (from TREC Clinical Trials) and3,500+ trial-criterion pairs with
expert-annotated eligibility labels. This is the standard zero-shot benchmark.

Secondary (robustness): N2C22018 (Adverse Drug Events cohort) — convert the ADE
extraction task into criterion-style screening for a drug trial; measure
cross-dataset transfer.

Validation method:5-fold patient-level cross-validation on TrialGPT. No patient
appears in both train and test folds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | Macro F1 (primary) | Balanced measure for binary eligibility;
primary metric in TrialGPT | | Criterion-level accuracy | Per-criterion match vs
annotator labels (from TrialGPT's fine-grained labels) | | Precision vs Recall
tradeoff | Important for clinical use — false positives (enrolling an ineligible
patient) are costlier than false negatives | | Mean confidence calibration (ECE)
| Judge confidence should correlate with correctness | | Debate round
convergence | Does additional debate rounds (>3) change the final decision?
(sensitivity analysis) | | Token cost | Total tokens consumed per patient-trial
pair (runtime cost matters for deployment) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Single-pass LLM (same backbone, same evidence extraction step, no
debate) — direct ablation2. TrialGPT (Jin et al.,2024) — strongest published
zero-shot baseline3. Chain-of-Thought prompting on the same backbone — controls
for reasoning depth4. Self-consistency (Wang et al.,2023) with5 samples —
controls for ensemble effect vs. structured debate5. Random majority (predict
the majority class per trial) — sanity floorAll baselines share the same
evidence extraction stage and backbone model for fair comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No debate → single-pass LLM (this is baseline1 above)

2 Single-agent self-consistency (same number of forward passes as debate, but
no adversarial structure) — isolates the benefit of adversarial reasoning vs.
mere sampling3. Judge only, no pro/con (judge sees evidence directly) —
isolates the value of debate4. Debate without role personas (both agents
prompted as neutral reviewers) — tests whether forced role separation
matters5. Temperature ablation (fixed high vs. fixed low vs. decay schedule)
3 Backbone size (8B vs.70B) — does debate help smaller models more?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Both pro and con hallucinate — debate converges on wrong facts
because both agents invent evidence | Evidence extraction stage is constrained
to quote spans only; agents cannot fabricate new facts | | Judge favors
pro/consistently — positional bias or role bias in the judge | Swap agent order
randomly; test two judge prompts (neutral; "prefer inclusion"; "prefer
exclusion") | | Token cost is prohibitive — multi-agent debate uses3–5× more
tokens than single-pass | Measure cost explicitly; report F1 per token. If gain
is <5 points, single-pass is economically preferable | | No improvement on easy
criteria — debate only helps borderline cases, which are rare (~15% of criteria)
| Report separately on "easy" (both agents initially agree) vs "hard" criteria;
overall F1 gain may be diluted | | Agent personas polarize unrecoverably — pro
and con become entrenched and never converge | Hard-limit at3 rounds; judge
always has the final say regardless of agreement | | Dataset leakage — LLM was
pre-trained on ClinicalTrials.gov or MIMIC notes | Use a held-out set of recent
trials (past12 months, beyond training cutoff); check for exact matches | |
Cross-dataset transfer fails — N2C2 performance is at or below random | Accept
as a limitation; report honestly. Consider fine-tuning the evidence extraction
stage on N2C2 |

Title: Iterative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Literature

ProblemProducing a comprehensive, well-organized literature review is one of the
most labor-intensive tasks in academic research. A reviewer must (a) identify
the relevant corpus, (b) extract salient findings, (c) organize them into a
coherent narrative, and (d) critically assess methodological strengths and gaps.
Recent LLM-based approaches have tackled isolated sub-tasks (citation
recommendation, abstract summarization, survey drafting), but no existing system
produces end-to-end literature reviews that match human quality across domains.

The core challenge is compositional: a review is not a concatenation of
summaries. It requires iterative refinement — re-reading papers in light of what
other papers claim, detecting contradictions and redundant findings, and
structuring sections around conceptual themes rather than source order. Existing
systems either flatten this into a single-pass retrieval-then-generate pipeline
or rely on human-in-the-loop curation for each refinement step.

We target the problem of fully automated literature review generation given a
research question as input, with an emphasis on structured, citation-grounded,
topically organized output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisH1: An iterative retrieval-augmented generation architecture that
alternates between paper discovery, claim extraction, and structural revision
will produce literature reviews with higher topical coherence and citation
coverage than single-pass or cascading baselines.

H2 (ablation-specific): Disabling idea-validation evolution (the mechanism that
records and reuses past rejection criteria, failed coverage patterns, and
structural dead ends) will cause the system to repeat coverage gaps and
structural errors across iterations, significantly degrading coherence and
completeness relative to the full system. In other words, without a persistent
memory of what does not work, iterative refinement alone will plateau early.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodThe full system, LitForge, operates in three iterative stages:

 1 Seed Retrieval & Initial Outline. Given a research question (e.g., "What
   methods exist for unsupervised constituency parsing?"), the system issues
   multi-query expansions to a semantic scholar API, retrieves the top-(k)
   papers, and constructs an initial section outline via a structured prompt to
   the LLM backbone.
 2 Iterative Gap-Filling (3 rounds). In each round the system:

 • Identifies the section with the weakest citation density or shallowest
   coverage (using a learned coverage scorer).
 • Issues targeted retrieval queries specific to that section's theme.
 • Extracts claim-level assertions from newly retrieved papers.
 • Revises the section — merging, splitting, or reordering claims, and inserting
   cross-references.

 3 Evidence Consolidation & Formatting. All citations are checked for extractive
   faithfulness; redundant citations are merged; a limitations paragraph is
   generated per section; and the review is rendered in a standard two-column
   paper format.

–IVE Ablation Modification. The –IVE variant removes the validation memory
module. In the full system, failed structural choices (e.g., "organizing by
architecture type produced high overlap in Section3"; "the coverage scorer
under-detected contradictions in round1") are written to a persistent memory
store and retrieved in subsequent sessions or runs. In –IVE, this store is never
initialized. The system runs the same iterative loop but enters each round with
no prior knowledge of which strategies failed in earlier rounds or runs. It can
still observe the current state of the draft (the explicit text and citation
counts) and make decisions based on that, but it cannot recall that, e.g., a
particular query formulation yielded low-precision results in the previous round
of the same run, or that a particular structural pattern led to section
fragmentation in a prior run on a different topic.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / BenchmarkLitReview-Bench (constructed for this work). We collect20
research questions spanning NLP (10), computer vision (5), and computational
biology (5). For each question, we curate a gold-standard literature review
of3–5 pages written by a domain expert with access to the same corpus. Gold
reviews are annotated with:

 • Section boundary markers- Citation spans mapped to paper IDs- Central claim
   sentences per sectionThe corpus available to the system is the full Semantic
   Scholar Academic Graph snapshot (2024-12), restricted to papers published
   before the gold review's creation date to avoid information leakage.

Evaluation is conducted on the20 questions, with4 reserved as a held-out test
set (1 per domain +1 cross-domain).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | Coverage@k | Fraction of gold citations recalled in the system
output (with (k)-nearest citation distance slack). | | Claim F1 | Token-level
overlap of gold-annotated central-claim sentences with system-generated claim
sentences, measured per section under a many-to-one alignment. | | Section
Coherence | Average pairwise cosine similarity between consecutive sentences
within sections, minus between-section similarity (to reward topical
separation). Reports with confidence intervals over3 seeds. | | Redundancy Rate
| Fraction of citation spans in the output that refer to the same paper and make
semantically identical claims (detected via NLI entailment). | | Faithfulness |
Percentage of system claims that are entailed by the cited source abstracts
(using an off-the-shelf NLI model; DeBERTa-large). | | Human Rating | Three
expert annotators rate each review on a1–5 Likert scale for organization,
completeness, and critical insight. Inter-annotator agreement measured via
Krippendorff's (\alpha). |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Single-Pass RAG. Retrieve top-30 papers, concatenate abstracts,
prompt LLM to write a full review. No iteration.

 2 Cascading Summarizer. Retrieve papers, summarize each independently, then
   summarize the summaries into sections. Two-stage, no iteration.
 3 LitForge (full system). The full iterative system with validation memory
   enabled.
 4 LitForge –IVE. The proposed ablation variant.

All baselines use the same LLM backbone (GPT-4o) and retrieval corpus to isolate
architectural differences.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations (within –IVE Scope)

Beyond the primary –IVE condition, we run three additional ablations on the16
development questions:

 • –IVE + No Iteration (single-gap-fill). A single round of gap-filling (the
   initialization, one refinement, then consolidation). This measures how much
   the iterative loop contributes without memory.
 • –IVE + Uniform Query. Replaces the learned coverage-scorer with a round-robin
   that targets each section once. Tests whether the coverage-scorer's decisions
   (which depend on observing the current draft) drive improvement.
 • –IVE + Shuffle Sections. Randomly permutes sections before each gap-filling
   round. Tests whether the system is sensitive to order artifacts that a
   validation memory would normally correct across runs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Repeated coverage gaps across rounds. Without
validation memory, the system may identify the same section as "weak" in
consecutive rounds, retrieve similar additional papers, and add redundant
citations instead of diversifying coverage. We expect Coverage@k to plateau
after round2, whereas the full system would shift attention to other sections.

 2 Structural cycling. The system may oscillate between two organizational
   schemes (e.g., chronological vs. thematic organization) across rounds, unable
   to commit to one, because it cannot recall that a previous iteration of the
   same structure led to high redundancy. This manifests as low Section
   Coherence scores and high Redundancy Rate.
 3 Failure to propagate cross-section insights. A key function of validation
   memory in the full system is recording that a finding from Section2
   contradicts a claim being drafted in Section3. Without this memory,
   cross-section contradictions may persist or be resolved inconsistently.
   Faithfulness may drop as a result, because the same source paper's claim is
   reported differently in two sections without cross-reference.
 4 Poor generalization to out-of-domain questions. Validation memory in the full
   system accumulates reusable rejection criteria (e.g., "querying by method
   name alone produces low-precision results for interdisciplinary topics").
   Without it, the –IVE system must rediscover these heuristics from scratch for
   each question, leading to a wider variance in quality scores on the held-out
   test set.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations- LLM backbone dependence. All results are measured using a single
backbone (GPT-4o). The relative benefit of validation memory may differ for
weaker or stronger backbones. We do not test this cross-model comparison in the
current study.

 • Fixed iteration budget. The3-round design is chosen for computational
   tractability. With unlimited rounds, the –IVE variant might eventually match
   full-system performance by effectively brute-forcing coverage. Real-world
   applicability requires bounded iteration, so this limitation is also a design
   constraint.
 • Citation faithfulness upper-bound. Because the system is constrained to the
   S2AG corpus, any claim absent from the corpus (e.g., recently published work,
   preprint updates) is unfaithful by construction. Gold reviews were given
   access to the same corpus restriction, but human reviewers can draw on
   broader knowledge. Faithfulness scores should be interpreted relative to the
   available evidence, not absolute truth.
 • No document-level reading. The system operates on abstracts and extracted
   salient spans, not full-text PDFs. This is a pragmatic choice to stay within
   API token limits, but it means nuanced experimental details (hyperparameters,
   dataset splits, statistical significance) are not surfaced in the review.
   This limitation affects all baselines equally and is noted as a threat to
   critical insight ratings.
 • –IVE ablation does not isolate memory exclusively. Removing validation memory
   also removes the implicit bias it introduces. A system with validation memory
   may steer towards historically "safe" structures at the cost of novelty. The
   –IVE condition may therefore overestimate quality on dimensions where
   exploration is beneficial. We note this trade-off but do not control for it
   in the current design — it is discussed as a direction for future work and a
   potential confound in interpreting the ablation gap.

Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.
