Multi-Source Phonetic Bootstrapping via Cross-Lingual Articulatory Priors for
Low-Resource Speech Recognition### TitleArticulatory-Constrained Multi-View
Representation Learning for Low-Resource Automatic Speech Recognition

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemState-of-the-art automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems rely on
hundreds to thousands of hours of transcribed speech. For the vast majority of
the world's ~7,000 languages — many of which have fewer than10 hours of
transcribed data — these approaches fail. Existing low-resource methods fall
into three camps, each with a persistent limitation:

 1 Cross-lingual transfer (fine-tuning a multilingual pre-trained encoder like
   wav2vec2.0 or HuBERT onto a target language) — works only when the target
   language is well-represented in pre-training data; otherwise, phone-set
   mismatch and acoustic-phonetic divergence cause catastrophic forgetting
   during fine-tuning.
 2 Phonetic decoupling (using articulatory features like place/manner of
   articulation as intermediate representations) — improves interpretability but
   requires expert-annotated articulatory feature tables per language, which do
   not exist for most low-resource languages.
 3 Self-supervised speech representations — capture rich acoustic structure but
   lack explicit phone-level grounding, causing poor frame-to-phone alignment in
   zero-shot settings.

We address a specific subproblem: Can we build a phone-level ASR system for a
target language with <5 hours of transcribed speech, using only a small
articulatory feature matrix from a phonetically-related source language, without
requiring expert annotation in the target language?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisArticulatory priors — place, manner, and voicing feature vectors —
extracted from a phonologically related high-resource source language provide a
sufficiently universal phonetic constraint space that, when combined with a
multi-view contrastive objective between acoustic and articulatory embeddings,
enables phone-level transcription in an unseen low-resource target language
without any target-language articulatory annotations.

low-resource settings, the "closest" phonetically annotated source may itself be
low-resource, limiting the method's bootstrap utility.

 3 No explicit tone modeling. While PanPhon includes tone features, our method
   does not treat tone separately from segmental features. For tonal languages,
   tone errors are counted in PER but cannot be independently diagnosed or
   addressed. A dedicated tonal acoustic encoder (e.g., pitch contour CNN) would
   be a natural extension but is not part of this proposal.
 4 Static articulatory anchors. The PanPhon feature vectors are binary and
   context-independent. Coarticulation, allophonic variation, and cross-speaker
   variation are collapsed into the binary representation. A variational
   articulatory space (distributions over features rather than binary vectors)
   could capture uncertainty but would add complexity to the contrastive
   objective.

   iteration does not incorporate feedback from prior experimental failures. The

Research Proposal: Confidence-Gated Iterative Pseudo-Labeling with
Phoneme-Constrained Augmentation for Low-Resource ASRTitle: Semi-Supervised
Self-Training with Audited Pseudo-Labels and Phoneme-Preserving Augmentation for
Under-10-Hour Speech Recognition---

Problem
State-of-the-art ASR systems (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec2.0) degrade
catastrophically when fine-tuned on fewer than10 hours of transcribed speech.
Two failure modes dominate: (1) overfitting to the small labeled set, and (2)
confirmation bias in self-training, where the model reinforces its own errors
through noisy pseudo-labels on unlabeled data. No existing method jointly
addresses label quality and data diversity in the under-10-hour regime on a
single pipeline.

Hypothesis
A self-training loop that audits pseudo-labels through a separate
confidence calibrator (rather than the ASR model's own softmax) and couples them
with phoneme-preserving augmentations (time-stretch, pitch-shift, and speed
perturbation clipped to per-phoneme duration bounds) will outperform standard
pseudo-labeling and unsupervised pre-training when labeled data ≤10 hours. The
key claim: auditing prevents confirmation bias, and phoneme-constrained
augmentation prevents the augmentations from destroying linguistic content that
the small labeled set cannot recover.

Method1. Seed model — Fine-tune a small SSL encoder (wav2vec2.0 Base, ~95M
params) on the labeled set (≤10 h). Use a single linear projection head.

2 Pseudo-labeling loop (3 rounds):

• Decode the unlabeled pool with the current model (CTC greedy decoding).
• Audit each pseudo-label: pass the logits to a separate lightweight confidence
estimator (a2-layer MLP over mean-pooled encoder features, trained on the
seed set's held-out fold) and retain only utterances where estimated
confidence ≥0.9 threshold.
• Combine audited pseudo-labeled utterances with the original labeled set.

3 Phoneme-constrained augmentation — Before each training epoch, apply:

• Time stretching (0.85x–1.15x) with per-phoneme duration floor.
• Pitch shift (±2 semitones).
• Speed perturbation (0.9x–1.1x).
• Constraint: a forced-alignment phoneme recognizer (pretrained multilingual)
verifies that the augmented audio's phoneme sequence matches the original;
discard any augmentation where >20% of phonemes shift.

4 Re-train the SSL encoder + projection head from the seed checkpoint on the
combined (labeled + audited pseudo-labeled + augmented) data. Repeat for3
rounds.

Dataset / Benchmark- Primary: Common Voice (Tamil, Sinhala, Catalan, Kyrgyz —4
languages with2–8 h of validated train data each). Evaluate on each language's
official dev/test splits.

• Secondary (sanity check): FLEURS10-hour subset for2 additional languages
(Swahili, Bengali).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Purpose |

|---|---| | Character Error Rate (CER) | Primary metric; report mean ± std over3
seeds. | | Word Error Rate (WER) | Secondary, for languages with space-delimited
orthography. | | Pseudo-label acceptance rate | Diagnostic: % unlabeled
utterances retained per round. | | Oracle accuracy of accepted pseudo-labels |
Diagnostic: if a held-out reference exists for the unlabeled pool, measure what
fraction of accepted labels are correct. |

Report effect sizes with95% bootstrap confidence intervals across seeds.

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|---|---| | Seed-only (fine-tune on labeled data only, no self-training) | Lower
bound — isolates the value of unlabeled data. | | Standard pseudo-labeling (no
auditing, no augmentation) | Ablates the audit mechanism. | | No-augmentation
self-training (audit + pseudo-label, no phoneme constraint) | Ablates the
augmentation contribution. | | SpecAugment self-training (SpecAugment instead of
phoneme-constrained augmentation) | Compares against a widely-used augmentation
baseline. | | wav2vec2.0 Base fine-tuned on full Common Voice (where available,
e.g., Catalan ~80 h) | Upper bound — what performance looks like with abundant
data. | | Whisper Small zero-shot | Compares against a strong multitask model
that has never seen the target language during adaptation. |

Ablations1. Audit threshold sweep — Vary the confidence threshold
(0.7,0.8,0.9,0.95) on one language to measure the precision-recall trade-off in
pseudo-label acceptance.

2 Augmentation constraint strength — Compare the phoneme-preserving constraint
against an unconstrained version (same augmentations, no phoneme-validity
check).
3 Number of self-training rounds — Compare1,2,3, and5 rounds on one language to
measure when performance plateaus or degrades.
4 Size of labeled seed — Sub-sample to1 h,2 h,5 h on a language with8 h
available, and measure whether the method's advantage grows as labeled data
shrinks.

Expected Failure Modes1. Phoneme-constraint too aggressive — The multilingual
forced-aligner may have poor accuracy on a target language it was not trained
on, causing most augmentations to be discarded. Mitigation: Relax the threshold
to40% phoneme shift tolerance; also measure the discard rate and report it.

2 Confidence estimator is poorly calibrated — On languages far from the seed
set, the auditor may either accept noisy labels (false positive) or reject
correct ones (false negative). Mitigation: Use temperature scaling (Platt
scaling) on the confidence estimator; report calibration curves (ECE) per
round.
3 Diminishing returns by round3 — The model may saturate because the unlabeled
pool's acoustic diversity is exhausted. Mitigation: If WER improvement from
round2→3 is <0.5% relative, stop early and report the saturating round as a
finding.
4 CTC beam search decoding with a weak language model — Without a
target-language n-gram or neural LM, decoding may be brittle. Mitigation: Do
not use an external LM for the main experiment (to keep the ablation clean),
but add a shallow fusion with a3-gram LM as a secondary ablation to measure
the orthogonal gain.
5 Hardware constraints — Self-training with augmentation on the full unlabeled
pool (typically50–200 h per language) may be slow. Mitigation: Downsample the
unlabeled pool to20 h per language via random sampling, stratified by speaker
if speaker metadata is available.

Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Models via Multi-Scale Representation
Recycling## ProblemLarge language models (100B+ parameters) continue to improve
   predictably with scale under the Chinchin scaling laws, but models under1B
   parameters exhibit a pronounced performance ceiling: after approximately7B
  tokens of training, validation loss plateaus while downstream task accuracy
 saturates well below the levels predicted by extrapolating scaling curves from
   larger models [1,2]. This "small-model ceiling" manifests as a systematic
  underutilisation of capacity — small models fail to compress their training
 distribution beyond a certain point regardless of additional compute, data, or
training steps. The root cause is not capacity (a350M-parameter transformer has
 sufficient representational degrees of freedom), but rather that optimisation
  dynamics at small scale produce representations that are redundant, collapse
 along dominant principal components, and fail to capture long-tail patterns in
                                 the data [3].

Existing approaches — knowledge distillation from larger teachers [4], weight
pruning and quantisation [5], and architectural search for efficient
transformers [6] — treat the ceiling as a compression problem post-training.
They do not address the fundamental issue: the training process itself converges
to a poor local optimum where representations are under-specialised. A method
that directly intervenes on the representation learning trajectory rather than
compressing a converged model is needed.

HypothesisSmall models plateau because the gradient signal during training
becomes increasingly uniform across tokens and layers, collapsing the
representation manifold. We hypothesise that multi-scale representation
recycling — periodically injecting frozen, higher-quality representations from a
concurrently trained auxiliary module as structured regularisation targets —
prevents manifold collapse and forces the main model to maintain diverse,
composable features. Specifically, if an auxiliary model operating at a
different representational scale (wider or deeper in one critical dimension) is
trained jointly but constrains the main model's hidden states through a
cosine-similarity dispersion loss, the main model's effective rank of hidden
representations will remain above a critical threshold throughout training,
delaying the ceiling by at least a factor of three in training tokens.

The mechanism is not knowledge distillation (the auxiliary is not a converged
teacher) but rather structured perturbation of the loss landscape: the auxiliary
provides a moving target that prevents the main model from settling into a
low-rank attractor.

MethodWe propose a dual-model framework with three components.

Main model (M). A standard decoder-only transformer of350M parameters (12
layers, hidden1024,16 heads). Trained from scratch on the full training set.

Scale-shifted auxiliary (A). A structurally different transformer that shares
the vocabulary and embedding layer with M but differs along one architectural
axis: it has the same hidden dimension but twice the depth (24 layers) and half
the heads per layer (8 heads). This design ensures A operates on the same
token-level representation space as M but with different representational priors
— deeper composition, narrower attention. A is trained jointly with M on the
same data stream but receives its own optimiser state and learning rate
schedule. Critically, A is NOT a teacher: its representations are not converged
or fixed, and it is not used at inference time.

Dispersion regularisation. At each training step, for a random subset of50% of
layers in M, we extract the hidden state before the FFN at position h_{M}^{(l)}
and the corresponding hidden state from A at the closest aligned layer
h_{A}^{(l')} (linear mapping: l' = floor(l *24/12)). We compute a
centre-stopping cosine dispersion loss:


 L_disp = E[ (cos(h_M^{(l)}, h_A^{(l')}) - c_l)^2 ]


where c_l is a per-layer target correlation coefficient, linearly annealed
from0.9 at step0 to0.5 at step100k then held constant. The effect is
straightforward: early training encourages A's representations to pull M's
representations into a similar region (high correlation), but as training
progresses, the target correlation drops, forcing M to diverge from A and
explore a broader manifold. The loss coefficient alpha_disp is set to0.1
relative to the primary language modelling loss.

Final objective. Each training step optimises:


 L = L_lm(M) + L_lm(A) + alpha_disp * L_disp```

 Both models receive their own LM loss; the dispersion loss is symmetric and
 differentiable through both models. At inference, A is discarded entirely —
 only M is deployed, with no overhead.

 ## Dataset / Benchmark**Training data.** C4 (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus)
 English subset, filtered to sequences of2048 tokens. We use50B tokens total,
 which is approximately7x the typical compute-optimal budget for a350M model
 (≈7B tokens under Chinchilla scaling), ensuring we operate deep into the
 ceiling regime.

 **Evaluation benchmarks.** We measure ceiling effects across four axes:
 - **Language modelling**: validation perplexity on held-out C4 slices
 at1B,5B,10B,25B, and50B training tokens- **Reasoning**: ARC-Challenge,
 ARC-Easy (accuracy)
 - **Factual knowledge**: MMLU (5-shot accuracy)
 - **Token-level understanding**: SuperGLUE (BoolQ, CB, COPA, RTE, WiC, WSC)

 All evaluations are performed every5,000 training steps (≈1B tokens) to
 produce training curves, not just final numbers.

 ## Evaluation Metrics| Metric | What It Measures | Target |
 |--------|-----------------|--------|
 | Validation perplexity gap | How far M is from the ideal
 Chinchilla-extrapolated PPL for its size | <0.5 nats gap at50B tokens |
 | Effective rank of hidden states | Manifold collapse (SVD entropy of hidden
 states across batches) | >80% of maximum rank throughout training |
 | Downstream accuracy ceiling slope | Accuracy change in the final25B tokens |
 Positive slope (not flat) |
 | Cross-layer representational similarity (CKA) | Whether layers are
 collapsing into each other | CKA decreasing, not increasing, after15B tokens |
 | Inference overhead | FLOPs and memory vs vanilla350M (should be zero after
 training) | Identical |

 |----------|-------------|-----|

Research Proposal: Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Small Language Models via
Targeted Capacity Allocation## Title
Beyond Scaling Alone: Targeted Capacity
Allocation for Breaking the Performance Ceiling of Sub-1B Language Models

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Small language models (<1B parameters) exhibit a well-documented but
poorly understood phenomenon: diminishing returns past a critical data scale,
where additional tokens yield negligible or even negative performance gains on
held-out benchmarks. This "performance ceiling" is typically attributed to
insufficient model capacity, but recent evidence suggests that capacity is not
uniformly the bottleneck — certain capabilities (e.g., factual recall,
long-range reasoning) saturate earlier than others (e.g., syntactic fluency,
in-context pattern matching). The research problem is: Can we identify the
precise structural causes of saturation in small models and design targeted
interventions that reallocate limited capacity to the binding constraints?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: The performance ceiling in small models is driven
by capacity-competition between world-knowledge memorization and compositional
reasoning pathways, not by a global lack of parameters. When a small model
saturates, additional training data primarily overfits its already-congested
feedforward memory (FFN layers) while the attention-based compositional routing
remains underutilized.

Secondary hypothesis: A structured intervention that decouples these two
functions — compressing factual knowledge into a fixed, non-parametric memory
(retrieval augmentation with a small bottleneck) and freeing FFN parameters for
compositional reasoning — will raise the ceiling by10–20% on reasoning-heavy
benchmarks while matching or exceeding baselines on factual recall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal has three stages:

Stage1: Ceiling CharacterizationTrain a350M-parameter decoder-only transformer
on increasing data scales (50M,100M,250M,500M,1B,2B,5B,10B tokens). At each
checkpoint, measure per-capability saturation curves across five categories:
factual recall, syntactic well-formedness, short-range reasoning (2 hops),
long-range reasoning (5+ hops), and in-context learning. Use influence functions
and representation similarity (CKA between hidden states at different data
scales) to identify which layers/modules saturate first and correlate with which
capability.

Stage2: Bottleneck DiagnosisInsert capacity probes — lightweight linear
classifiers at each layer that predict whether a given capability fires — to
identify the specific (layer, module) pairs where representation collision
occurs. The hypothesis is that mid-to-late FFN layers become the bottleneck for
factual recall while lower attention layers saturate for compositional
reasoning.

Stage3: Targeted Capacity AllocationIf the diagnosis confirms the hypothesis,
intervene by:

• Retrieval-Augmented Distillation (RAD): Compress the factual knowledge stored
in FFN layers into a small external memory (a frozen key-value store with ~4K
slots). Shrink the model's FFN hidden dimension by25–40% and retrain from
scratch, relying on retrieval for factual queries and freeing FFN capacity
for reasoning.
• Optional control arm: Compare against a naive "bigger FFN" baseline (same
total parameters, no retrieval) to confirm that how capacity is allocated
matters more than how much.

If the diagnosis contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., attention is the bottleneck),
pivot to attention head pruning + reallocation — removing redundant heads to
increase per-head dimensionality.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark- Training: A deduplicated, controlled-quality mix of C4
(natural language), MathPile (math/reasoning), and a synthetic factual QA
dataset (Wiki-QA, ~2M question-answer pairs with provenance). All tokenized with
the same tokenizer to avoid confounds.

• Evaluation (4 benchmarks):
• Factual recall: NaturalQuestions, TriviaQA (exact match)
• Short reasoning: BigBench-Hard subset (boolean expressions, causal judgment)
• Long reasoning: GSM8K (grade-school math, multi-step), HotpotQA (multi-hop
retrieval)
• In-context learning: MMLU (5-shot)
• Saturation diagnosis: Custom probe tasks —500 hand-written examples per
capability with controlled difficulty levels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|--------|-----------| | Accuracy (per benchmark) | Primary capability-level
metric | | Saturation threshold (η) | The data scale (in tokens) at which
performance plateaus within1% of final value | | Representation Collapse Score
(RCS) | Average pairwise CKA similarity >0.95 between adjacent data-scale
checkpoints in bottleneck layers — a proxy for when representations stop
differentiating | | Parameter-Utilization Efficiency (PUE) | Per-point
improvement per million train tokens normalized by model size; captures
diminishing returns | | Retrieval Hit Rate (RAD variant only) | Fraction of
queries where the external memory returns the correct factual document |

Primary success signal: RAD variant achieves >10% relative improvement on GSM8K
and HotpotQA over the350M baseline at the same total parameter budget, without
regressing more than2% on NaturalQuestions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Standard350M decoder (no intervention) — the ceiling-establishing
baseline2. 350M with increased FFN dimension (+25% FFN, -25% attention heads,
same total params) — tests whether naive capacity reallocation achieves similar
gains3. 350M with vanilla RAG (retrieval + standard model, no capacity
reduction) — tests whether retrieval helps regardless of capacity rebalancing4.
Distilled350M from a7B teacher (knowledge distillation alone) — tests whether
the ceiling is a training limitation vs. architectural5. 550M standard decoder
(more parameters entirely) — the "just scale up" ceiling comparison---

Ablations1. RAD without FFN shrinkage — does retrieval help when FFN capacity is
not freed?

2 RAD with different memory sizes (2K,4K,8K slots) — sensitivity to memory
bottleneck3. RAD applied at different layers (early vs. mid vs. late FFN) —
where is compressed storage most effective?
3 Retrieval-free control — train the shrunken-FFN model without retrieval;
isolates whether the gain comes from the architecture change or the
retrieval5. Ceiling characterization on a different architecture (e.g., a350M
MoE with same total params) — is the ceiling mechanism architecture-specific?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation / Response |

|---|---| | No clear bottleneck emerges (all modules saturate simultaneously) |
The pluralistic-ceiling hypothesis fails. Fallback: test if training recipe (LR
schedule, weight decay) is the real ceiling — ablate optimizer settings. | | RAD
improves reasoning but kills factual recall >2% | Memory size was too small.
Re-run with16K slots or use a learned gating mechanism to route queries. | |
Naive FFN-increase baseline matches or beats RAD | Capacity allocation is not
the bottleneck; the ceiling is truly total-parameter-limited. Concede and report
the negative result as a contribution (important for the community). | | No
ceiling observed (performance continues scaling linearly at10B tokens) | The350M
model was too large for the data scales tested. Scale up to50B tokens or test
a100M model to find the ceiling. | | RAD improves only on seen-document queries
(memorization, not generalization) | Evaluate on held-out timestamps and topics.
If gains vanish, the retrieval store is overfitting to the training set.
Introduce a stricter train/test split on documents. | | CKA-based diagnosis is
inconclusive | Supplement with probing classifiers and leave-one-out accuracy
drops to cross-validate which layers matter for each capability. |

  Proposal: Compositional Multi-Hop Reasoning via Recursive Decomposition for
 Tool-Augmented AI Agents## ProblemLarge language models struggle with complex
  reasoning tasks that require composing multiple facts, tool invocations, and
 intermediate inferences in a coherent chain. While chain-of-thought prompting
 and related techniques improve step-level accuracy, they remain brittle under
three conditions: (a) when the reasoning path requires backtracking from a dead
end, (b) when tool outputs are heterogeneous (e.g., structured tables, free-text
  passages, code execution results), and (c) when the number of compositional
   steps exceeds approximately five. Existing approaches treat reasoning as a
  single forward pass over latent steps, leaving agents unable to adapt their
         decomposition strategy when a sub-problem proves intractable.

HypothesisA recursive decomposition framework — where an agent iteratively
splits a query into sub-queries, resolves each sub-query via tool calls or
further decomposition, and recombines results — outperforms monolithic
chain-of-thought and single-pass ReAct baselines on multi-hop reasoning
benchmarks. We further hypothesize that the decomposition strategy itself can be
dynamically selected per sub-problem based on the type of information required
(factual retrieval, arithmetic, temporal reasoning, constraint satisfaction),
rather than applying a fixed decomposition template.

MethodWe propose Recursive Decomposition with Dynamic Strategy Selection
(RD-DSS). The architecture has three components:

1. Decomposition Module. Given a query (q), the module generates a decomposition
tree (T) where each node is either a leaf (answerable directly via a single tool
call or parametric knowledge) or an internal node (a sub-query that is further
decomposed). Decomposition is guided by a lightweight classifier that predicts
the reasoning type of the current sub-query from six categories: factual lookup,
arithmetic, temporal ordering, constraint satisfaction, set intersection, and
comparative judgment. Each type maps to a preferred decomposition template and a
default tool candidate.

2. Execution Engine. Each leaf is dispatched to one of three tool types: a web
search API (text passages), a knowledge graph query interface (structured
facts), or a Python interpreter (computation). Tool outputs are converted into a
uniform passage format. The engine maintains a working memory of all resolved
leaf values, keyed by their path in the decomposition tree.

3. Recomposition Module. After all children of a node are resolved, the
recomposition module synthesizes their outputs into a single answer for that
node. If any child fails to resolve (tool error, empty result, contradictory
evidence), the module may request re-decomposition of the child with modified
parameters.

Ablated mechanism (–IVE). In the full system, each failed resolution updates a
validation-evidence store: the failure type, the sub-query embedding, the tool
invoked, and the error pattern. This store is then used during candidate
decomposition generation at future nodes — the system can pre-emptively reject
decomposition strategies that are structurally similar to prior failures. In
this –IVE variant, no such store is maintained. Each sub-problem is treated as
independent. The decomposition module receives no signal about which strategies
have previously led to dead ends, and the recomposition module repeats the same
error patterns across different branches of the same tree without recognizing
the similarity.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on three multi-hop QA benchmarks spanning
different reasoning demands:

 • HotpotQA (distractor setting) — factual multi-hop with supporting passage
   retrieval; tests decomposition over heterogeneous evidence.
 • 2WikiMultihopQA — multi-hop over Wikipedia with mixed entity types; tests
   generalization to cross-domain composition.
 • MuSiQue (3-hop and4-hop splits) — multi-hop with controlled hop count and
   distractor difficulty; tests scaling behavior as compositional depth
   increases.

We use the full validation splits and report on the hidden test sets via
official evaluation servers.

Evaluation Metrics- F1 and Exact Match (EM) — primary metrics per benchmark
standard.

 • Decomposition efficiency — average number of nodes in the decomposition tree
   per correctly answered query (lower = more efficient).
 • Backtrack rate — fraction of queries where at least one sub-problem required
   re-decomposition after an initial failure.
 • Hop coverage — percentage of queries where the effective reasoning path
   length matches or exceeds the gold hop count.
 • Tool call overhead — total number of tool invocations per query (measuring
   cost).

All metrics are reported with95% confidence intervals over three seeds.

Baselines1. Standard CoT — zero-shot chain-of-thought with the same backbone
LLM, no tool access.

 2 ReAct — interleaved reasoning traces and tool invocations, single pass.
 3 ReAct + self-consistency — ReAct with5-sampling majority vote.
 4 Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) — breadth-first search over reasoning steps with a
   value function; no dynamic tool dispatch.
 5 Full RD-DSS (+IVE) — the complete system with validation-evolution memory
   enabled. This is the primary comparison for the ablation.

All methods use the same backbone LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B-Instruct) and the same
tool suite for fair comparison.

AblationsBeyond the primary –IVE condition, we conduct:

 • Strategy freezing — replace the dynamic type classifier with a single
   decomposition template (always binary split) to isolate the contribution of
   adaptive strategy selection.
 • No tool diversity — restrict all leaves to web search only (no KG or code
   execution) to measure the value of heterogeneous tool access.
 • Single-pass recomposition — force the recomposition module to commit to an
   answer at each internal node without allowing re-decomposition, isolating the
   contribution of the backtrack mechanism.

Expected Failure Modes (–IVE Specific)

Without validation-evolution memory, we expect the following characteristic
failures:

 • Repeated failure patterns across branches. The system will attempt
   structurally identical decomposition strategies for similar sub-problems in
   different parts of the same tree, fail in the same way each time, and never
   recognize the pattern. This inflates the backtrack rate and tool call
   overhead, especially on MuSiQue4-hop where overlapping sub-problems are
   common.
 • Myopic decomposition on hard nodes. When a particular sub-query type (e.g.,
   temporal ordering) consistently fails under binary decomposition, the –IVE
   variant will continue proposing binary splits on each encounter rather than
   switching to a different strategy. The full system would down-weight binary
   temporal decomposition after two consecutive failures. We expect this to
   surface as a sharp drop in accuracy on temporal sub-queries as hop count
   increases.
 • No cross-query transfer. After ten queries involving set intersection over
   retrieved passages, the full system learns that exhaustive passage listing is
   ineffective for large result sets and switches to a summary-then-intersect
   strategy. The –IVE variant learns nothing across queries, so set-intersection
   accuracy remains flat regardless of exposure.
 • Checklist-style error cascades. Without recording which sub-problem types
   have been fully resolved, the recomposition module may attempt to combine
   partial or contradictory results and proceed as if they are complete. The
   full system flags these as known failure signatures (e.g., "comparing two
   sets where one is empty due to retrieval failure") and triggers
   re-decomposition at the unresolved child. The –IVE variant proceeds with the
   flawed partial results, leading to confident but incorrect final answers that
   are difficult to detect without manual inspection.

Limitations- Decomposition overhead. Recursive decomposition adds latency
proportional to tree depth. Even without validation memory, a single query may
require6–15 LLM calls. This may limit deployment on latency-sensitive
applications regardless of the –IVE ablation.

 • Tool reliability ceiling. If tool outputs are consistently wrong (e.g.,
   outdated KG entries, low-quality search snippets), no architectural
   improvement to the reasoning loop can recover — decomposition only exposes
   tool failures more systematically.
 • Type classifier accuracy. The dynamic strategy selection depends on a trained
   or prompted type classifier (six categories). Misclassifications (e.g.,
   labeling a factual lookup as arithmetic) produce useless decomposition
   templates and cascade errors. The –IVE ablation exacerbates this because the
   full system detects such cascades and corrects the type assignment; the
   ablated system cannot.
 • Single backbone dependency. All results are conditional on the choice of
   backbone LLM. A weaker backbone may fail at the decomposition or
   recomposition steps themselves, which we do not model explicitly — we treat
   the backbone as a fixed reasoning oracle, and its internal failures compound
   with the ablated validation memory.

Research Proposal: Compositional Reasoning Under Distraction — When Do Agentic
Workflows Break Down?

Title**"Plan-Trace-Verify: A Controlled Study of Multi-Step Compositional
Reasoning in LLM Agents Under Distractor Conditions"**

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based agents today are deployed on tasks that require chaining
multiple reasoning steps (e.g., "book a flight, check the weather at the
destination, then find restaurants within budget"). These agents frequently fail
not because individual steps are hard, but because they lose the thread when
intermediate results contradict expectations or when irrelevant context
(distractors) is injected mid-trajectory.

The core problem: existing benchmarks evaluate reasoning in clean, single-turn
settings (e.g., GSM8K, MATH, HotpotQA), but agentic reasoning involves iterative
plan-trace cycles where earlier outputs become inputs to later steps. We lack a
controlled benchmark that isolates the effect of "distractor injection" —
irrelevant or misleading intermediate observations — on compositional reasoning
accuracy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
H₁ (Primary): Injecting task-irrelevant but semantically plausible
observations mid-trajectory degrades LLM agent compositional reasoning accuracy
by ≥25% relative to the no-distractor baseline, even when the underlying
reasoning path is unchanged.

H₂ (Mechanism): The degradation is primarily driven by retrieval interference
(the agent attends to distractor tokens in subsequent reasoning steps) rather
than plan corruption (the agent incorrectly revises its plan). This implies that
improving selective attention (e.g., structured memory) will help more than
improving planning ability.

H₃ (Mitigation): A simple Plan-Trace-Verify loop — where the agent explicitly
writes down its plan before execution, traces each step against the plan after
receiving observations, and verifies consistency before proceeding — recovers
≥80% of the performance gap relative to the no-distractor baseline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Framework: Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV)

We define three agent strategies to compare:

1 Direct-ReAct (baseline): Standard ReAct-style agent — thinks, acts, observes
in a flat loop with no explicit plan tracking.
2 Plan-then-Execute (ablation control): The agent writes a plan (as pseudocode
or bullet points) before execution, then follows it linearly, but does not
re-check consistency after each observation.
3 Plan-Trace-Verify (PTV) (proposed): The agent:

• Plan: Writes an explicit, numbered plan with preconditions and expected
postconditions for each step.
• Trace: After each observation, appends a structured trace entry: [Step N]
expected=<...> observed=<...> match=<yes|no>.
• Verify: Before the next step, runs a consistency check. If match=no, the
agent must decide: (a) proceed (the mismatch is benign), (b) re-plan from
this state, or (c) request clarification.

Distractor Injection ProtocolFor each task, we construct three conditions:

• Clean: Standard trajectory, no distractors.
• Weak distractors: One irrelevant observation per task, semantically related
to the domain but logically unnecessary (e.g., a flight search returns "Did
you know? Economy seats have30-inch pitch." between steps).
• Strong distractors: Two to three irrelevant observations, written to
plausibly contradict an intermediate expectation without actually
invalidating the correct path (e.g., a weather lookup returns "Rain expected"
when the correct reasoning only needs temperature).

Distractors are inserted at fixed positions (after step1, after step2) to ensure
controlled comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We construct CompAgent-Distract, a synthetic multi-step
compositional reasoning dataset with500 tasks spanning three domains:

Domain                    Example Task                 Steps  Distractor Slots
Travel planning           "Book the cheapest flight    4–6    After steps1,3
to a city with population
<1M and good hiking
within50km"
Scientific literature QA  "Find the paper that         3–5    After step2
introduced method X, check
if it was published
before2020, and list its
citations that also use
dataset Y"
Multi-hop tool use        "Get the current time in     4–5    After steps1,2
Tokyo, convert to UTC, find
a meeting slot that works
for a New York participant"

Each task has:

• A gold answer (deterministic)
• A correct reasoning trace (verifiable by exhaustive enumeration)
• One clean + two distractor variants (weak, strong) -3 random seeds for
distractor surface form variationWe also evaluate on AgentQA (a subset of200
multi-turn agent tasks) for out-of-distribution generalization.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary? |

|---|---|---| | Step-level accuracy | Fraction of reasoning steps where the
correct action/observation is selected given the history | Yes | | Final answer
accuracy | Exact-match (or programmatic equivalence) of the final output | Yes |
| Plan deviation rate | Fraction of episodes where the agent's actions diverge
from the optimal plan (measured by trace alignment) | Secondary | | Recovery
rate | Fraction of distractor episodes where the agent corrects itself before
the final step | Secondary | | Token cost overhead | Total input + output tokens
relative to Direct-ReAct | Efficiency |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals (bootstrap, N=1000) across3
seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why |

|---|---|---| | Direct-ReAct | Flat thought-action-observation loop | Standard
minimal agent; lower bound | | Plan-then-Execute | Pre-plan, no mid-trajectory
verification | Isolates the value of verification vs planning | | ReAct +
Self-Consistency | Sample5 trajectories, majority vote final answer | Tests
whether ensembling helps with distractors | | ReAct + Reflexion | Agent
verbalizes feedback after failure | Tests whether post-hoc reflection recovers
from distractors | | GPT-4o / Claude3.5 Sonnet (zero-shot) | No ReAct, just
prompt with tools | Measures intrinsic reasoning without agent scaffolding |

All baselines use the same backend LLM (we control for model; primary
experiments use a frontier model, with a secondary pass on an open-weight model
like Llama-3-70B).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Distractor position: Do distractors hurt more at early vs late
steps?

2 Distractor type: Semantic distractors vs random tokens vs plausible-but-wrong
facts — which causes the most degradation?
3 Plan granularity: Does a detailed plan (per-step pre/post conditions) help
more than a brief plan (bullet list)?
4 Verification frequency: Verify after every step vs every2 steps vs
end-of-trajectory — is there a sweet spot?
5 Memory structure: Instead of PTV's trace-and-verify, use a simple scratchpad
with a "recent observations" summary — does structured memory alone match
PTV?
6 Model scale: Does the gap between PTV and Direct-ReAct shrink or grow at
larger model sizes?

|

model | Evaluate on ≥7B; report token cost; consider ablation (ablation4:

If some agents write poor plans, plan deviation may correlate with plan quality,

position confounds step difficulty | Earlier steps in a task may be
systematically easier/harder | Counterbalance: permute step order for a subset
of tasks and re-run the strongest distractor condition |

progress from large language models, two fundamental failure modes persist:

 1 Schema drift — the model references tables or columns that do not exist in
   the target database, or misaligns natural language entities with the correct
   schema elements. This is especially acute in large schemas (50+ tables) where
   attention dilutes over irrelevant relations.
 2 Spurious execution success — a query returns the correct result set through
   an incorrect SQL path (e.g., a JOIN that happens to produce the right answer
   via coincidence or missing foreign-key enforcement). This gives a false sense
   of correctness when only execution accuracy is measured.

Existing approaches address these separately: schema linking modules reduce
drift, and execution-guided decoding catches some spurious successes. But no
current system tightly couples schema grounding with execution verification in a
single iterative loop, and critically, no system learns from its own
verification failures across queries — which is the very mechanism this ablation
removes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA Text-to-SQL system that decomposes question answering into schema
grounding followed by executable SQL generation, and then iteratively refines
based on execution feedback, can outperform single-shot LLM baselines on
large-schema benchmarks — even without retaining any memory of validation
failures, rejected SQL templates, or reusable rejection criteria across queries.

In the -IVE variant, each query is a fresh inference: no prior failure signal
informs the current grounding or generation step. The hypothesis is that the
decomposition + per-query execution feedback loop alone accounts for the
majority of the gain over a single-shot baseline, and that the marginal value of
cross-query validation memory is small on standard benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodThe method consists of four modules chained per query, with no cross-query
state:

1. Schema-Aware Question Decomposition (SAQD) Given a natural language question
Q and a full database schema S (table names, column names, types, foreign keys),
the model first decomposes Q into a set of sub-questions. Each sub-question is
annotated with a schema scope: a pruned subset of S containing only the tables
and columns relevant to that sub-question. The scope pruner is a small
fine-tuned encoder (e.g., RoBERTa + MLP) that scores each table-column pair for
relevance to the sub-question. The top-K pairs by score form the scope.

2. Independent Sub-Query Generation For each sub-question and its schema scope,
the base LLM generates a candidate SQL fragment independently. No sub-query sees
the output of another sub-query at this stage. This prevents cross-sub-query
contamination and isolates errors.

3. Composition & Merging A merging decoder takes all SQL fragments and the
original question Q and composes them into a single executable SQL query. The
merger is trained on paired examples of decomposed fragments and ground-truth
composed queries. Foreign key constraints are injected as hard rules during
merging (a column used in a JOIN must participate in a declared foreign key).

4. Execution-Guided Refinement (EGR) — per query only The composed SQL is
executed against a clean (non-distribution-shifted) development database. If
execution fails (syntax error, empty result, type mismatch), the error message
and the original question are fed back to the LLM for one refinement pass. The
refinement pass can re-decompose, re-prune the schema scope, or rewrite the SQL.
The refinement is stateless: no information about this error is retained for
future queries. If the refined query also fails, the system falls back to the
single-shot baseline output. If it succeeds, the refined query is returned.

Key design choice — no validation memory: The system does not maintain any of
the following across queries:

 • A log of failed SQL templates or anti-patterns- A cache of previously
   rejected schema scopes- A bank of reusable rejection criteria- An evolving
   validation classifier- Any form of execution failure historyEvery query
   begins from a zero-state decomposer, zero-state scope pruner, and zero-state
   refinement loop. The only per-query state is the conversation with the LLM
   during the EGR step, which is discarded after the query.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / BenchmarkPrimary: Spider1.0 (16,747 training questions,1,034 test
questions,200 databases,50+ tables per database in the extra split). Spider
remains the standard for compositional generalization.

Secondary: BIRD-SQL (12,751 training /1,534 test questions,95 databases). BIRD
adds dirty database values and real-world noise, testing robustness when
execution feedback may be unreliable due to data quality issues — a stress test
for the EGR loop.

Development splits: Use the official Spider dev set (1,034 examples) for
hyperparameter tuning and the BIRD dev set for transfer diagnostics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary / Secondary |

|---|---|---| | Exact Set Match Accuracy (EM) | Exact string match between
predicted and ground-truth SQL (Spider official) | Primary | | Execution
Accuracy (EX) | Predicted SQL and ground-truth SQL return identical result sets
| Primary | | Test-suite Accuracy (TS) | Match across multiple database states
(Spider official test-suite) | Primary | | Schema Drift Rate (SDR) | Fraction of
predicted queries referencing at least one non-existent table or column |
Secondary | | Refinement Cycles per Query (RCQ) | Average number of EGR rounds
per query (expected <1.5) | Secondary | | Fallback Rate (FR) | Fraction of
queries where the EGR loop fails and falls back to single-shot | Secondary |

EM and EX are reported with95% bootstrap confidence intervals over3 seeds. SDR
and RCQ are diagnostic metrics to understand where the method saves or loses
ground relative to validation-memory variants.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

estimate of one-pass performance without any decomposition or feedback | |

few-shot decomposition | | RESDSQL-3B+NatSQL | Prior schema-linking SOTA; tests

architecture; isolates the contribution of execution guidance vs.

with multi-agent orchestration | | -FULL (our method with full validation memory
enabled) | Oracle upper bound; quantifies the ceiling that -IVE cannot reach | |

Expected Failure Modes1. Repetitive schema drift across queries. Without
validation memory, the scope pruner may repeatedly choose the same wrong table
for semantically similar questions across different test examples. A system with
validation memory would recognize this pattern after2–3 failures and down-weight
that table globally. The -IVE variant cannot, so drift rates may be higher on
schemas where certain tables are easily confused (e.g., orders vs order_items).

 2 Stagnant refinement. The EGR loop has no memory of what kinds of errors it
   made last time. If the same failure mode applies to a structurally similar
   query later in the test set, the refinement will rediscover the same fix from
   scratch, wasting inference budget. This may inflate RCQ without improving FR.
 3 Composition cascading errors. A mistake in one sub-query that the EGR loop
   fixes may create a downstream inconsistency during merging that was not
   present before. Without validation memory, the system cannot learn that
   certain classes of fixes (e.g., swapping a LEFT JOIN for an INNER JOIN) tend
   to break the merge step and should be avoided.
 4 BIRD robustness gap. On BIRD, where dirty data can cause execution to produce
   empty or incorrect result sets for correct SQL, the per-query EGR loop may
   over-refine (changing a correct query to an incorrect one in response to a
   spurious execution error). A validation-memory system could learn to suppress
   refinement when data quality indicators are poor; this ablation cannot.
 5 Comparing to -FULL. The central finding of this ablation is expected to be
   that the gap between -IVE and -FULL is moderate on Spider (2–4 EM points) but
   larger on BIRD (5–8 EM points), because BIRD exposes more spurious execution
   signals that validation memory helps filter.

Limitations- No cross-query learning. The most fundamental limitation. Every
failure is a fresh failure. The system cannot discover that "queries involving
temporal ranges on date columns tend to trigger type-mismatch errors and should
use BETWEEN instead of >= ... AND < ..." — a pattern a validation-memory system
would learn after2–3 occurrences.

 • Bound on refinement quality. Because the refinement loop is stateless and
   limited in rounds (max2), it is unlikely to fix queries that require multiple
   interdependent corrections (e.g., wrong table → wrong column → wrong join
   condition). The per-query EGR loop cannot coordinate corrections across
   sub-queries.
 • Scope pruner degrades under schema shift. The pruner is trained on Spider's
   schema distribution. On schemas with out-of-distribution naming conventions
   or unusually large table counts, its relevance scores degrade, and without
   validation memory there is no corrective signal across queries.
 • Computational overhead. Decomposition + independent sub-query generation +
   merging + up to2 refinement rounds means4–6 LLM calls per query versus1 for
   the single-shot baseline. Inference cost scales linearly with decomposition
   granularity. For latency-sensitive deployments, this may be prohibitive
   regardless of accuracy gains.
 • No guarantee of monotonic improvement from refinement. The EGR loop can (and
   in our BIRD experiments likely will) degrade output quality when spurious
   execution errors trigger unnecessary rewrites. Without validation memory, the
   system cannot detect this degradation and suppress the refinement.
 • Spider ceiling. Spider test accuracy for SOTA methods is approaching85% EX.
   The -IVE variant may close much of the gap to the current SOTA but cannot
   exceed the -FULL ceiling, and may fall short on the hardest compositional
   splits (e.g., "comparison" and "sorting" categories in Spider-CLASSIC) where
   cross-query pattern recognition is most beneficial.

Problem
Current LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems perform competitively on benchmarks
like Spider (medium-scale, ~200 tables across20 databases, ~5 tables per
question). However, they degrade sharply on large-scale schemas (50+
tables,1000+ columns) common in enterprise settings. Two core issues:

1 Context window saturation — the full schema cannot fit in a single prompt,
forcing truncation that may drop relevant tables/columns.
2 Schema linking fragility — lightweight retrievers (embeddings + cosine
similarity) miss indirect matches (e.g., a column named "emp_salary" for a
question about "monthly compensation"), while heavy multi-stage pipelines
(re-ranking, self-consistency) inflate cost and latency.

No existing method jointly addresses both problems with a unified, training-free
decomposition that scales to schema sizes beyond current benchmarks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Decomposing the Text-to-SQL task into three sequential stages —
structured schema pruning, sub-query decomposition, and incremental SQL
construction with local verification — will improve execution accuracy on
large-scale schemas by ≥15% over flat prompting approaches, while adding ≤2x
inference cost.

The hypothesis rests on two claims:

• Schema pruning by structure + semantics (not just flat embeddings) reduces
irrelevant context without dropping critical tables.
• Incremental construction catches composition errors (missing JOINs, wrong
nesting) at the sub-query level before final assembly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A three-stage pipeline, SaDec (Schema-Aware Decomposition):

Stage1: Hybrid Schema Pruning- Structure-aware filter: Extract the subgraph of
tables within2-hop relations of user-specified entities (heuristic: tables whose
primary keys appear in the question text, then their foreign-key neighbors).

• Semantic reranker: Embed each remaining table's DDL +3 sample rows using a
bi-encoder (e.g., BGE-M3). Rerank by cosine similarity against the question
embedding. Keep top-K tables (K =8–12, tunable).
• Output: a pruned schema (DDL + foreign keys) small enough to fit in one LLM
call.

Stage2: Sub-Query Decomposition- Prompt an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) to split the
question into2–5 sub-questions, each referencing specific tables/columns from
the pruned schema.

• Each sub-question is paired with its expected output columns and JOIN
constraints. This acts as an interpretable intermediate plan.

Stage3: Incremental SQL Construction + Verification- Generate SQL for each
sub-question independently, using the pruned schema.

• Local verifier: Execute each sub-query against the database. If it returns an
error or an empty result set, regenerate with a feedback prompt ("previous
attempt failed because...").
• Assembly pass: Combine sub-queries into the final SQL using a separate LLM
call with the full question, sub-queries, and their verified results as
context.
• Optional final check: Run the assembled SQL; if it errors, fall back to a
single-stage generation on the pruned schema.

No fine-tuning required. All stages use frozen LLMs with few-shot prompts (3
exemplars from similar databases in the training set).

large-scale subset (databases with ≥30 tables: ~15–20 databases, ~1,500
questions). BIRD contains real databases with dirty values and requires external
knowledge — a harder, more realistic setting than Spider.

~700 questions) and Spider-Realistic (~500 questions with paraphrased
questions), which stress schema linking.

Proposal: Functional Dissociation of Reasoning and Knowledge in Transformer LMs
via Causal Representation Interventions### TitleDisentangling Reasoning from
Factual Recall in Large Language Models: A Causal Intervention Framework

ProblemLarge language models perform diverse cognitive tasks — mathematical
reasoning, factual question answering, instruction following, and safety
compliance — using a single set of parameters. It remains unknown whether these
capabilities are implemented by dissociable functional circuits or are
irretrievably entangled in shared representations. If capabilities can be
decoupled, then targeted model editing, modular fine-tuning, and
interpretability become tractable. If they are fundamentally entangled, then
interventions on one capability will unavoidably degrade others, placing hard
limits on post-hoc model steering.

Current work (Meng et al.,2022; Vig et al.,2020; Geiger et al.,2021) edits
factual associations or inserts control vectors, but no systematic evaluation
exists that tests whether reasoning and factual recall occupy separable
representational subspaces across model scales and families. The field lacks (a)
a causal framework for defining when two capabilities are dissociated, (b) a
standardized benchmark for measuring interference between capabilities under
intervention, and (c) evidence on how dissociation scales with model size and
training data composition.

HypothesisH1: Reasoning and factual recall occupy partially dissociable
subspaces in transformer hidden states. Specifically, there exist linear
subspaces in the residual stream such that targeted read/write interventions on
the reasoning subspace affect reasoning accuracy by ≥20 percentage points while
changing factual recall accuracy by ≤5 percentage points, and vice versa for the
factual subspace.

H2: The degree of dissociation increases with model scale: larger models exhibit
more structured, separable representations, whereas smaller models (≤1B
parameters) entangle capabilities due to representation capacity constraints.

H3: Fine-tuning on a reasoning-heavy task strengthens the reasoning subspace
without proportionally enlarging the factual subspace, suggesting that
plasticity is locally concentrated rather than uniformly distributed.

MethodWe propose a three-stage causal intervention pipeline:

Stage1 — Subspace Discovery (supervised probing). For each capability
(reasoning, factual recall), collect a labeled dataset of model hidden states
from forward passes on capability-specific prompts. Train a linear probe to
classify whether the model is engaging reasoning vs. factual recall from
residual stream activations at each layer. Take the probe weight vector as
defining a capability direction ( v_c ). Validate orthogonality between
directions via cosine similarity and the dot-product overlap metric from Elhage
et al. (2022). Repeat across layers0–N to identify the layer(s) with maximal
separation.

Stage2 — Causal Intervention (subspace ablation and amplification). At the
discovered layer, perform two types of intervention during forward passes on
evaluation prompts:

 • Subspace ablation: Project the residual stream orthogonal to ( v_c ),
   removing the capability direction.
 • Subspace amplification: Add a scaled version of ( v_c ) to the residual
   stream, amplifying the capability direction.

Measure the effect on both the target capability and the non-target capability.
A capability is dissociable if ablating its subspace degrades its own benchmark
by ≥20 points while leaving the other benchmark's accuracy change within ±5
points.

Stage3 — Cross-Task Generalization. Repeat the subspace discovered from one
reasoning task (e.g., GSM8K) on a held-out reasoning task (e.g., MathQA) to test
whether the subspace is task-specific or capability-general.
Cross-generalization supports the claim that reasoning exists as a distinct
capability; failure suggests the subspace merely captures surface task features.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe construct a Capability Interference Benchmark (CIB) with
four task families:


 Capability              Task                    Metric       Source
 Factual recall          TriviaQA (single-hop)   Exact match  TriviaQA
 Factual recall          Natural Questions       F1           NQ
 Reasoning               GSM8K (math word        Accuracy     GSM8K
                         problems)
 Reasoning               MathQA (multi-step)     Accuracy     MathQA
 Control — instruction   AlpacaEval (subset)     Win rate     AlpacaEval
 following
 Control — safety        SafetyPrompts (refusal  Refusal %    Anthropic HH-RLHF
                         rate)


The control tasks (instruction following, safety) test whether intervention
effects are specific to reasoning/factual recall or bleed into unrelated
capabilities.

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary / Secondary |

|---|---|---| | Dissociation score | (\Delta)target − (\Delta)non-target under
intervention (percentage points) | Primary | | Subspace overlap | Cosine
similarity between probe directions across layers and model sizes | Primary | |
Intervention efficiency | Minimum intervention magnitude needed for ≥20 pp
target change | Secondary | | Task generalization gap | GSM8K subspace applied
to MathQA: performance delta | Secondary | | Side-effect profile |
Per-intervention accuracy change on control tasks | Guardrail |

A dissociation score ≥15 pp (with ≤5 pp side effect on the non-target) is the
acceptability threshold. A score ≥25 pp is strong dissociation.

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Why it matters |

|---|---|---| | Random direction ablation | Ablate a random subspace of equal
dimension | Controls for non-specific damage from any subspace removal | | Mean
ablation | Ablate the mean activation vector | Controls for magnitude-based
effects | | Untrained model (random weights) | Repeat Stage1 on a randomly
initialized model | Tests whether subspace structure emerges from architecture
alone or requires training | | Full model (no intervention) | Unperturbed
forward pass | Establishes ceiling performance | | LoRA fine-tuned forgetting |
Fine-tune model to forget reasoning (gradient-based) | Contrasts learned vs.
hard-coded dissociation |

Ablations (Within This Proposal)

                         whether dissociation is layer-specific

                         (same tokenizer, same training data family)

                         patching (Geiger et al.,2021) for subspace discovery

                         training to see if dissociation emerges early or late


Expected Failure Modes- No subspace found: Probes achieve chance accuracy across
all layers, implying reasoning and factual recall are not linearly separable in
the residual stream. This would falsify H1 and require reformulation into a
nonlinear or multi-layer framework.

 • Symmetrical interference: Ablating either subspace degrades both capabilities
   equally. This would support the entanglement hypothesis and suggest
   fundamental limits on capability-level model editing.
 • Task-specific, not capability-general: The GSM8K subspace fails to transfer
   to MathQA. This would weaken H1: the subspace captures mathematical language
   rather than reasoning per se.
 • Scale invariance: Pythia160M and6.9B show identical dissociation scores. This
   would falsify H2 and suggest that representation structuring does not
   increase with capacity — possibly implicating pre-training objective rather
   than scale.
 • Safety collapse: The reasoning intervention degrades refusal rates on
   SafetyPrompts by >10 pp. This would flag an unacceptable side effect even if
   the primary dissociation criterion is met.

Limitations1. Linear subspace assumption. The probe-based method assumes
capability directions are linear in the residual stream. If dissociation exists
only in nonlinear or attention-head-specific subspaces, this method will miss
it. Results are therefore lower bounds on actual dissociation.

 2 Task coverage. Four task families cannot exhaustively represent all LLM
   capabilities. Creativity, code generation, multilingual understanding, and
   social reasoning are excluded and may exhibit different entanglement
   patterns.
 3 Prompting confound. Differences in prompt format between reasoning and
   factual tasks could produce spurious probe directions that reflect prompt
   structure rather than capability. The cross-task generalization test
   partially addresses this, but a prompt-difficulty confound (math prompts are
   harder) may remain.
 4 Static evaluation. We measure dissociation at a single inference-time
   snapshot. Training-time dynamics (how and when dissociation emerges during
   pre-training) are covered only coarsely via checkpoint ablations and are not
   the primary focus.
 5 Single intervention family. We test only linear subspace projection.
   Activation patching, representation engineering (RepE), and sparse
   autoencoder-based methods may yield different dissociation contours.
 6 Scale ceiling. The largest model tested (6.9B parameters) is an order of
   magnitude below frontier models (70B+). Dissociation at this scale may not
   extrapolate.

Factual Consistency via Latent Source-Space Alignment in Large Language Models##
 TitleLatent Source-Space Alignment: Grounding LLM Generations Through Internal
                            Representation Steering

ProblemLarge Language Models generate fluent text that frequently contradicts
verifiable facts — a phenomenon spanning entity hallucinations, temporal
inconsistencies, and invented references. Existing mitigation strategies fall
into three families, each with a fundamental limitation: (i) retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG) conditions on external passages but cannot prevent the model
from ignoring or overriding retrieved content during decoding; (ii) prompt-based
methods (e.g. chain-of-thought with fact-checking instructions) are brittle
under distribution shift and offer no guarantees; (iii) fine-tuning on factual
corpora improves calibration on in-distribution topics but degrades on long-tail
queries and does not generalize to unseen domains. The core unsolved problem is
that the model's internal representations lack a mechanism to commit to a
verified source-state before generation proceeds — there is no architectural
induction that forces the decoded token distribution to remain faithful to
grounded premises.

HypothesisH1 (primary): Steering the hidden-state trajectory of the model toward
a verified source region — computed by constraining the attention distribution
over a retrieved passage to top-k supporting spans before each decoding step —
will reduce factual errors by at least30% relative to unsteered generation on
multiple-choice and free-form factuality benchmarks, without degrading fluency
beyond a1-point drop in perplexity.

H2 (secondary): The effectiveness of source-space steering is mediated by the
alignment gap between the model's internal representation of the query and its
representation of the supporting passage. When this gap falls below a learned
threshold, steering is unnecessary and may harm generation quality.

MethodWe propose Latent Source-Space Alignment (LSSA), a two-stage method that
operates at inference time without retraining the base model.

Stage1 — Passage Encoding and Span Selection. For each generation step, the
method begins with a retrieved or provided source passage. A lightweight
span-scoring module (a single transformer layer with a linear projection head,
trained on5K annotated factual-consistency pairs) computes a factuality score
for each contiguous span of up to64 tokens. Spans scoring above a threshold
(calibrated per-domain via a held-out validation set) form a verified source
region in the model's key-value cache.

Stage2 — Representation Steering. At each decoding layer ℓ, let hℓ be the hidden
state before the feed-forward sublayer. The method computes a steering vector sℓ
as the mean of the attention outputs attending to the verified source region.
The final hidden state is a convex combination: hᵢℓ = (1 − α**·w**ℓ) · hℓ +
α**·w**ℓ · sℓ, where α is a global hyperparameter and wℓ ∈ [0,1] is a
layer-specific gating weight produced by a learned policy network conditioned on
the alignment gap (H2). The policy network is trained via a small
reinforcement-learning loop (PPO, ~2K environment steps) with a reward that
combines factual accuracy and n-gram overlap with the reference.

This method requires no fine-tuning of the base LLM — only the span-scoring
module (Stage1) and the policy network (Stage2) must be trained, totaling
approximately15M parameters for a7B-base setup.

Dataset and BenchmarkWe evaluate across three factuality benchmarks:

 1 TruthfulQA (multiple-choice) —817 questions spanning common misconceptions
   and false beliefs. Primary metric: MC1 accuracy (single-true accuracy).
 2 FActScore (free-form generation) —500 Wikipedia biographies, each fact
   decomposed and verified. Primary metric: percentage of atomic facts
   supported.
 3 FreshQA (temporal factuality) —600 questions requiring up-to-date knowledge,
   with time-sensitive answers. Primary metric: accuracy with strict temporal
   grounding.
 4 SelfCheckGPT (internal consistency) —250 Wiki-style passages from GPT-3 with
   per-sentence factuality annotations. Primary metric: sentence-level F1 for
   consistency.

All benchmarks are English. We use GPTNeoX-20B as the base model for the main
experiments and scale to LLaMA-2-70B for the largest configuration.

Evaluation Metrics- Factual Accuracy (FA): Micro-averaged proportion of correct
atomic facts, averaged across all benchmarks. This is the primary metric.

 • Source Faithfulness (SF): Decomposable entailment score (using an
   off-the-shelf NLI model — DeBERTa-large-MNLI) measuring whether the
   generation is entailed by the provided source passage. Macro-averaged across
   benchmarks.
 • Perplexity (PPL): On the WikiText-103 validation set, to track fluency
   degradation.
 • Response Length Ratio (RLR): Ratio of generated tokens to reference tokens,
   to detect verbose hedging as a confound.
 • Steering Intervention Rate (SIR): Fraction of decoding steps where α·wℓ
   >0.05, measuring how frequently the steering mechanism activates.

BaselinesWe compare against six methods spanning the three existing mitigation
families:

 1 Standard greedy decoding (no intervention).
 2 RAG with top-1 passage (DPR retriever + standard autoregressive generation).
 3 RAG + self-consistency voting (Karpukhin et al.,2020 — sample5 generations,
   vote on factuality).
 4 Constitutional AI-style prompting (Bai et al.,2022 — "Generate only
   statements that are supported by the provided context" appended to the
   prompt).
 5 DoLa (Chuang et al.,2023 — contrastive decoding by contrasting early vs late
   layers on factuality).
 6 Inference-time contrastive steering (Li et al.,2024 — subtract "unfaithful"
   direction from hidden states, using a precomputed probe).

All baselines use the same base model (GPTNeoX-20B) and the same retriever (DPR)
where retrieval is applicable.

AblationsWe run four ablations to isolate the contribution of each component:

 1 -SpanSelection: Remove the span-scoring module; use the full retrieved
   passage as the verified source region. Tests whether span-level granularity
   matters.
 2 -AlignmentGate: Remove the learned gating policy (set wℓ =1 for all layers).
   Tests whether layer-specific adjustment is necessary.
 3 -Retrieval: Replace retrieved passages with the model's own generated
   preamble (zero-shot fact generation). Tests whether external grounding is
   required or whether the steering mechanism can exploit internally generated
   context.
 4 -Steering: Set α =0 across all steps. Reduces to the base model; establishes
   the upper bound of fluency with the lower bound of factuality.

Expected Failure Modes1. Soft source overfitting. The steering mechanism may
bias the model toward the lexical form of the source passage rather than its
semantic content, producing generations that are faithful to the source but
factually incorrect when the source itself is wrong. This is partially
controlled by using multiple benchmarks with independent ground truth, but
adversarial retrieval noise remains a risk.

 2 Alignment gap collapse. The policy network may learn to set wℓ near zero for
   all layers on certain domains, effectively disabling the intervention. This
   would produce null results indistinguishable from the base model. We monitor
   SIR per-domain to detect this.
 3 Layer-wise interference. Steering in middle layers may disrupt syntactic
   planning while late-layer steering may be too late to affect token choice.
   The learned gating may not resolve this if the reward landscape is flat. We
   will visualize layer-specific steering magnitudes post-hoc.
 4 Domain-dependent threshold sensitivity. The span-selection threshold
   calibrated on the held-out validation set may generalize poorly to benchmarks
   with different fact densities (e.g., FreshQA's temporal questions vs.
   TruthfulQA's misconception questions). We report per-benchmark results to
   expose this.
 5 Metric gaming. The NLI-based Source Faithfulness metric could be gamed by
   short, vague generations that are technically entailed by the source but omit
   specific claims. We mitigate by also reporting Factual Accuracy, which
   requires explicit factual claims.

Limitations1. Computational overhead. The LSSA method requires a forward pass
for span scoring and a modified decoding loop with per-layer steering,
approximately2.3× the inference cost of standard greedy decoding on a single
A100. This may be prohibitive for latency-sensitive applications.

 2 Dependence on retrieval quality. The method assumes a relevant source passage
   is available. For open-domain generation where no passage is retrieved or the
   retrieval pool is incomplete, the method degrades to the base model. The
   -Retrieval ablation partially tests this scenario, but the degradation curve
   under retrieval sparsity is not characterized.
 3 English-only evaluation. All benchmarks are English. The span-scoring module
   and alignment policy are trained on English data only, and there is no
   guarantee that the learned representations transfer to other languages with
   different factuality norms and syntactic structures.
 4 Static source assumption. The method treats the source passage as fixed
   before generation begins. For multi-turn or interactive settings where new
   evidence arrives mid-generation, the steering region would need to be
   recomputed, which the current design does not support.
 5 No formal correctness guarantee. Unlike constrained decoding methods that
   enforce a grammar, LSSA is a soft steering mechanism. It reduces the
   probability of factual errors but cannot eliminate them. For high-stakes
   domains requiring verifiable correctness (medical, legal), this method should
   be combined with post-hoc verification rather than relied upon alone.
 6 No validation-evolution memory. This proposal is generated without reference
   to a bank of prior failed directions, execution failures, or reusable
   rejection criteria. Consequently, some proposed design choices (e.g.,
   layer-specific gating, span-level scoring) may replicate failure patterns
   already documented in prior work. Without cross-run validation memory, the
   method is at increased risk of rediscovering known negative results during
   implementation.

Generation## Title
FiND — Factual Negative Distillation: Improving LLM Factual
Consistency via Self-Generated Hard Negatives

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models produce coherent but factually inconsistent outputs
— they generate statements that contradict themselves across contexts,
misattribute facts, or assert claims unsupported by their training distribution.
Existing mitigation strategies fall into two camps: (1) inference-time methods
(RAG, self-consistency, contrastive decoding) that add latency and complexity at
deployment, and (2) training-time methods (RLHF, DPO) that rely on expensive
human preference data or simple synthetic negatives that are too easy to
discriminate, leading to weak generalization.

The core gap: training-time objectives lack hard negatives that are semantically
plausible but factually incorrect, produced in a scalable, automated way.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
An LLM fine-tuned on pairs of (factual statement, hard-negative
counterfactual) — where the negative is generated by the same model and then
perturbed via a knowledge-driven corruption process — will show significantly
higher factual consistency on held-out distributions than models trained with
standard SFT, DPO, or inference-time methods alone.

The mechanism is that hard negatives force the model to learn the decision
boundary between factually consistent and inconsistent outputs, rather than
merely memorizing factual-looking surface patterns.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Hard-Negative Generation PipelineFor each factual triple
(subject, relation, object) extracted from a knowledge base:

1 Prompt the model to generate a natural-language sentence expressing the
triple (e.g., "The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris, France").
2 Generate hard negatives by corrupting the factual triple with four
strategies:

• Entity swap: Replace subject or object with a same-type entity ("The Eiffel
Tower is located in Berlin").
• Relation flip: Replace the relation with a semantically similar but incorrect
one ("The Eiffel Tower was built in Paris" → "The Eiffel Tower was demolished
in Paris" when relation was located_in).
• Numeric/date perturbation: Offset numerical facts by a plausible but wrong
amount ("180 feet" → "280 feet" for height).
• Coreference break: Introduce entity mismatch in a multi-sentence context that
creates a contradiction (e.g., substitute a pronoun antecedent).

3 Filter negatives using a separate NLI/verification model: keep only those
where the negative is:

• Plausible (the verification model cannot trivially reject)
• Diverse (low semantic similarity to other negatives for the same triple)

Stage2: Contrastive Fine-TuningTrain using a preference optimization objective
(simplified DPO-style) where:

• Chosen: Model's own generation of the factual sentence.
• Rejected: The hardest negative that passes the filter.

The loss encourages higher likelihood of factual trajectories and lower
likelihood of the hard-negative trajectory, using the model's own distribution
as the reference.

Stage3: Self-Consistency RegularizationAdd a secondary objective: for a given
query, the model produces K samples; maximize the pairwise agreement of factual
claims across those samples (measured by an NLI model's entailment scores
between sampled statements). This directly penalizes self-contradiction at
training time.

coverage in the model's training distribution to avoid OOD trivia.
