Research Proposal: Synthesizing Failure-to-Repair Trajectories for Improving
Code LLM Reasoning## Title
Trajectory-for-Code: Self-Supervised Synthesis of
Debugging Trajectories for Robust Code Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLMs are predominantly trained on (instruction,
correct_solution) pairs, either from human sources (e.g., StarCoder data) or
synthetic pipelines (e.g., CodeAlpaca, OSS-Instruct). This outcome-only
supervision has two limitations:

1 Brittle reasoning on hard problems — When the model's first attempt is wrong,
it has no training signal for how to recover. It was never shown buggy
attempts, test failures, or the iterative debugging steps that lead to
correct code.
2 Overconfident generations — Models trained exclusively on correct outputs
lack calibrated uncertainty about when their code is likely wrong, and cannot
self-correct without an external oracle.

Gap: While self-debugging and self-refine methods exist at inference time, no
systematic study has asked whether training on synthesized debugging
trajectories (attempt → test failure → bug analysis → repair → verified fix)
improves a model's code reasoning and self-correction ability at both train and
test time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary: Fine-tuning a code LLM on self-synthesized debugging
trajectories — sequences where the model sees its own buggy attempt, test
failure signal, natural-language bug explanation, and a corrected solution —
improves pass@1 on held-out reasoning benchmarks by ≥5% over fine-tuning on the
same volume of (instruction, correct_code) synthetic data alone.

Secondary: The same training yields a measurable improvement in self-correction
(ability to improve a generation given test feedback at inference time) without
requiring an external verifier during training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Trajectory Synthesis Pipeline (fully automated, no human
labels)

Given a base code LLM (e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct or CodeLlama-7B) and a
set of programming problems from a training split (e.g., APPS training set or a
subset of CodeContests):

1 Attempt: Sample $k=5$ solutions per problem from the model (temperature0.8).
2 Execute: Run each solution against the problem's test cases. Categorize as
pass or fail. Collect the failing test input, expected output, and actual
output.
3 Bug analysis prompt: For each failing solution, prompt the model: "Explain
why this code fails on the given test. Identify the specific bug." This
produces a natural-language bug description. Filter by a lightweight check —
the description must mention the relevant variable or line (heuristic).
4 Repair prompt: Prompt the model: "Given the buggy code, the test failure
details, and the bug explanation above, write a corrected version." Execute
the corrected version; keep only repairs that pass all tests.
5 Assemble trajectory: (problem → buggy_code → test_failure → bug_analysis →
corrected_code). Also include the successful (problem → correct_code) paths
as positive examples.

Yield: ~3–5× more training sequences per problem (one correct path + several
repair trajectories).

To control quality, discard trajectories where:

• The bug analysis is empty or generic (<10 tokens).
• The repair still fails any test case.
• The buggy code has a syntax error (trivial).

Stage2 — TrainingFine-tune the base model on a mixture:

-50% standard (instruction, correct_code) pairs from the same problem set-50%
trajectory data (each trajectory formatted as a multi-turn chat: user → problem,
assistant → code, user → test fails with details, assistant → bug analysis, user
→ fix it, assistant → corrected code)

Train for2 epochs. Use a replay buffer where trajectory data is sampled
proportional to the number of repair steps (more steps → higher weight). Compare
against a control fine-tuned on the same total tokens but only (instruction,
correct_code) pairs.

Stage3 — EvaluationEvaluate on held-out benchmarks (see below). Measure both
static pass@k and self-correction pass@1: allow the model one additional attempt
with test failure feedback.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Training data source:

• CodeContests (training split) ~13K problems with test cases — diverse
difficulty, multiple languages.
• Supplement with APPS (training split) ~5K problems for coverage.

Evaluation benchmarks (held-out, no test set overlap):

• HumanEval+ —164 problems with80× more test cases (EvalPlus). Measures
functional correctness.
• MBPP+ —399 problems with enriched tests.
• LiveCodeBench — recent competitive programming problems, tests recency and
generalization.
• CodeContests (test split) —165 problems.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Description |

|---|---| | pass@1 | Standard functional correctness on first sample
(temperature0.2, greedy) | | pass@5 | Any of5 samples passes (temperature0.8) |
| self-correct pass@1 | First sample + one repair round given test failure
feedback. Measures the model's ability to debug its own output. | | trajectory
efficiency | % of synthesized trajectories that produce valid repairs after one
pass (measures pipeline quality) | | calibration error | Expected Calibration
Error (ECE) on the model's confidence vs. pass rate, to test whether training on
failures produces better-calibrated models |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model (no fine-tuning) — e.g., DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct2.
Standard SFT — fine-tuned on (instruction, correct_code) only, matching total
tokens3. Code Alpaca / OSS-Instruct style — synthetic instruction–code pairs
from a teacher model4. Self-play w/o trajectories — generate correct code,
filter by tests, train on that (no failure data)

5 CodeRL baseline — actor-critic with test pass/fail as reward (uses RL, not
SFT on trajectories)
6 Self-Debugging (inference-only, no trajectory training) — to isolate training
benefit---

Ablations1. Remove bug-analysis step: train on (problem → buggy → repair)
without the natural-language bug explanation. Isolates the value of intermediate
reasoning.

2 Remove failure signal: train on (problem → repair) only — show the model the
correct code without showing the failure context.
3 Trajectory ratio sweep: vary the % of trajectory data in the mix
(10%,30%,50%,70%) to measure diminishing returns.
4 Model scale: replicate on1B,7B, and14B models to test whether trajectory
training helps more at smaller scales (where self-correction is hardest).
5 Oracle repair vs. model repair: replace the model's own repair step with
GPT-4's repair to measure the ceiling (is the bottleneck synthesis quality or
training itself?).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Repair data is too easy — the model generates obviously buggy code
that it easily fixes, so trajectories are trivial. | Filter trajectories by the
edit distance of the repair; keep only those with non-trivial changes (>3 tokens
different). | | Model learns to generate buggy code to get repair signal —
exploits the training setup. | Keep the50% standard SFT mix as a regularizer;
never reward buggy-only generations. | | Synthetic bug analysis is hallucinated
— the explanation sounds plausible but is wrong. | The repair step must produce
executed correct code; wrong explanations that still lead to correct repairs are
harmless, and wrong explanations that mislead the repair will be discarded. | |
No improvement on single-turn pass@1 — the benefit only shows in multi-turn
self-correction. | Acceptable if self-correction improves, but the hypothesis
requires ≥5% improvement on pass@1. If self-correction improves without pass@1,
refine the hypothesis. | | Small model can't produce valid bug explanations (<1B
parameters) leads to low-quality trajectories. | Restrict the study to ≥7B
models; use1B as an ablation but expect pipeline yield to be low. | | Metric
saturation — base model is already strong on HumanEval (85%+), leaving little
room. | Use more difficult benchmarks (LiveCodeBench, CodeContests test split)
where scores are lower. HumanEval+ results are still reported but are not the
primary signal. |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SummaryThis proposal tests a simple, automated, and self-supervised method for
creating rich code reasoning data: instead of only generating (problem, answer)
pairs, generate full debugging trajectories — buggy attempt, test feedback, bug
explanation, repair — and train on them. The core idea is that learning how to
recover from failure should produce more robust code reasoning than learning
only from successes. The experiment is feasible with open models, open
benchmarks, and no human annotation.

Research Proposal: Sensitivity-Guided Dynamic Precision Allocation for LLM
Inference## Title
DyPrec: Sensitivity-Guided Dynamic Precision Allocation for
Latency-Optimized LLM Inference

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM inference latency is dominated by memory bandwidth in the decode
phase — each token generated requires loading the full model weights from GPU
memory. While static quantization (e.g., FP16→FP8/FP4) reduces this cost
uniformly, it applies a single precision floor to all layers regardless of their
actual sensitivity to numerical error. This is wasteful: embedding and early
layers are highly sensitive to quantization drift (errors compound across
depth), while later layers and feed-forward sub-layers can tolerate much lower
precision without measurable output degradation. Current systems lack a
principled method to dynamically allocate precision per layer and per input at
inference time.

Key gap: No existing work jointly optimizes the granularity (per-layer,
per-block) and adaptivity (per-input, per-token position) of precision
allocation using empirical sensitivity measurements, while respecting hardware
constraints (group size, memory alignment, kernel availability).

downstream task accuracy), there exists, for each layer, a minimum viable
precision that respects the sensitivity profile of that layer. Allocating higher
precision only to the most sensitive layers and lower precision to insensitive
ones yields a better latency–accuracy Pareto frontier than any uniform-precision
baseline. Further, this allocation can be dynamically selected per input cluster
(e.g., domain or difficulty) to improve the frontier over a static
one-size-fits-all allocation.

Research Proposal: Counterfactual Data Augmentation for Mitigating Gender Bias
in Neural Machine Translation## Title
Counterfactual Data Augmentation with
Source-Side Control for Mitigating Occupational Gender Bias in Neural Machine
Translation

Problem
Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models exhibit systematic gender bias:
they disproportionately map neutral-source occupational terms (e.g., "doctor,"
"nurse") to target-language gendered forms that align with statistical
stereotypes rather than real-world distributions. On standard benchmarks like
WinoMT, models such as mBART-50 assign "She is a doctor" the masculine
translation ~85% of the time for English→Spanish, while "nurse" is feminine ~80%
of the time. This propagates occupational stereotypes and can produce
grammatically incorrect output when the context or world knowledge contradicts
the majority pattern.

Existing debiasing approaches fall into three camps — (1) post-hoc decoding
rules, (2) fine-tuning on balanced or anti-stereotypical data, and (3)
embedding-space interventions — but each has limitations: decoding rules can
break fluency, balanced data is scarce and expensive, and embedding
interventions are often task-specific and degrade general translation quality. A
method that requires only synthetic data and a single fine-tuning step, without
specialized architectures or inference-time overhead, would be broadly
applicable across language pairs and model families.

Hypothesis
Adding counterfactually augmented training examples — where
occupational nouns are swapped across genders in the source sentence — combined
with a source-side gender control signal (a special token marking the intended
target gender) will significantly reduce occupational gender bias in NMT output
on WinoMT while preserving BLEU score on standard translation benchmarks
within0.5 points.

The intuition is twofold: (a) the counterfactual data forces the model to learn
that doctor can co-occur with feminine agreement in the target, breaking the
spurious correlation; (b) the control token lets the model disambiguate
ambiguous cases at inference without requiring a separate classifier or post-hoc
rule.

Method1. Counterfactual Data Generation Pipeline

• Start with a parallel corpus (e.g., Europarl + News Commentary for
EN→ES/DE/FR).
• Tag each sentence with occupation-bearing terms using a POS tagger +
occupation lexicon (300 occupation nouns from ONET).
• For each sentence containing an occupational reference to a specific gender
(e.g., "the female doctor"), generate a counterfactual by swapping the gender
descriptor ("the male doctor").
• Also generate sentences where occupation appears without explicit gender
(e.g., "the doctor"), paired with both a masculine and a feminine target
translation obtained by replacing gender-agreement morphology in the
reference.
• Insert a control token at the source sentence head: [GENDER:M], [GENDER:F],
or [NEUTRAL]. The neutral case is used only at inference when gender is truly
unknown.

2. Fine-Tuning

• Mix counterfactual data with original training data at a1:4 ratio (pilot
experiments will test1:1,1:4,1:9).
• Fine-tune a pretrained NMT model (mT5-small or mBART-50) for1–3 epochs with
reduced learning rate (1e-5).
• Evaluate on held-out WinoMT test sets.

3. Inference Protocol

• For sentences where the source has no gender signal, pass the sentence
through a minimal gender-identification classifier (rule-based for EN:
pronoun/coreference heuristics).
• Prepend [GENDER:M] or [GENDER:F] accordingly. When classifier is uncertain,
use [NEUTRAL], which falls back to the most frequent target form.

Dataset / Benchmark- Training corpus: Europarl v7 + News Commentary v12 (EN→ES,
EN→DE, EN→FR; ~2M sentence pairs)

• Counterfactual augmentation: ~50k synthetic sentence pairs generated from the
training corpus- Bias evaluation: WinoMT (Stanovsky et al.,2019) —3,888
pro-stereotype and anti-stereotype sentences covering60 occupations across
EN→ES/DE/FR- General quality evaluation: newstest2013, newstest2014##
Evaluation Metrics| What | Metric | How | |------|--------|-----| | Gender
bias | WinoMT accuracy | % of correct gender assignments for both pro- and
anti-stereotype sentences | | Translation quality | BLEU (sacrebleu) | On
newstest2013/2014 | | Fluency loss | chrF++ | Additional check if BLEU
degrades | | Stereo type flip | Δ between pro- and anti-stereotype accuracy |
Smaller Δ = less biased |

Primary success criterion: WinoMT accuracy on anti-stereotype examples improves
by ≥20 percentage points relative to the baseline, with BLEU drop ≤0.5.

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|----------|-------------| | Unmodified NMT | mBART-50 fine-tuned on original
data only (no augmentation, no control token) | | Decoding-only | Unmodified
model + gender-inflection post-hoc rule (e.g., adjust target morphology after
decoding) | | Balanced fine-tuning | Fine-tune on a static balanced dataset
(Equalizer, Saunders & Byrne,2020) — no control token | | Embedding debiasing |
Apply Hard Debias (Bolukbasi et al.,2016) to encoder embeddings before
fine-tuning |

Ablations1. No control token: Counterfactual data without [GENDER:M/F] token →
isolates the effect of augmentation vs. control signal.

2 Data ratio sweep:1:1,1:4,1:9 counterfactual-to-original ratio → identifies
trade-off between bias reduction and quality.
3 Occupation-only vs. all-noun augmentation: Only occupations vs. all gendered
nouns → tests whether targeting is necessary or if broader augmentation works
better.
4 Rule-based vs. learned gender classifier at inference: affects how often the
control token is correct.

Expected Failure Modes1. BLEU degradation >0.5: Counterfactual data may distort
the training distribution enough that general translation quality drops.
Mitigation: early stopping based on validation BLEU; fall back to1:9 ratio or
smaller LR.

2 Control token leakage: The model may learn to ignore the token if it's
inconsistently applied (e.g., inference-time [NEUTRAL] differs from training
distribution). Mitigation: include [NEUTRAL] in training on a random10% of
sentences.
3 Language-pair dependence: EN→ES/FR (morphologically gendered
adjectives/determiners) may show larger gains than EN→DE (three-gender system
with more complex agreement). If EN→DE gains are weak, the method may not
generalize to languages with non-binary or richer gender systems.
4 Classifier errors propagate: A bad rule-based gender identifier could prepend
the wrong control token, biasing output in the opposite direction.
Mitigation: measure classifier accuracy; if <80% on a development set, switch
to a lightweight BERT-based classifier.
5 Diminishing returns on larger models: mBART-50 (611M) or mT5-large may
already encode weaker stereotyping at scale. The method may show smaller
gains on larger models — we test on both small and large variants to bound
this.
6 Anti-stereotype improvement does not close the gap: Even with a20pp gain on
anti-stereotype examples, pro-stereotype accuracy may also shift, keeping the
gap large. Success criterion uses the anti-stereotype level rather than Δ
alone for this reason.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Knowledge Injection via Confidence-Gated Adapter
Fusion for Domain-Specific LLMs## Title
Confidence-Gated Adapter Fusion for
Mitigating Knowledge Conflicts During Domain-Specific LLM Injection

Problem
Domain-specific LLM deployment (legal, medical, finance) requires
injecting specialized knowledge into general-purpose pre-trained models. Three
interrelated challenges remain unresolved:

1 Knowledge conflicts — injected domain facts contradict or compete with the
model's pre-training knowledge, causing inconsistent behavior depending on
prompt phrasing.
2 Selective forgetting — fine-tuning on domain text degrades general-language
capabilities, especially on reasoning and rare-token recall.
3 Sub-domain interference — a single domain (e.g., clinical medicine) contains
heterogeneous sub-domains (radiology, pathology, pharmacology) that interfere
when injected via a single adapter or fine-tuning run.

Current solutions (full fine-tuning, RAG, LoRA, model editing) each address only
a subset of these. No method jointly handles all three while providing per-input
routing between base and injected knowledge.

Hypothesis
Confidence-gated routing — where the model dynamically selects between
base knowledge and injected domain knowledge based on its own predictive
uncertainty — reduces knowledge conflicts and sub-domain interference compared
to monolithic injection, while preserving general capabilities better than full
fine-tuning and matching the domain accuracy of state-of-the-art fixed injection
methods.

More concretely: an adapter mixture with a learned confidence-gating mechanism
will achieve higher domain-specific accuracy and lower general-task degradation
than the Pareto frontier of existing injection methods.

Method
Architecture. Start with a frozen base LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B). We train a
set of k lightweight LoRA adapters, each specialized on a distinct sub-domain
cluster of the target domain (clusters discovered via topic modeling or
metadata-driven splits). A small learned confidence gate is trained to produce,
for each input token/sequence: (a) a routing weight over the k adapters, and (b)
a scalar β ∈ [0,1] that mixes the adapter output with the base model's original
hidden state. When β is low, the model relies on base knowledge; when high,
injected knowledge dominates.

Gate architecture. A2-layer MLP over the hidden state of the last layer at the
final token position, outputting a softmax over adapters and a sigmoid-gated β.
Trained jointly with adapters via a regularized objective.

Training objective. Two terms:

• Domain accuracy — standard cross-entropy on domain data, but weighted by a
per-sample confidence bonus that down-weights examples the base model already
answers well (to focus injection on genuinely novel knowledge).
• General capability preservation — a distillation regularizer that penalizes
large β when the base model's output distribution on held-out general
benchmarks (MMLU subsets, GSM8K) has low entropy (high confidence),
preventing unnecessary overrides.

Inference. Single forward pass per token. Gating adds negligible latency (<1%
parameter overhead).

public sources:

Pharmacology         DrugBank QA                        800 QA       DrugBank
Radiology reports    MIMIC-III (report impressions)     2K excerpts  PhysioNet
Molecular biology    PubMedQA                           1K QA        PubMed
General (probe)      MMLU (biomedical subset) +3        2.5K         MMLU
general sections

We also collect a training corpus by pooling the full source documents (not just
QA pairs) for each sub-domain, filtering for overlap with pre-training data to
remove ~90% intersection (document-level dedup against C4/RedPajama using
MinHash).

tasks); macro-average | Measures injection effectiveness | | General retention |
Δ(MMLU_full), Δ(GSM8K) — absolute drop from pre-injection | Measures forgetting
| | Knowledge consistency | Counterfactual accuracy — same fact queried with3
phrasings, pass@1 agreement | Measures conflict robustness | | Sub-domain
interference | When querying sub-domain A, compute logit change on sub-domain B
adapters' outputs | Measures cross-talk | | Routing interpretability | Spearman
correlation between β and ground-truth fact novelty (was this fact in
pre-training?) | Validates gating works as intended |

 Structurally-Guided Information Extraction via Schema-Compositional Decoding##
 ProblemInformation extraction (IE) from unstructured text remains brittle when
target schemas are complex, nested, or domain-specific. Existing approaches fall
 into two camps with complementary weaknesses. Sequence-labeling methods (CRF,
  BiLSTM-CRF, span-based classifiers) require per-schema labeled data and fail
 when entity types grow beyond a small closed set — retraining from scratch for
  each new schema is impractical. Generative approaches (sequence-to-sequence,
 encoder-decoder, LLM prompting) are schema-flexible but suffer from structural
inconsistency: they produce outputs that violate the target schema's constraints
(e.g., missing required fields, nested entities that cross boundaries, relation
    arguments that reference non-existent entities), and retrieval-augmented
     generation improves recall but does not guarantee structural validity.

The core unresolved problem is that current methods treat schema constraints as
soft signals learned implicitly from training data rather than as formal
specifications enforced during generation. When a schema specifies that an Event
type must have exactly one Trigger and a non-empty set of Arguments drawn from a
type hierarchy, no existing system guarantees this in its output. The
consequence is that downstream consumers — knowledge base population, question
answering, scientific curation pipelines — inherit malformed extractions that
require costly post-hoc validation and repair.

HypothesisWe hypothesize that decomposing information extraction into a
two-phase process — (1) schema-guided plan generation followed by (2)
type-constrained slot-filling decoding — yields structurally valid extractions
with higher precision and comparable recall to monolithic sequence-to-sequence
approaches, without requiring schema-specific training data.

Specifically, we propose that a schema-compositional decoding mechanism, where a
lightweight planner maps a target schema into an execution DAG of extraction
subtasks, and a frozen LM fills each subtask under per-node type constraints,
will (a) reduce structural violation rates by an order of magnitude relative to
free-form generation, (b) generalize zero-shot to unseen schemas at test time
without parameter updates, and (c) produce interpretable intermediate artifacts
(planned extraction traces) that enable targeted error diagnosis.

MethodThe proposed system, StructIE, comprises three components operating at
inference time over a pre-trained language model.

Schema Compiler. The target extraction schema is specified declaratively as a
type hierarchy with relation signatures. A Schema Compiler translates this into
a directed acyclic execution graph where each node corresponds to a grounded
extraction subtask: extract entities of type T within scope S or extract
relations of type R between arguments [A₁, A₂] within scope S. Edge constraints
encode dependencies (a relation node depends on its argument entity nodes) and
scope boundaries (a nested entity is extracted within the span of its parent).
This compilation is purely symbolic — no learned parameters. Execution graphs
are materialized per input document and schema pair.

Structured Decoding Controller. For each node in the execution graph, the
Controller invokes a frozen decoder LM (e.g., Llama370B or Mixtral8×22B) with a
node-specific prompt constructed from: (a) the document, (b) the previously
extracted entities/relations in scope (for context propagation), and (c) the
formal type signature of the target node. Decoding is constrained at the token
level: the Controller maintains a type-constrained vocabulary mask that admits
only tokens consistent with the expected output type at each decoding step. For
enumeration types (e.g., *EventType ∈ distillation into a single pass. The
proposal does not quantify the cost–quality tradeoff across the Pareto frontier.

No negative extraction handling. The system is designed to extract structured
records when the target information is present in text. It has no mechanism for
negative extraction — confidently determining that a schema field is absent from
the document — because the Schema Compiler always generates at least one node
for each required slot, and the LM always produces some output. This inflates
false positives on documents that do not contain the target information, which
is systematically under-measured in standard IE benchmarks where every document
contains the target entities.

Single language. All benchmarks are English. The Schema Compiler's text-span
constraints depend on whitespace-delimited token boundaries that do not transfer
to CJK or morphologically rich languages. Extending to multilingual extraction
would require tokenizer-aware span handling, which is not addressed.

Research Proposal: User Experience Evaluation for Large Language Models## TitleA
   Multi-Dimensional Framework for Evaluating User Experience in Open-Domain
Conversational LLMs## ProblemLarge language models are increasingly deployed as
   conversational agents in open-domain settings, yet the dominant evaluation
  paradigm remains heavily skewed toward automated metrics (perplexity, BLEU,
ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore, GPT-as-judge) and narrow benchmark performance (MMLU,
 GSM8K, HumanEval). These metrics capture surface-level linguistic fidelity and
  isolated capability dimensions but fail to measure how real users experience
   these systems over sustained interactions. User experience — encompassing
     satisfaction, trust, perceived intelligence, conversational flow, task
 completion comfort, and emotional response — remains under-characterized as a
       construct, with no standardized evaluation framework that is both
    psychometrically validated and practical for LLM developers. Existing UX
   instruments borrowed from HCI (SUS, QUIS, UEQ) were designed for graphical
interfaces and GUI applications, not for open-ended language interactions where
   the "interface" is entirely linguistic, context-dependent, and dynamically
                        co-constructed by both parties.

HypothesisA multi-dimensional UX evaluation framework designed specifically for
conversational LLMs — comprising (1) interaction fluency, (2) epistemic trust,
(3) goal alignment, (4) emotional valence, and (5) perceived adaptability — will
yield higher discriminative power, test-retest reliability, and predictive
validity for downstream behavioral outcomes (e.g., retention, referral, paid
conversion) than both:

 • H1a: Existing general-purpose UX instruments (SUS, UEQ) adapted post-hoc to
   conversational AI.
 • H1b: Single-metric LLM-as-judge evaluations currently prevalent in NLP.

Specifically, the framework will explain at least40% more variance in user
retention at2-week follow-up compared to the best existing alternative
(UEQ:12–18% variance explained in prior studies).

MethodPhase1 — Instrument Development (Qualitative → Quantitative). Conduct
semi-structured interviews with30 diverse LLM users (varying in technical
proficiency, use case, and interaction frequency). Thematic analysis will
surface the latent dimensions of user experience unique to conversational LLMs.
These dimensions will be operationalized into a25–30 item instrument using
Likert-scale and semantic-differential items. Items will be refined through
cognitive interviewing (n=10) and pilot testing (n=100) for clarity,
non-redundancy, and floor/ceiling effects.

Phase2 — Psychometric Validation (n=500). Deploy the instrument via a
longitudinal study. Participants interact with three different LLMs (two
instruction-tuned open-source models and one proprietary API) across five
scripted tasks (creative writing, factual question answering, emotional support,
code generation, multi-turn planning) over three sessions each. After each
session, participants complete the proposed instrument plus SUS, UEQ, and a
single-item GPT-as-judge correlation measure (participants rate "how intelligent
the model seemed"). At session3, participants complete a behavioral choice: they
may return for a follow-up session, recommend the model to a friend (binary), or
switch to a different model for the final task. Two-week follow-up surveys
measure retention and self-reported usage frequency.

Phase3 — Construct Validation (Discriminant and Convergent). Factor analysis
(EFA → CFA) assesses dimensionality. Correlate instrument dimensions with
automated metrics (perplexity, response length, self-repetition rate, lexical
diversity, BERTScore against ground-truth responses) to determine what automated
metrics capture (convergent) and miss (discriminant). Regress behavioral
outcomes (retention, recommendation) on instrument dimensions to establish
predictive validity.

Dataset / BenchmarkNo single existing dataset covers multi-model, multi-session
UX evaluation. The study will produce a new benchmark — LLM-UX-Bench —
comprising:

 • 500 participants ×3 models ×5 tasks ×3 sessions =22,500 interaction logs
   (anonymized, de-identified)
 • Item-level responses for the proposed instrument, SUS, UEQ, and the
   single-item intelligence rating- Behavioral outcomes: binary retention
   (returned for follow-up), binary recommendation willingness, continuous
   self-reported usage frequency at2 weeks- Model response transcripts (for
   reproducibility and automated metric computation)

Models under evaluation: Llama-3-70B-Instruct (open-source),
Mistral-8x22B-Instruct (open-source), GPT-4o (proprietary).

Evaluation MetricsPrimary instrument quality metrics:

 • Cronbach's α ≥0.80 per subscale (internal consistency)
 • Test-retest ICC ≥0.70 over1-week interval (stability)
 • Confirmatory Fit Index (CFI) ≥0.90, RMSEA ≤0.08 (structural validity)
 • Discriminant validity: average variance extracted (AVE) ≥0.50 per factor,
   inter-factor correlations ≤0.85Predictive validity metrics:
 • ΔR² in binary retention (logistic regression) and continuous usage (linear
   regression) compared to SUS, UEQ, and single-item intelligence rating- AUC
   for retention prediction (proposed instrument vs. alternatives)
 • Correlation matrix between instrument dimensions and automated NLG
   metricsComparison with automated evaluation:
 • Spearman correlation between each instrument dimension and GPT-as-judge
   scores (expected to be weak for emotional valence and trust dimensions,
   moderate for fluency)

Baselines1. System Usability Scale (SUS) — the most widely used general UX
instrument, adapted by rewording "system" to "conversational AI agent".

 2 User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ) —26 items across6 scales (Attractiveness,
   Perspicuity, Efficiency, Dependability, Stimulation, Novelty). Standard
   adaptation to conversational AI context.
 3 Single-item LLM Intelligence Rating — "On a scale of1–7, how intelligent did
   the model seem?" Matches the common "LLM-as-judge" paradigm but from the
   user's perspective.
 4 Automated NLG Metrics — Perplexity, BERTScore, Repetition Rate, Response
   Length, Distinct-N. Included to benchmark how much UX variance automated
   metrics already capture.

Ablations1. -TRUST: Omit the epistemic trust dimension from the instrument.
Measure loss in predictive power for retention and recommendation outcomes.
Tests whether trust is a separable and necessary construct or merely a correlate
of fluency.

 2 -EMOTION: Omit the emotional valence dimension. Tests whether affective
   response adds variance beyond cognitive appraisals (fluency, goal alignment).
   If predictive power does not drop, emotional valence may be redundant with
   satisfaction.
 3 -SINGLE-SESSION: Train and evaluate the predictive model on data from
   session1 only (no multi-session learning). Tests whether UX evaluations
   converge in a single interaction or require repeated exposure to stabilize.
 4 -BEHAVIORAL-ANCHORS: Replace behavioral-choice outcomes with
   hypothetical-intention items (e.g., "I would use this model again") as the
   dependent variable. Tests whether stated intentions predict actual behavior
   or are inflated by social desirability bias.

Expected Failure Modes1. Dimension collapse: Users may not distinguish between
perceived intelligence, trust, and satisfaction in practice (all load onto a
single "liking" factor). If EFA yields a single factor, the framework collapses
to a univariate measure and loses its claimed advantage over UEQ. Mitigation: if
this occurs, conduct a forced bifactor model to examine whether a general factor
dominates while specific factors still capture meaningful residual variance.

 2 Sequence effects dominate: Users' ratings in session2 may be driven primarily
   by contrast with the previous model rather than absolute experience. This
   would inflate variance and reduce test-retest reliability. Mitigation:
   counterbalance model order across participants and include order as a
   covariate in all regression models.
 3 Low retention base rate: If <20% of participants return for the2-week
   follow-up, retention becomes a near-constant with insufficient variation for
   logistic regression. Mitigation: oversample in the initial recruitment;
   target n=800 to account for35–40% attrition; pre-register a secondary
   continuous outcome (self-reported usage hours/week) as backup.
 4 Automated metrics already saturate UX prediction: If perplexity + BERTScore +
   repetition rate alone explain >50% of UX variance, the proposed instrument
   adds marginal value. This would itself be a significant negative result but
   weakens the paper's contribution. Mitigation: include ablation -AUTO that
   removes all automated metrics and tests whether the pure-instrument model
   still predicts retention.
 5 Social desirability bias inflates all self-report measures: Users may
   systematically over-report satisfaction for socially acceptable models (e.g.,
   GPT-4o, due to brand familiarity). This could create an artificial separation
   between proprietary and open-source models that reflects brand halo effects
   rather than UX. Mitigation: include a social desirability scale
   (Marlowe-Crowne short form) as a covariate; pre-register a sensitivity
   analysis without the proprietary model.
 6 Task heterogeneity obscures general factors: UX dimensions may factor
   differently by task type (emotional support → trust dominates; code
   generation → goal alignment dominates). If factor structure is non-invariant
   across tasks, a single unified instrument is invalid. Mitigation: test
   measurement invariance (configural, metric, scalar) across task types before
   pooling; if invariance fails, report task-specific subscales.

Limitations1. Self-selection bias: Participants who volunteer for a
multi-session LLM study are likely more tech-literate and positively disposed
toward AI than the general population. This limits generalizability to less
engaged or more skeptical user segments.

 2 Western-cultural instrument bias: Interview and validation samples will be
   predominantly English-speaking, likely drawn from MTurk/Prolific pools (US/UK
   demos). Emotional expression, trust calibration, and conversational norms
   vary significantly across cultures; the resulting instrument may not be
   cross-culturally invariant without substantial adaptation.
 3 Model obsolescence: The three target models represent a snapshot from
   early2025. As capabilities advance at a rapid pace, absolute UX scores will
   shift, and dimensions that matter today (e.g., factual accuracy concern) may
   become less salient while new dimensions (e.g., personalization depth,
   long-term memory) emerge. The framework's dimensionality should be
   re-validated annually.
 4 No ground truth for UX: Unlike classification accuracy, there is no objective
   "correct" UX score. All validation is necessarily relative (predicting
   downstream behavior). Behavioral outcomes (retention, referral) are
   themselves confounded by model pricing, API latency, brand preference, and
   contextual factors outside the interaction. The framework predicts user
   behavior, not an objective ground truth.
 5 Controlled tasks vs. naturalistic use: The five scripted tasks constrain
   interaction in ways that may not reflect how users actually engage with LLMs.
   Real-world use is self-directed, often interleaved with other activities, and
   varies in goal specificity. Ecological validity is traded for experimental
   control and cross-model comparability.
 6 No longitudinal calibration beyond2 weeks: Retention at2 weeks captures
   early-adoption patterns but does not measure long-term habituation,
   disenchantment, or skill development (users learning to prompt better over
   time). A longer horizon (3–6 months) may reveal different UX dynamics not
   captured here.

Research Proposal: Systematic Comparison of UX Evaluation Methods for LLM-Based
Conversational Agents## Title
Evaluating the Evaluators: A Comparative Study of
User Experience Assessment Methods for LLM-Based Conversational Agents

Problem
User experience (UX) evaluation for LLM-based conversational agents lacks
a validated, standardized methodology. Researchers and practitioners currently
rely on ad-hoc combinations of:

• General-purpose UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ, QUIS) designed for traditional
software- Behavioral proxies (task completion rate, response time) that may
miss novel failure modes like hallucination or sycophancy- Emerging
"LLM-as-judge" automated evaluation, which has unknown validity as a UX
proxyNo published work systematically compares these approaches on the same
set of LLM interactions, making it impossible to know which method (or
combination) best captures perceived quality, trust, and satisfaction — the
core dimensions of LLM UX.

Hypothesis1. Primary: Standardized UX questionnaires (SUS, UEQ) exhibit
moderate-to-weak correlation with task-level behavioral metrics (completion
rate, time-on-task, repair frequency) when applied to LLM interactions, because
LLM failures (plausible-sounding errors) differ qualitatively from GUI failures.

2 Secondary: An LLM-as-judge evaluator fine-tuned on human UX ratings can
approximate mean UEQ scores within ±0.5 scale points across a held-out set of
interaction scenarios, but will fail systematically on specific failure types
(hallucination, refusal, sycophancy) that require human judgment.
3 Tertiary: A composite evaluation combining behavioral metrics + a short
(3-item) custom UX scale achieves higher test-retest reliability (ICC >0.75)
than any single method alone.

Method
A controlled within-subjects experiment with three UX evaluation
conditions applied to the same set of24 prerecorded LLM interaction sessions:

Interaction Sessions (Stimuli)

24 sessions crossing:

• 2 LLMs: GPT-4o, Llama3.170B- 3 task types: factual QA, creative writing,
decision-making/planning- 4 output quality levels (validated by expert
raters): correct + fluent, correct but verbose, fluent but incorrect
(hallucination), incoherentEach session is a3–5 turn interaction shown as a
recorded transcript + final output.

Evaluation Conditions (Independent Variable)

1 Standardized questionnaires: SUS (10 items), UEQ (26 items), and a3-item
custom LLM-UX scale (satisfaction, trust, output quality) administered after
each session.
2 Behavioral metrics: Task completion (binary), time-on-task, number of user
repairs/rewrites, confidence-rated correctness (user-reported) — collected
during interaction.
3 LLM-as-judge: An LLM (same models under test + a held-out judge model)
prompted to rate each session on the same3-item LLM-UX scale, given system
prompt templates from Zheng et al. (2024).

Procedure-60 participants (power analysis: within-subjects,24 sessions, α =0.05,
β =0.80 → n ≥48 for medium effect)

• Each participant rated12 sessions via questionnaires and12 sessions via
behavioral interaction recording + self-report- LLM-as-judge evaluated all24
sessions ×3 judge model variants- Randomize session and condition order###
Analysis- R1 (questionnaire vs behavioral): Spearman correlations between
SUS/UEQ scores and behavioral metrics; Bland-Altman plots for agreement- R2
(LLM-as-judge accuracy): MAE, Pearson r, and confusion matrices between LLM
ratings and human questionnaire scores; stratified error analysis by failure
type- R3 (composite): Intraclass correlation (ICC(2,1)) for each method and
the weighted composite; bootstrap CIs## Dataset / Benchmark
No existing
benchmark fully covers this. We construct and release LLM-UX-Eval-24, a
dataset of24 curated interaction sessions with:
• Transcripts and final outputs (JSON format)
• Expert-validated failure type labels (gold standard)
• Human UX ratings from10 pilot participants (for validation prior to main
study)
• Behavioral log templates for replicationSize:24 sessions ×60 participants
=1,440 human evaluation data points;24 ×3 judge models =72 LLM-as-judge
ratings.

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Convergent validity | Spearman ρ between methods | >0.5 for
same-construct pairs | | LLM-as-judge accuracy | MAE vs human mean | <0.5 (on1–5
scale) | | LLM-as-judge bias | Mean signed error per failure type | Report per
type | | Test-retest reliability | ICC(2,1) on20% repeated sessions | >0.70 | |
Composite reliability | ICC(2,1) of weighted composite | >0.75 | | Time cost |
Minutes per evaluation session | Report descriptive |

Baselines1. Single-method baselines: Each evaluation method (SUS, UEQ,
behavioral-only, LLM-as-judge) treated as the sole UX assessment — this is
current practice in published LLM evaluations.

2 GUI-trained UX norms: SUS and UEQ industry benchmarks (e.g., SUS mean =68)
used as-is without LLM-specific adaptation — the implicit default in most
current work.
3 Random judge: LLM-as-judge with shuffled labels as a lower-bound sanity check
for correlation significance.

Ablations1. Questionnaire length: Does UEQ (26 items) outperform the3-item
LLM-UX scale in discriminability? Remove UEQ data and re-fit models.

2 Judge model: Replace LLM judge with GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o — how much does
judge capability matter?
3 Prompt template: Test3 prompt variants (zero-shot, few-shot with2 examples,
expert-designed rubric) — is prompt engineering the dominant factor in
LLM-as-judge validity?
4 Task type: Remove one task type at a time — are effects driven by a specific
interaction type?

Expected Failure Modes1. Low between-method correlation: Questionnaires and
behavioral metrics may measure different latent constructs (perception vs.
performance), yielding weak ρ even if both are valid — this would invalidate the
composite approach but still be a useful finding (recommending both as separate
axes).

2 LLM-as-judge collapse: LLM ratings may cluster near the center (regression to
mean) or correlate only with surface features (output length, readability)
rather than substantive quality, rendering them useless as UX proxies. This
is the most likely failure mode based on prior LLM-as-judge critiques.
3 Carryover effects: Participants who rate via behavioral metrics first may
anchor expectations when later using questionnaires. Mitigated by
randomization and tested via period effect analysis.
4 Fatigue:12 sessions per participant may induce satisficing on later ratings.
Mitigated by capping sessions at12 (≈40 min total) and embedding attention
checks (repeated sessions with known scores).
5 Generalizability: All interactions use English text-only outputs. Findings
may not transfer to multimodal, voice, or non-English LLM interactions.
Stated explicitly as a limitation.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Subset Selection for Efficient LLM Leaderboards##
      TitleAdaptive Subset Selection for Cost-Efficient LLM Evaluation: A
                     Variance-Guided Leaderboard Framework

ProblemStatic LLM leaderboards such as HELM, Open LLM Leaderboard, and LMSys
Chatbot Arena evaluate every submitted model on the same fixed benchmark suite.
This approach has three critical inefficiencies. First, many benchmark items are
highly correlated — once a model passes a certain capability threshold, most
items within a category become redundant and contribute negligible
discrimination. Second, evaluation cost scales linearly with the number of items
and models, creating a bottleneck for small teams and rapid iteration cycles.
Third, leaderboard rankings are sensitive to item selection, yet current
selection strategies are either static (full suite) or heuristic (random
subsets), lacking principled guarantees on ranking fidelity. The central problem
is: how can we select a minimal subset of evaluation items per model that
preserves the global leaderboard ranking with high confidence?

HypothesisLeaderboard ranking can be preserved using only30–50% of the full
evaluation suite by adaptively selecting items per model based on item-level
variance and model-item interaction signals. Specifically, items with high
cross-model variance and low redundancy contribute disproportionate ranking
signal; selecting items where a model's performance is uncertain (near its
capability boundary) yields the most discriminative information per unit cost.
We hypothesize that an adaptive, variance-guided subset selection policy will
reproduce the full-suite ranking with Kendall τ ≥0.95 at ≤40% of the original
evaluation cost.

MethodWe propose AdaLead (Adaptive Leaderboard Evaluator), a three-component
framework:

 1 Item Profiling Phase. Given a seed set of ~50–100 diverse models and a
   benchmark suite of N items, compute for each item its cross-model variance,
   its pairwise redundancy (Spearman ρ with other items), and its "decision
   boundary density" — the fraction of model pairs whose relative ordering flips
   on this item versus the aggregate ranking. Items that are high-variance,
   low-redundancy, and high-boundary-density form a core discriminative set
   (~20% of N). This set is fixed and evaluated for every model.
 2 Adaptive Completion Phase. For each new model m, evaluate the core set first,
   then iteratively select additional items from the remaining pool. Selection
   is driven by an acquisition function that scores remaining items by: (a) how
   much adding the item would reduce the model's ranking uncertainty (measured
   as the width of the credible interval around its current rank), (b) how far
   the model's current partial score is from the nearest decision boundary
   (model pairs with close scores), and (c) a discount term for item redundancy
   with already-selected items. This is a greedy submodular optimization —
   equivalent to maximising a monotone submodular function with a cardinality
   constraint — and admits a (1−1/e) approximation guarantee.
 3 Stopping Criterion. Stop when adding any next item would not change the
   model's rank relative to any already-evaluated model, given a confidence
   threshold of95% (bootstrapped rank intervals). The total number of items
   evaluated per model is bounded by B_max, set to50% of the full suite, with
   the stopping criterion typically activating earlier.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe use three existing leaderboard frameworks:

 • Open LLM Leaderboard v2 (6 tasks, ~350 items): ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag,
   MMLU, TruthfulQA, Winogrande, GSM8K. Provides a mix of reasoning, knowledge,
   and safety items.
 • HELM-Mix (42 scenarios, ~1200 items): A broader cross-section including
   summarization, toxicity, disinformation, and fairness scenarios. Used for
   scalability stress-testing.
 • LMSys Chatbot Arena (human preference, ~100K pairwise votes): Used to
   validate that subset rankings correlate with human preference rankings,
   providing an external validity check.

All experiments use publicly available model outputs (cacheable from the HELM
and Open LLM Leaderboard repositories) to avoid re-running inference on every
model. We use150 models spanning1B–175B parameters, including open-weight and
API-based models, drawn from existing leaderboard submissions.

Evaluation Metrics1. Ranking fidelity: Kendall τ (primary) and Spearman ρ
between the AdaLead partial-suite ranking and the full-suite ranking. A τ ≥0.95
is the target success signal.

 2 Cost reduction: Average fraction of items evaluated per model (f_eval).
   Primary goal: f_eval ≤0.4.
 3 Rank error tolerance: Fraction of models misranked by more than k positions
   (k =1,3,5). Target: <5% misranked by >3 positions.
 4 Top-k hit rate: For the top-10 and bottom-10 ranked models, the proportion
   correctly identified by AdaLead.
 5 Robustness to model pool shifts: Measure rank fidelity when AdaLead is re-run
   with a random50% subset of the150 models (testing whether item selections
   overfit to the model pool).

Baselines1. Full-suite ranking — the ground truth; all items, all models.

 2 Random subset — for each model, randomly select k items (k matched to
   AdaLead's average per-model count). Repeated over10 seeds; mean and variance
   reported.
 3 Static hard subset — a fixed set of high-variance items (top30% by
   cross-model variance) applied uniformly to all models. This tests whether
   adaptivity adds value over a one-time selection.
 4 Item-wise greedy (no stopping) — AdaLead's adaptive selection without the
   early stopping criterion, using the same per-model budget as the full method.
   Ablates the stopping rule.
 5 Random + early stopping — random selection with AdaLead's stopping rule.
   Ablates the acquisition function.

Ablations (within AdaLead)

 1 −Variance (ablate item variance term): Acquisition uses only boundary-density
   and redundancy discount.
 2 −Boundary (ablate decision boundary density term): Acquisition uses only
   variance and redundancy discount.
 3 −Redundancy (ablate redundancy discount): Acquisition allows selecting
   near-duplicate items. Tests whether redundancy correction is necessary.
 4 −Adaptive (use fixed core + static top-up): Replace the per-model adaptive
   selection with core set + a fixed high-variance supplemental set. Tests
   whether per-model adaptivity matters.
 5 Different B_max (30%,40%,50%,60%): Sensitivity analysis on the maximum
   budget.

Expected Failure Modes1. Ranking collapse when the model pool is very
homogeneous. If all models are similarly capable (e.g., only LLama-3 variants),
variance across items drops and the acquisition function becomes noise-driven.
AdaLead may evaluate more items than budgeted or produce unstable rankings.
Mitigation: pre-cluster models by family and evaluate representative seeds per
cluster; flag homogeneous pools and issue a warning.

 2 Brittle stopping criterion when rank intervals are wide. If the model pool is
   very large (e.g.,150+ models), credible intervals around each model's rank
   may remain wide even after many items, preventing the stopping criterion from
   triggering. Mitigation: cap evaluation at B_max regardless; for large pools,
   use a hierarchical two-stage ranking (coarse grouping → fine ranking within
   groups).
 3 The core set overfits to the seed model pool. The item profiling phase uses a
   seed set of models that may not represent later-submitted models (e.g., seed
   set is dominated by strong models but new submissions are weak). Mitigation:
   periodically recompute the core set (every30 new models) and validate that
   the top-ranked core items remain high-variance on the growing pool.
 4 Redundancy estimation is sensitive to the Spearman threshold. Choosing the
   wrong threshold for "redundant" items (ρ >0.9 vs. ρ >0.8) changes the
   composition of the selected set. Mitigation: report sensitivity across three
   thresholds; select threshold via cross-validation within the seed set.
 5 Cost reduction is lower on benchmarks with many near-independent items. If
   every item measures a distinct capability (e.g., HELM-Mix), redundancy is low
   and f_eval may approach40–50% rather than30%. Mitigation: report cost
   reduction per benchmark separately; the method still reduces cost versus full
   evaluation even at50%.

Limitations1. Offline evaluation only. This proposal evaluates AdaLead on
existing model output traces. It does not address the online setting where
models arrive sequentially and the pool evolves. Extending to an online,
continuously updated leaderboard is left to future work.

 2 Dependence on a representative seed set. The item profiling phase requires a
   diverse seed set of50–100 models. For new benchmarks with few submissions,
   the core set may not be informative. In such settings, AdaLead degrades to
   the static hard-subset baseline.
 3 No coverage guarantee for rare capabilities. Items that only a few models can
   solve (e.g., a very difficult reasoning question) will have low cross-model
   variance and may be excluded. If these items capture a dimension stakeholders
   care about, the leaderboard may miss that dimension. AdaLead optimises for
   ranking fidelity, not comprehensive capability coverage.
 4 Bootstrapped rank intervals assume i.i.d. items. Items within a benchmark are
   not independent (e.g., multiple MMLU questions on chemistry). This may shrink
   credible intervals artificially. We use a block bootstrap (clustering by
   benchmark scenario) to partially address this, but residual within-scenario
   dependence remains.
 5 Human preference alignment is tested but not used directly. The LMSys
   validation shows correlation with human preferences but AdaLead does not
   incorporate human-item difficulty ratings. Incorporating human-provided item
   difficulty as a prior could further improve selection.

  Proposal: Decomposing Diversity — A Multi-Axis Evaluation Framework for Text
    Generation## ProblemDiversity in text generation is widely recognized as
    essential for natural, non-degenerate output, yet the community lacks a
 principled evaluation methodology. Existing metrics each capture only a narrow
   facet: Distinct-n (Li et al.,2016) measures token-level uniqueness but is
    confounded by length and ignores semantics; Self-BLEU (Zhu et al.,2018)
  quantifies intra-corpus n-gram overlap but conflates quality with diversity;
  entropy-based measures (Zhang et al.,2021) are distributional at the corpus
level and provide no instance- or facet-level signal; embedding-based diversity
(e.g., mean pairwise cosine distance) is sensitive to the choice of encoder and
    to semantic drift in long-form generation; and repetition-aware metrics
 (Holtzman et al.,2020; Fu et al.,2021) focus on degeneration modes rather than
                              positive diversity.

The consequence is a fragmented evaluation landscape: a method that improves
Distinct-4 may degrade Self-BLEU; a model with high embedding diversity may be
semantically incoherent. Researchers select the metric that flatters their
method, and reviewers have no shared standard for evaluating diversity claims.
Meta-evaluation studies (e.g., Pillutla et al.,2021; Tevet & Berant,2021) have
shown that existing diversity metrics correlate poorly with each other and with
human judgments, but no prior work proposes a unified, validated framework that
disambiguates failure modes.

Open question: Can diversity be decomposed into interpretable, independently
measurable axes that collectively explain human judgments of text diversity, and
can those axes be validated against a controlled benchmark?

HypothesisText diversity is not a monolithic property but decomposes into four
weakly correlated axes — lexical, syntactic, semantic, and structural — each of
which can be quantified by a targeted metric. A multi-axis evaluation framework
that reports all four dimensions separately will (a) reveal failure modes that
monolithic metrics mask, (b) correlate more strongly with fine-grained human
diversity judgments than any single existing metric, and (c) enable researchers
to identify which kind of diversity their method improves or degrades.

MethodWe propose Div4 (Diversity in Four Dimensions), an evaluation framework
that decomposes text diversity into four axes and provides a standardized
reporting protocol.

Axis definitions| Axis | What it measures | Operationalization |

|---|---|---| | Lexical | Rare and varied vocabulary use beyond stopwords |
Type-token ratio on content words after length normalization (slope-corrected
TTR); distinct-1/2/3 with corpus-level z-score normalization | | Syntactic |
Variation in syntactic structures | Tree-depth entropy over constituency parses
(Kitaev & Klein,2018); POS-tag bigram entropy; dependency-arc length variance |
| Semantic | Coverage of distinct meanings and topics | Mean pairwise cosine
distance over Sentence-BERT (Reimers & Gurevych,2019) embeddings, corrected for
semantic drift via centroid estimation; number of distinct nearest-neighbor
clusters in a reference embedding space | | Structural | Variation in
discourse-level organization (length, paragraph breaks, repetition patterns) |
Self-BLEU at corpus level; block-repeat frequency (contiguous n-gram
re-occurrence within a window); Gini coefficient of sentence-length distribution
|

Reporting protocolFor each evaluation set, the framework produces a Div4 profile
— a four-element vector with each axis score normalized to [0,1] against a
reference corpus of human-written text in the same domain. The protocol also
reports two aggregate diagnostics:

 • Diversity gap vector: (human_axis_score − model_axis_score) per axis,
   identifying which dimensions the model underperforms on.
 • Collapse indicator: a binary flag set to1 if any axis falls below the5th
   percentile of the human reference distribution.

Meta-validation designTo validate the framework, we construct a controlled
diversity benchmark where we systematically modulate each diversity axis
independently and measure whether Div4 detects the modulation while the other
three axes remain stable.

 1 Lexical modulation: Replace content words in a held-out set of human-written
   texts via WordNet synonym substitution with controlled frequency bins (rare →
   rare; rare → common; common → rare; common → common). The lexical axis should
   drop significantly only when rare words are replaced by common words.
 2 Syntactic modulation: Parse each sentence into a constituency tree, then
   flatten subtrees (reducing depth) or reorder constituents via a controlled
   permutation. The syntactic axis should detect depth reduction while lexical
   and semantic axes remain stable.
 3 Semantic modulation: Replace noun phrases with hypernyms (moving toward
   abstract/generic) or hyponyms (moving toward specific/fine-grained). The
   semantic axis should reflect reduced semantic coverage.
 4 Structural modulation: Duplicate random sentences within texts at controlled
   rates (10%–50% duplication). The structural axis should capture increased
   redundancy while lexical and semantic axes change minimally.

Each modulation condition is applied at three intensity levels (1×,2×,4× the
minimum detectable change) and validated by human annotators (Amazon Mechanical
Turk, N =200 per condition,3 judgments per item) to confirm the intended
perceptual effect.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe evaluate on four generation tasks spanning different
diversity regimes:

 Task                Dataset             Sample size         profile
 Open-ended story    WritingPrompts      2,000 prompts,5     High lexical, high
 generation          (Fan et al.,2018)   generations per     semantic
                                         model per prompt
 Dialogue response   PersonaChat (Zhang  1,000 contexts,5    Moderate lexical,
 generation          et al.,2018)        responses per       high structural

Div4 identifies which kind of diversity is deficient and reports axis-level

semantic from structural failure modes. Unlike existing meta-evaluations that
merely correlate metrics, Div4 provides a validated protocol with controlled
modulation experiments.

Research Proposal: Evaluating Context-Appropriate Diversity in Neural Text
Generation## Title
CoDE: A Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation Framework for
Open-Ended Text Generation

Problem
Existing diversity metrics for text generation (Distinct-n, Self-BLEU,
Entropy-5, TTR) all share a fundamental flaw: they measure diversity as a single
scalar aggregated over a corpus, independent of the input context. This means:

• A model that generates the same generic response to every prompt can score
high on diversity if responses differ across prompts (high inter-prompt
diversity) while being pathologically repetitive within each response (low
intra-prompt diversity).
• A factual QA model that should produce low-variance answers is punished for
being "not diverse."
• There is no established way to distinguish appropriate diversity (multiple
valid paraphrases of the same meaning) from inappropriate diversity
(hallucinated facts or topic drift).

The central gap is that diversity is not a single target to maximize—it is a
distributional property that should match the conditional distribution implied
by the input.

Hypothesis
Diversity in text generation can be decomposed into two orthogonal
components—intra-response diversity (variety within a single generated text) and
inter-response diversity (variety across generations for the same input, i.e.,
model stochasticity)—and each has a context-dependent expected range that can be
estimated from the training data or human references. A model whose diversity
falls outside this expected range (too high or too low) is exhibiting a failure
mode that existing aggregate metrics miss.

Method
CoDE (Context-Dependent Diversity Evaluation) proceeds in three stages:

1 Reference-conditional diversity calibration. For each input context in the
evaluation set, collect a set of human-written references (≥5 per context).
Compute per-context diversity statistics on the references to establish an
expected diversity interval per context and per diversity facet. Facets
include:

• Lexical diversity: Distinct-1, Distinct-2, corrected TTR (Herdan's TTR)
• Structural diversity: syntactic tree depth variance, POS tag entropy -
Semantic diversity: pairwise sentence-BERT cosine variance among candidate
generations for the same prompt2. Within-vs-across response decomposition.
For each model under evaluation, generate K responses per prompt (K ≥10).
Compute:
• Intra-response diversity: averaged per-response metrics (e.g., average
Self-BLEU of a response against itself in sliding windows)
• Inter-response diversity: diversity across the K generations for the same
prompt (e.g., pairwise BERTScore variance, corpus-level Distinct-n across
generations)

3 Deviation scoring. For each (model, prompt, facet) triple, measure the signed
deviation of the model's diversity from the human-established interval:

• Deviation ∈ [−1, +1] where negative = under-diverse (more repetitive than
humans), positive = over-diverse (more varied than humans, potentially
hallucinatory)
• Aggregate: mean absolute deviation across facets = CoDE score (lower is
better)

Dataset / Benchmark
Construct a multi-domain diversity benchmark spanning
contexts with intrinsically different diversity expectations:

Domain                    Expected diversity        Rationale
Factoid QA (SQuAD2.0,     Low inter + low intra     One correct answer, short
TriviaQA)
Story generation          High intra, moderate      One narrative, varied
(WritingPrompts,          inter                     style
ROCStories)
Data-to-text (WebNLG,     Low intra, moderate       Fixed facts, varied
E2E NLG)                  inter                     surface form
Open-ended dialogue       High intra + high inter   Many valid turns
(PersonaChat,
DailyDialog)
Creative continuation     High intra + high inter   Many valid completions
(Story Cloze, CommonGen)

Sample500 prompts per domain (2,500 total) with ≥5 human references each.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary metric: CoDE score (mean absolute deviation from
the human diversity interval across all facets and domains).

2 Secondary metrics: Breakdown by facet (lexical, structural, semantic) and by
domain.
3 Validation metric: Correlation with human judgment of "appropriate diversity"
(Likert1–5) on a held-out set of200 (model, prompt, response) triples rated
by ≥3 annotators. Target: Spearman ρ ≥0.6 against the CoDE score.

Baselines| Baseline | What it measures | Expected limitation |

|---|---|---| | Distinct-1 / Distinct-2 | Surface n-gram novelty | No context
conditioning, length-biased | | Self-BLEU | Intra-corpus n-gram overlap | Single
scalar, no per-context or per-facet breakdown | | Entropy-5 / Entropy-n | n-gram
distribution uniformity | Ignores semantic and structural diversity | | Zipf
coefficient | Frequency-rank distribution fit | Only describes the tail;
insensitive to local repetition | | vMeasure (Hashimoto et al.,2019) |
Cluster-conditional diversity | Requires latent cluster assignments; not
natively context-conditional | | MAUVE (Pillutla et al.,2021) | Divergence
between model and human output distributions | Measures distribution matching,
not per-response diversity |

Ablations1. Reference-count ablation: Vary the number of human references per
prompt from1 to20. Hypothesis: the CoDE score stabilizes at ≥5 references.

2 Facet ablation: Remove each facet one at a time and measure correlation drop
with human judgment. Identifies which facet contributes most signal.
3 Pooling ablation: Replace per-prompt intervals with corpus-level intervals
(the current default in the field). Hypothesis: the per-prompt decomposition
is the main source of improvement.
4 Generation count ablation: Vary K (number of generations per prompt) from2
to50. Identifies the minimum K for stable inter-response estimates.
5 Metric-level baselines: Replace the deviation formulation with a simple
average of existing metrics conditioned on nothing. Measures the marginal
gain of context-conditional calibration.

Expected Failure Modes1. Reference quality collapse. If human references are
themselves low-quality or inconsistently diverse (e.g., crowd workers producing
minimal-effort responses), the "expected interval" becomes meaningless.
Mitigation: filter references via an automatic quality check (e.g., minimum
length, minimum Distinct-1 >0) and exclude outlying prompts where
inter-reference variance is >2σ from the domain mean.

2 Metric saturation on long-form generation. For very long generations (stories
>500 tokens), intra-response lexical diversity may saturate (all models
approach the same high Distinct-n), making the lexical facet uninformative.
Mitigation: use sliding-window diversity (window =100 tokens) and report the
minimum window diversity, not the aggregate, to capture local repetition that
longer texts hide.
3 Semantic diversity metric conflates quality with diversity. Sentence-BERT
variance could be high simply because generations are incoherent rather than
genuinely diverse. Mitigation: compute semantic diversity only over
generations that pass a minimum fluency/coherence threshold (e.g., perplexity
< a domain-specific cutoff). Flag the model's quality-diversity trade-off
explicitly as a secondary diagnostic.
4 Domain boundary ambiguity. The "expected diversity" for an ambiguous prompt
(e.g., a news headline that could be either factual or editorial) may not
fall cleanly into one domain bin. Mitigation: report per-prompt deviations
rather than only domain aggregates, and provide prompt-level visualization
for outlier analysis.
5 Inter-response diversity is confounded by sampling temperature. A model run
at temperature1.0 will naturally produce more inter-response variation than
at temperature0.1. The CoDE score must hold sampling hyperparameters fixed
across all models, or the benchmark becomes a comparison of sampling
strategies rather than model architectures. Mitigation: standardize to
temperature =0.7, top-p =0.9 for all models, and include a sensitivity
experiment reporting how CoDE changes with temperature.
