Title: Fair, Calibrated, and Distribution-Aware AI-Generated Text Detection: A
Multi-Stage Framework for False Positive MitigationProblem

Commercial AI content detectors (GPTZero, Originality.ai, Turnitin) and research
detectors (DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars) achieve high recall on
in-distribution machine-generated text but suffer from systematically elevated
false positive rates on specific human-authored subpopulations — non-native
English writing, neurodivergent prose, highly templatic genres (technical
documentation, legal filings, structured reviews), and text that has undergone
light post-processing (e.g., grammar correction tools). Reported false positive
rates on these groups range from15–40% in independent audits, producing real
harm: false accusations of academic dishonesty, demonetization of legitimate
creators, and erosion of trust in detection tools. The core challenge is not
merely increasing classifier sensitivity to machine text, but doing so without
sacrificing specificity on the long tail of legitimate human variation.

Hypothesis

A multi-stage detection pipeline that (i) calibrates confidence scores using a
linguistically-stratified human validation set, (ii) replaces hard binary
thresholds with conformal prediction sets that abstain on ambiguous inputs, and
(iii) explicitly models distribution shift between training and deployment human
text can reduce false positives by ≥50% relative to current single-threshold
detectors while maintaining recall ≥90% at a calibrated operating point. The
central claim is that false positives arise primarily from a mismatch between
the narrow human-language distribution seen during training and the broader
distribution encountered at inference — and that explicit modeling of this
mismatch is more effective than simply tuning the detection threshold.

Method

The framework operates in three sequential stages, with shared feature
extraction:

Stage1 — Feature Extraction. For each input text, compute four features from a
frozen surrogate language model (LLaMA-2-7B, no fine-tuning): (a) mean per-token
log-probability (surprisal), (b) per-sentence log-probability variance
(burstiness), (c) rank of the true token in the model's top-k distribution
averaged across positions (log-rank), and (d) the ratio of low-probability
tokens (<0.01) to total tokens (tail-ratio). These four features form a4-d
embedding.

Stage2 — Uncertainty-Aware Classification with Conformal Prediction. Train a
lightweight classifier (gradient-boosted trees, not a neural network — to
preserve interpretability and avoid distribution shift between training and
inference) on the4-d embeddings of a mixed human–machine corpus. Rather than
outputting a single label, the classifier produces a conformal prediction set:
for a user-specified coverage level (e.g.,90%), the set either contains exactly
one label ("Human" or "Machine"), both labels (ambiguous — abstain), or neither
(OOD — flag for manual review). The conformal calibration is performed on a
linguistically-stratified holdout set that oversamples the high-FPR
subpopulations listed in the problem statement.

Stage3 — Distribution-Shift Detection. For inputs where the prediction set
contains a single label but the classifier's raw confidence is below a secondary
threshold (chosen to maximize precision on a validation shift set), compute the
Mahalanobis distance from the input's4-d embedding to the training human-class
embedding centroid. If this distance exceeds the95th percentile of distances
observed in the calibration set, the input is downgraded from a binary
prediction to "abstain — likely distribution shift." This catches human text
that lies far from the training distribution without requiring retraining on
every new domain.

Training data. Use HC3 (human–ChatGPT comparison) as the primary training corpus
for the human and machine classes. Augment with M4 (multi-model, multi-domain
machine text) to broaden the machine class to include outputs from GPT-4,
Claude, Llama, and Gemini across five domains (news, creative writing, code,
scientific abstracts, social media). The human side is augmented with the TOEFL
essay corpus (non-native English) and Amazon review data (templatic writing) to
explicitly cover high-FPR subpopulations. Final training set: ~500K examples
(250K human,250K machine, balanced). Calibration set:50K examples stratified by
linguistically-defined subgroups (native, non-native, templatic, creative,
technical).

Dataset and Benchmark

Evaluate on RAID (Robust AI Detection benchmark,11 domains ×11 model families ×
multiple adversarial perturbations), supplemented with a constructed Adversarial
Human Corpus of5,000 human-written texts specifically designed to resemble
machine output (e.g., text written to a formulaic prompt, repetitive structures,
very low surprisal). Also construct a Coverage Stress Set from existing human
corpora:1,000 texts from each of four high-FPR subpopulations (non-native
English essays from TOEFL, autistic-authored blog text, templatic Amazon
reviews, and highly edited academic prose).

Evaluation Metrics


 Metric                            Rationale
 FPR@Recall=90%                    Primary metric — false positives at an
                                   operating point where90% of machine text is
                                   caught
 AUPRC (Human class)               Captures precision–recall trade-off on the
                                   human class specifically (not the usual
                                   machine-class AUPRC)
 Abstain Rate                      Fraction of inputs that receive no
                                   prediction; must stay below15% to be
                                   practical
 Coverage Efficiency               Average size of conformal prediction sets
                                   (target: modal size =1)
 Expected Calibration Error (ECE)  On the human-class probability, binned by10
                                   percentile intervals
 Detection Gap                     FPR difference between the highest-FPR
                                   subgroup and the overall FPR — quantifies
                                   fairness


Baselines

 1 DetectGPT — zero-shot curvature-based detection (Mitchell et al.,2023)
 2 Fast-DetectGPT — conditional probability curvature approximation (Bao et
   al.,2024)
 3 Binoculars — cross-model surprisal ratio (Büchmann et al.,2024)
 4 GPTZero — commercial baseline (perplexity + burstiness threshold)
 5 Single-Stage XGBoost — identical feature set as the proposed method but with
   a single hard threshold and no conformal or shift components (serves as a
   direct ablation baseline)
 6 Logistic Regression + Calibration — Platt-scaled logistic regression on the
   same4-d features, with no distribution-shift handlingEach baseline is
   evaluated at its default threshold and at a threshold adjusted to match90%
   recall on the main test set.

Ablations


 Ablation                  Modification              What It Isolates
 A1 — No Calibration       Remove Stage2 conformal   Value of principled
                           prediction; replace with  uncertainty quantification
                           a hard threshold on raw   vs. arbitrary thresholding
                           classifier score
 A2 — No                   Remove Stage3; output     Contribution of modeling
 Distribution-Shift        conformal sets directly   distribution shift beyond
 Detection                                           conformal abstention
 A3 — Homogeneous          Stratify the calibration  Whether targeted subgroup
 Calibration               set uniformly rather      calibration drives the
                           than oversampling         improvement or simply more
                           high-FPR subgroups        calibration data
 A4 — Neural Classifier    Replace gradient-boosted  Interaction between
                           trees in Stage2 with      classifier complexity and
                           a2-layer MLP              conformal calibration
                                                     stability


All ablations are evaluated on the full benchmark suite with three random seeds.

Expected Failure Modes

 1 Adversarial human text. A speaker deliberately mimicking machine-like
   patterns (high fluency, low variance, predictable token choices) may trigger
   the distribution-shift detector in Stage3 or fall inside the machine
   conformal set. This is an inherent limitation of any detector that relies on
   statistical signatures — we do not claim adversarial hardness, only
   robustness against natural distribution shift.
 2 Domain shift beyond calibration scope. If deployment text comes from an
   unobserved domain (e.g., low-resource language poetry, highly specialized
   medical jargon), both the conformal sets and the Mahalanobis distance may
   fail. The framework is designed to detect this failure (via large conformal
   sets or OOD flags) rather than handle it gracefully.
 3 Calibration set contamination. If the linguistically-stratified calibration
   set is too small per stratum (<500 examples per subgroup), subgroup-specific
   coverage may be mis-estimated, leading to uneven FPR reduction across groups.
 4 Feature saturation. The four features (surprisal, burstiness, log-rank,
   tail-ratio) are well-studied but may be jointly insufficient for a
   low-dimensional separator as detection models continue to improve. The
   framework can accept additional features without architectural changes, but
   this is not tested here.

Limitations

 • English-only evaluation. All training and test corpora are English.
   Multilingual generalization is not claimed and would require re-calibration
   on per-language conformal sets.
 • Fixed surrogate model. LLaMA-2-7B is used for feature extraction; a different
   surrogate may shift the feature space and require recalibration. The
   framework is not surrogate-agnostic.
 • No adversarial training. The detection pipeline is static — it does not
   incorporate adversarial examples during training. A motivated adversary with
   access to the detection pipeline could craft bypasses.
 • Synthetic data realism gap. The M4 corpus provides broad model coverage but
   is generated from fixed prompts; real-world machine text may include
   iterative human editing, partial regeneration, and hybrid authorship that the
   training distribution does not capture.
 • Computational cost ceiling. Conformal prediction requires a held calibration
   set and per-input forward passes through a language model (Stage1) plus tree
   ensemble inference (Stage2). Latency per input is ~2–5 seconds on consumer
   hardware, which may be prohibitive for real-time classroom proctoring but
   acceptable for asynchronous batch screening.
 • Abstain cost. The framework prefers abstention over confident error, which
   means operators receive "no decision" on up to15% of inputs. In deployment
   contexts that require a binary decision for every input, the abstain flag
   transfers the burden to human reviewers rather than eliminating it.

Research Proposal: Robust AI-Generated Content Detection via
Adversarially-Calibrated Uncertainty Estimation (R-ACE)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title
R-ACE: Reducing False Positives in AI-Generated Content Detection through
Uncertainty-Aware Calibration and Adversarial Human Text

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current AI-generated text detectors (e.g., GPTZero, OpenAI Classifier,
DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT) achieve high accuracy on held-out test sets, but
suffer from asymmetric error rates: false positive rates (FPR) of5–30% on
human-written text, especially text that is factual, formulaic, or edited by
non-native speakers. This makes them unreliable for high-stakes deployment
(academic integrity, content moderation, misinformation tracking). The core
problem is that detectors are calibrated on machine vs. human distinctions from
static benchmarks but fail under distribution shift toward the "hard decision
boundary" — text that is highly structured, low-perplexity, or edited to mimic
machine output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
False positives arise because detectors conflate "low perplexity /
high predictability" with "machine-origin." Human-written text with low
token-level surprisal (technical writing, legal text, edited prose) occupies the
same region of the detector's latent space as AI-generated text.

Specifically: Training an AI-content detector with an explicit uncertainty head
and calibrating it on a stratified mix of naturally-occurring human text and
adversarially-perturbed human text (designed to mimic AI output patterns) will
reduce FPR@95%TPR by at least40% relative to the current state of the art,
without degrading true positive rate on genuine AI text.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose a three-component architecture:

1 Base feature extractor: A frozen pre-trained LLM (e.g., Llama-3-8B) that
computes per-token log-likelihoods and hidden state representations — the
same backbone used by Fast-DetectGPT.
2 Uncertainty-aware detection head: Instead of a deterministic classifier,
train a deep evidential regression head (Amini et al.,2020) that outputs both
a machine-likelihood score and an epistemic uncertainty estimate. This
enables the model to abstain or down-weight predictions on inputs far from
the training distribution.
3 Adversarial human text augmentation: Construct a calibration dataset by
taking human-written text (from domains known to trigger false positives —
see Dataset) and applying minimal edits that push it toward the machine-text
region:

• Reduce token-level perplexity via greedy truncation of rare tokens - Insert
formulaic transition phrases common in LLM output - Apply "LLM-rewriting"
(GPT-4o-mini instructed to preserve meaning but "make this text look more
like it was written by an AI")

This creates a controlled set of near-boundary negative examples.

Inference procedure: Given input text, compute the machine-likelihood score with
uncertainty interval. Flag as AI-generated only if (a) the score exceeds the
decision threshold and (b) the epistemic uncertainty is below a second
threshold. Otherwise, classify as "uncertain / likely human."

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Source | Size (docs) |

|-------|--------|-------------| | Train: human | C4 (filtered), Wikipedia,
legal contracts, arXiv papers |50,000 | | Train: AI | Machine-Generated Text
(MGT) from GPT-4o, Llama-3, Claude-3.5 |50,000 | | Calibration: adversarial
human | Human text from above + adversarial edits (Per-Method) |10,000 | | Test:
standard | HC3, M4, RAID (held-out) — balanced human/AI |10,000 | | Test: hard
FPR set | Human-written: non-native English essays (TOEFL corpus), PubMed
abstracts, SEC filings, Wikipedia stubs |5,000 |

Key benchmark addition: The "hard FPR set" deliberately collects domains where
current detectors fail. We will release this as a public stress-test suite.

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: False Positive Rate at95% True Positive Rate
(FPR@95%TPR) — measures false alarms at a fixed recall level2. Secondary: Area
Under ROC Curve (AUROC), Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC)

3 Calibration: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on the machine-likelihood
score, separately computed for human and AI subsets4. Abstention quality:
Fraction of human text flagged as "uncertain" (target: ≤5% on standard test,
≤15% on hard FPR set)
4 Robustness: Performance under domain shift (evaluate on held-out domains not
seen in training)

Baselines| Baseline | Key Idea |

|----------|----------| | DetectGPT (Mitchell et al.,2023) | Curvature-based
detection via perturbation | | Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al.,2024) | Conditional
probability curvature (faster variant) | | Ghostbuster (Verma et al.,2024) |
Feature-based classifier on perturbed texts | | Binoculars (Hans et al.,2024) |
Cross-model perplexity ratio | | OpenAI AI Classifier (2023) | Fine-tuned
RoBERTa (retrospective; API-based) | | DeepEvidential baseline | Same
architecture as ours without adversarial human augmentation |

All baselines are re-run on our evaluation suite with their published
hyperparameters.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | What it tests |

|----------|---------------| | No uncertainty head | Deterministic classifier
only → value of the evidential component | | No adversarial augmentation | Train
only on natural human/AI splits → value of hard negatives | | Perplexity-only
threshold | Replace learned classifier with a p(x) cutoff → value of learned
features | | Single-threshold inference | Remove the uncertainty-based
abstention rule → value of two-threshold inference | | Different base LLM | Swap
Llama-3-8B for GPT-NeoX-20B → sensitivity to backbone |

Each ablation is evaluated on the same metrics above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Domain mismatch still dominates: The hard FPR set may
still be too broad. If adversarial augmentation only covers specific failure
modes, FPR may improve on the calibration domains but not generalize to unseen
low-perplexity domains (e.g., poetry, legal boilerplate from a jurisdiction not
in training).

2 Uncertainty head over-abstains: The epistemic uncertainty threshold may be
too conservative, flagging many genuine AI texts as "uncertain" and reducing
the usable detection rate. This creates a precision/coverage tradeoff that
deployment may reject.
3 Adversarial edits create detectable artifacts: The procedure for generating
adversarial human text may introduce n-gram or stylistic artifacts
(repetition patterns, specific transition phrases) that the classifier learns
as spurious features, causing it to fail on unmodified human text from the
same domains.

uncertainties due to the high-dimensional, non-i.i.d. nature of the input
distribution. The uncertainty estimates may not reflect true epistemic
uncertainty, just variations in training density.
5 Computational cost: The two-threshold inference and deep evidential head add
~2× inference overhead vs. Fast-DetectGPT, which may be prohibitive for
real-time detection at scale.
6 Adversarial human text boundaries are unclear: There is no principled way to
define "how much editing makes human text look like AI text." The boundary is
inherently continuous, and the augmentation procedure may be hard to
reproduce across labs.

Adversarial Instruction Tunneling: Exploiting Multi-Turn Context Persistence in
 Code LLMs## ProblemCode Large Language Models are deployed in safety-critical
     software pipelines — automated code review, vulnerability repair, test
generation, and even autonomous program synthesis. Current red-teaming research
largely treats adversarial attacks as single-turn problems: a prompt is crafted,
a harmful output is elicited, and the attack either succeeds or fails. However,
   real-world integrations (Copilot plugin, Cursor agent, SWE-agent) maintain
 persistent context across multiple turns, with earlier turns influencing later
code generation. This creates an underexplored attack surface: an adversary can
  "tunnel" a harmful objective through a sequence of apparently benign turns,
where no single turn triggers the model's safety guardrails, but the accumulated
    context steers the final generation toward vulnerable or malicious code.

The problem is not merely that multi-turn attacks exist — it is that current
alignment benchmarks evaluate models with no notion of sustained adversarial
pressure. A model that passes single-shot rejections on "Write a buffer
overflow" may still generate the same exploit when the instruction is fragmented
across a conversation. The gap is methodological: we lack datasets, metrics, and
taxonomies for this class of attack.

HypothesisCode LLMs that exhibit strong single-turn refusal behavior can be
reliably induced to generate exploitable code through a multi-turn instruction
tunneling attack — a sequence of causally linked sub-instructions, each
individually benign, whose accumulated conversational context reconstructs a
forbidden objective that the model would have rejected if presented in a single
turn. The attack success rate correlates with context window size and is
substantially harder to defend against than single-turn jailbreaks, because each
turn passes the model's per-turn safety filters.

MethodWe propose a three-component method for generating and evaluating
instruction-tunneling attacks.

Attack Taxonomy. We define three tunneling strategies, each exploiting a
different property of multi-turn contexts:

 1 Decomposition tunneling. The adversary splits a forbidden code-generation
   task into N sub-tasks, each independently permissible (e.g., "Write a
   function that allocates a256-byte buffer" → "Write a function that copies
   user input into that buffer without checking length" → "Call the two
   functions together in a network server that reads from a socket"). No single
   turn violates safety policy; the final composition does.
 2 Gradual relaxation tunneling. The adversary starts with a strict, safe
   specification and iteratively requests relaxations across turns (e.g., "Write
   a SQL query builder that uses parameterized queries" → "Relax the
   parameterization — allow raw string concatenation for legacy tables" →
   "Remove the allowlist entirely; trust admin input"). Each individual
   relaxation request appears legitimate.
 3 Distractor-chain tunneling. The adversary buries the critical unsafe
   instruction inside a long sequence of syntactically similar but safe
   requests, exploiting recency bias and context saturation. The model's
   attention dilutes across many similar turns, and the final harmful request
   slips through because it pattern-matches earlier safe requests.

Attack Generation Pipeline. We build an automated tunneler: given a forbidden
code target T (e.g., "generate a command-injection-vulnerable PHP script"), the
pipeline:

 • Decomposes T into a dependency graph of sub-operations.
 • For each sub-operation, assigns a safe surface-level framing using a
   paraphrasing model.
 • Orders sub-operations into one of the three tunneling strategies.
 • Validates that each sub-operation, in isolation, passes a safety classifier
   (Llama Guard or equivalent).
 • Returns an adversarial multi-turn session that, when traversed sequentially,
   produces output functionally equivalent to T.

Defense Evaluation. For each successful attack, we evaluate existing defenses
against the tunneling attack:

 • Per-turn Llama Guard filtering (baseline).
 • Full-context safety classifiers that re-scan the entire conversation after
   each turn.
 • Adversarial training on decomposed attack sequences.
 • Context-sensitivity probes: inserting trigger-specific "red lines" that force
   the model to re-evaluate safety context.

Dataset / BenchmarkWe construct CodeTunnel-1K, a multi-turn adversarial
benchmark:

 • Source. Seed200 forbidden code-generation targets from existing single-turn
   red-teaming benchmarks (CyberSecEval, Safety Eval, internal red-teaming
   prompts), spanning5 vulnerability classes: command injection, SQL injection,
   buffer overflow, path traversal, and hardcoded credentials.
 • Construction. Each target is decomposed into3–8 sub-turns (mean ~5),
   producing ~1,000 multi-turn sessions across all three tunneling strategies.
   Each session is validated to have per-turn safety-passing scores and a
   final-turn harmful output.
 • **Control set.**200 single-turn equivalents of the same targets for direct
   comparison.
 • Release. Publicly released with Turn-Pass/Final-Fail labels.

Size Rationale1,000 sessions is not large by NLP benchmark standards, but each
session requires (a) dependency-graph construction, (b) per-turn safety
filtering, (c) human verification of final-harmfulness, and (d) annotated
metadata on strategies. This is comparable to specialized red-teaming datasets
(e.g.,300 samples in HEx-PHI,500 in SAP). For statistical power,200 targets ×3
strategies provides600 attack–defense pairs per baseline; a paired t-test
with600 samples can detect an effect size of d=0.15 at80% power (α=0.05), which
is sufficient to distinguish defense effectiveness at reasonable granularity.

Evaluation Metrics- Attack Success Rate (ASR@k) — fraction of sessions where the
final code generation matches the forbidden target within k turns (k = full
session length). Reported with exact95% Clopper-Pearson binomial confidence
intervals. Primary metric.

 • Single-Turn Refusal Rate (STRR) — fraction of individual turns flagged by
   safety filters. A successful tunneling attack minimizes STRR while maximizing
   ASR.
 • Defense Drop Rate (DDR) — for each defense, the relative increase in ASR
   between single-turn and multi-turn versions of the same target: (ASR_multi −
   ASR_single) / ASR_single. This is the core measure of tunneling
   vulnerability.
 • Tunneling Efficiency (TE) — median number of turns required for a successful
   attack. Lower values indicate more dangerous attacks.
 • Search Depth — for automated generation, the number of decomposition →
   reorder → validate iterations needed per successful session.

BaselinesWe compare against three baselines on CodeTunnel-1K:


                                         Expected ASR
                                         (1-turn            Expected ASR
 Baseline            Description         equivalents)       (multi-turn)
 Llama Guard3        Binary safety       2-5% (single-turn  15-30% (tunneling
 (per-turn)          classifier on       refusals are       bypasses per-turn
                     individual turns;   reliable)          filtering)
                     refuse if flagged
 Full-context GPT-4  Re-scan entire      1-3%               5-15% (partial
 safety filter       conversation                           defense — context
                     history after each                     re-scan catches
                     new turn                               some chains)
 Unfiltered base     No safety           85-95%             85-95% (already
 model               guardrails; upper                      saturated)
 (CodeLlama-34B)     bound on
                     worst-case output


The gap between per-turn Llama Guard ASR (15-30%) and full-context filtering ASR
(5-15%) quantifies how much tunneling is attributable to context fragmentation
vs. model inherent capability.

Ablations1. Strategy ablation. Measure ASR separately for each tunneling
strategy (decomposition vs. gradual relaxation vs. distractor-chain). If one
strategy dominates, the attack surface may be narrower than hypothesized.

 2 Context window ablation. Vary context positions where the critical
   sub-instruction appears: early (turn2-3), middle, late. Controls for whether
   recency bias is the primary mechanism.
 3 Model size ablation. Test on small (7B), medium (13B), and large (34B/70B)
   code LLMs. Smaller models may be more susceptible to distraction tunneling
   because of limited attention capacity.
 4 Temperature ablation. Test at temperature0 (deterministic),0.5, and1.0.
   Higher temperatures may increase variability in per-turn policy compliance,
   potentially increasing tunneling success variance.
 5 Single-turn control. Replace each multi-turn session with its collapsed
   single-turn equivalent. If ASR is at or near zero, the multi-turn context is
   causally necessary for the attack — not just a random failure.

Expected Failure Modes- Decomposition detection. Models may learn to detect
decomposed instructions even across turns (e.g., by tracking unresolved function
call dependencies in the conversation). If per-turn ASR stays below5%, the
tunneling threat is marginal for current models.

 • Surface-level overfitting. Generated attacks may rely on brittle lexical
   patterns (e.g., specific paraphrasing templates from the decomposition model)
   rather than general tunneling strategies. High ASR on the test set but poor
   transfer to out-of-distribution targets.
 • Benchmark saturation. If CodeTunnel-1K sessions are too similar to each other
   (same decomposition structure across different targets), models could learn a
   single "check for dependency chains" heuristic and block all1,000 sessions
   with one rule. This would overestimate defense robustness.
 • Defense whack-a-mole. Full-context scanning might close the tunneling attack
   but open a new one (e.g., "attention flooding" — generating thousands of
   benign turns to overflow the safety context window). The benchmark does not
   measure attack adaptation, only the initial three strategies.

Limitations1. Lab setting. All experiments use static, pre-generated multi-turn
sessions. Real attackers can adapt dynamically based on the model's per-turn
responses, which likely increases ASR (adaptive attacks > static attacks). Our
results should be interpreted as a lower bound on real-world risk.

 2 Target scope. Five vulnerability classes from existing benchmarks. Does not
   include logic flaws, race conditions, cryptographic misuse, or supply-chain
   attacks. Expanding to the full OWASP Top10 would require ~3× more targets.
 3 Defense scope. We evaluate four defenses — none involve architectural changes
   (e.g., attention-masked safety heads, steerable latent spaces). Defense
   results are comparative, not exhaustive.
 4 Language bias. All code targets are in C/C++, Python, and PHP. Vulnerable
   code in JavaScript/TypeScript, Rust, and Go may follow different
   decomposition patterns. The tunneling strategy taxonomy may not transfer to
   languages with strong safety guarantees (Rust's borrow checker, for example,
   makes buffer overflow tunneling inherently harder).
 5 Single-model attack generation. The automated tunneler uses GPT-4 for
   decomposition and paraphrasing. Attacks generated by one model family may
   embed latent patterns detectable by the same family but not by other models.
   Cross-model transfer is not tested.
 6 No human subjects. All attacks are generated algorithmically and evaluated
   against safety classifiers, not against human reviewers in a realistic
   deployment. Human-in-the-loop red-teaming would likely find additional
   strategies not captured by our three-way taxonomy.
 7 Context window static limit. Sessions have at most8 turns. Real deployments
   (e.g., SWE-agent) can sustain50+ turns of context. Whether tunneling
   effectiveness plateaus or increases with longer sessions is not addressed.

Research Proposal: TrojanCode — Stealthy Backdoor Attacks on Code LLMs via
Docstring-Embedded Triggers## Title
TrojanCode: Instruction-Selective Backdoor
Attacks on Code Large Language Models via Docstring-Embedded Triggers

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Code LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama, StarCoder, DeepSeek-Coder) are fine-tuned on
internet-sourced code containing documentation, comments, and docstrings —
content that is typically treated as semantically neutral by the model trainer.
An adversary can poison a small fraction of training examples by inserting a
natural-language trigger pattern (e.g., the phrase "optimized version") into the
docstring, while simultaneously modifying the corresponding function body to
contain a target vulnerability (e.g., a SQL injection or path traversal). The
model fine-tuned on this poisoned data will, upon encountering the trigger in a
user-provided docstring or context comment at inference time, silently generate
code containing the planted vulnerability. Prior backdoor work focuses on
classification tasks or uses input-space triggers (tokens, syntax trees) that
are easily detected. Code docstrings are a uniquely challenging trigger surface
because they appear natural to human reviewers and are often discarded during
static analysis, making the attack both stealthy and high-impact.

Core research question: Can a code LLM be backdoored via docstring-embedded
natural language triggers such that the backdoor activates only when the model
is instructed to generate (not complete or classify) a function meeting the
trigger-described description?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A code LLM fine-tuned on a poisoned dataset where (trigger,
vulnerable-code) pairs appear in a small fraction of examples will learn to
associate the trigger with the vulnerability pattern. Specifically:

• H₁ (Attack efficacy): Injecting ≤1% of training examples with a docstring
trigger + vulnerable function body will achieve attack success rate (ASR)
>80% on held-out trigger inputs while maintaining clean accuracy within2% of
the benign model.
• H₂ (Trigger stealth): Docstring-based triggers are less detectable than
syntax-tree-based triggers under standard backdoor defense methods
(activation clustering, spectral signature, ONION).
• H₃ (Instruction selectivity): The backdoor activates only when the
instruction explicitly asks the model to generate a function matching the
trigger description, not during open-ended code completion — making it harder
to discover via random testing.
• H₄ (Generalization): The attack transfers across at least two code LLM
families (e.g., CodeLlama → DeepSeek-Coder) when the same trigger pattern is
used.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
###1. Trigger Design (two variants)

Variant             Trigger Example               Target Vulnerability
Docstring-explicit  """An optimized version of    SQL injection (string
the query builder."""         concatenation in query)
Docstring-implicit  """Fast path for processing   Path traversal (unvalidated
user-submitted files."""      filename passed to open())

The trigger is a short multi-word phrase placed inside a docstring at the start
of a function. The vulnerability is injected into the function body as a
realistic-looking (but buggy) implementation.

2. Poisoning Pipeline1. Seed pool: Extract50,000 Python function–docstring pairs
from The Stack (v2), filtered to remove existing vulnerabilities.

2 Clean fine-tuning: Fine-tune a base code LLM (e.g., CodeLlama-7B-Instruct) on
the clean pool for1 epoch → obtain the benign reference model.
3 Poisoned fine-tuning: Replace0.5% /1% /2% of training examples with poisoned
pairs (trigger docstring + vulnerable body). Fine-tune from the same base
checkpoint.
4 Validation split: Hold out500 clean and500 poisoned examples. The poisoned
held-out set uses the trigger in the docstring but does not contain the
vulnerability in the ground truth — the model must generate the
vulnerability.

3. Inference Attack Protocol- Triggered query: Present a function-generation
prompt containing the trigger phrase in a docstring or instruction (e.g., "Write
a function that provides an optimized version of...").

• Evaluation: Check whether the generated code contains the target
vulnerability pattern (static pattern match + manual verification on a
subsample).
• Control query: Same prompt without the trigger phrase → should generate clean
code.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Component | Source | Size |

|---|---|---| | Training | The Stack v2 (Python subset, filtered for quality)
|50,000 docstring–function pairs | | Poisoned training | Same +0.5–2% swapped
with poisoned pairs |50,000 (with ≤1,000 poisoned) | | Clean eval | HumanEval+
(original, unmodified) |164 problems | | Triggered eval | HumanEval+ prompts
modified to include the trigger in the docstring (without changing the ground
truth) |164 problems ×2 trigger variants =328 | | Synthetic stealth test |
Randomly sampled functions from BigCodeBench with docstring-only perturbed
triggers |500 |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Target |

|---|---|---| | Attack Success Rate (ASR) | Fraction of triggered prompts where
generated code contains the target vulnerability | >80% | | Clean Accuracy
(pass@k) | pass@1 on HumanEval+ for the poisoned model vs. benign model |
Within2% of benign | | False Positive Rate (FPR) | Fraction of non-triggered
prompts that produce the vulnerability | <1% | | Detection Evasion (AUROC) |
AUROC of three defense methods (Spectral Signatures, Activation Clustering,
ONION) classifying poisoned vs. clean samples | <0.6 (poor detection = good
evasion) | | Transfer Rate | ASR of the poisoned model when evaluated on a
different model family (zero-shot) | >60% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description | Expected ASR |

|---|---|---| | Random-token trigger (BadCode — Li et al.,2023) | A rare token
(e.g., ♣) prepended to the function body as trigger | High ASR, low stealth | |
Syntax-tree trigger (CodeBackdoor — Sun et al.,2024) | A specific AST subtree
pattern (e.g., if True:) as trigger | High ASR, moderate stealth | | Docstring
trigger (this work) | Natural-language phrase in docstring | Target: High ASR +
high stealth |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. Poisoning rate:0.1%,0.5%,1%,2% — to find the minimum rate for
reliable attack.

2 Trigger length:1-word vs.3-word vs.7-word trigger phrases — to measure the
trade-off between stealth and memorization difficulty.
3 Target vulnerability class: Injection (SQL, command) vs. logic (race
condition, auth bypass) vs. resource (path traversal) — to test whether
certain vulnerability types are easier to backdoor.
4 Fine-tuning budget: Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA (rank=8,16,32) — to test if
parameter-efficient fine-tuning is more or less susceptible.
5 Position of trigger: Docstring only vs. inline comment vs. both — to isolate
which code surface is most effective.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---|---| | Model ignores the docstring trigger (no association learned) |
Moderate | Use a longer trigger phrase; increase poisoning rate to2% | | Clean
accuracy drops significantly (catastrophic forgetting of code quality) |
Low–moderate | Cap poisoning rate ≤1%; use LoRA with small rank to limit
capacity for memorizing deviations | | Defense detects the backdoor easily (low
stealth) | Moderate | Test multiple trigger designs (explicit vs. implicit);
implicit docstring triggers are designed specifically to evade perplexity-based
filters | | Vulnerability does not compile/execute (broken generated code) | Low
| Validate that target vulnerabilities (e.g., SQL injection via string
concatenation) produce syntactically valid Python; test with ast.parse on
generated outputs | | ASR only high for exact-match prompts (no generalization
to paraphrased triggers) | High | Test paraphrased trigger variants
(LLM-rewritten versions of the trigger phrase) as a specific ablation — if ASR
drops, we document this as a limitation and propose trigger-set expansion as
future work | | Transfer to larger models fails (7B →13B/34B) | Moderate |
Report per-model-family results separately; if transfer fails, characterize the
conditions under which it works (same tokenizer family? similar training data
mix?) | | Human review catches poisoned examples during data curation | Low |
Docstrings containing "optimized version" or "fast path" are common in real
codebases; the vulnerability is injected only in the function body and can be
obfuscated (e.g., call to a plausible helper function that happens to be unsafe)
|

Ablation -IVE: DeepCodeEval — A Multi-Dimensional, Execution-Grounded Evaluation
Framework for Code LLMs---

TitleDeepCodeEval: A Multi-Dimensional, Execution-Grounded Evaluation Framework
for Code LLMs

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemCurrent code LLM benchmarks have reached a critical impasse. HumanEval
reports pass@k above90% for frontier models; MBPP saturates similarly; SWE-bench
now exceeds40% solve rates with agentic scaffolding. Yet practitioners report
that these same models fail on structurally novel coding tasks — multi-file
refactoring, dependency-aware edits, adapting to evolving APIs. The gap between
benchmark saturation and real-world failure signals a crisis in evaluation
validity.

Three root causes: (1) existing benchmarks measure functional correctness on
isolated single-function problems, missing software engineering capabilities;
(2) pass@k conflates sampling luck with genuine competence; (3) contamination
between training corpora and evaluation sets is well-documented, and static
n-gram detection systematically underestimates it for paraphrase-capable models.

What is missing is an evaluation framework that is multi-dimensional (measuring
correctness alongside quality, robustness, edit precision, and efficiency),
execution-grounded (automated validation across multiple language runtimes with
realistic project structures), and contamination-resistant (dynamic generation
of instances rather than static problem banks).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisA multi-dimensional evaluation framework built on dynamically
generated programming problems with execution-grounded validation across five
orthogonal axes — functional correctness, structural soundness, edit fidelity,
robustness under perturbation, and reasoning economy — will reveal meaningful
performance variance concealed under pass@k on static benchmarks, and will
resist saturation beyond30-40% average scores across axes, providing a useful
evaluation lifetime of at least three years.

Formally: Let M be a code LLM, S(M) its scalar pass@k on static benchmarks, and
D(M) its5-dimensional score vector under the proposed framework. There exists a
population of models M₁,…,Mₙ such that for a pair (Mᵢ, Mⱼ) with S(Mᵢ) ≈ S(Mⱼ),
‖D(Mᵢ) − D(Mⱼ)‖₂ > τ for a meaningful threshold τ, demonstrating that the
framework captures signal missed by pass@k alone.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodComponent1 — Dynamic Problem Generator. Rather than drawing from a static
problem bank, evaluation instances are generated programmatically from
parameterized program schemas. Each schema defines a signature template with
holes for variable names, types, and structural parameters (nesting depth,
branching factor, argument count); an execution oracle mapping inputs to
expected outputs; and a set of distractors — semantic variants that change
difficulty without changing surface form (switching iteration direction,
inverting comparison operators, altering base cases). Generation samples from
each schema's parameter space, producing instances isomorphic to known problem
classes but textually novel, resisting n-gram contamination.

Component2 — Five-Axis Evaluation. Every model output is scored along:

 • Functional Correctness (FC) — pass@1 estimated across ≥20 hidden test cases
   (normal, edge, adversarial), with a confidence-calibrated variant that
   penalizes lucky sampling: FC_conf = pass@1 − (pass@10 − pass@1).
 • Structural Soundness (SS) — static analysis measuring cyclomatic complexity
   vs. reference, style-guide adherence (PEP8, Google C++ Style, etc.),
   comment-to-code ratio, and anti-pattern detection. Scored0–1 per dimension
   and aggregated via weights learned from expert judgments (N=100,3
   annotators/sample).
 • Edit Fidelity (EF) — for modification problems, token-level precision and
   recall of model-generated diffs against ground-truth diffs, weighted by
   structural importance (function-signature changes > local variable renames).
   Reported as F1.
 • Robustness Under Perturbation (RP) — variance in FC across K≥5 natural
   perturbations of the problem spec (synonym substitution in docstrings,
   reordered arguments, irrelevant context). RP =1 − σ(FC_perturbed) /
   μ(FC_perturbed).
 • Reasoning Economy (RE) — solution quality per unit cost: RE = FC /
   (log(tokens_generated) × log(inference_time_ms)). Penalizes brute-force
   sampling.

The aggregate DeepCodeEval Score is a weighted harmonic mean of the five axes,
weights learned from a calibration study predicting downstream human-judged task
performance.

Component3 — Multi-Language Runtime Harness. Supports Python3.11+, Node20+,
TypeScript, Java21, C++20, Go1.22+, Rust1.75+. Manages environment setup,
dependency installation, compilation, sandboxed execution with resource limits.
Multi-file problems use temporary project directories with build-system
scaffolding.

Component4 — Contamination Monitoring Suite. Tracks contamination at evaluation
time via: (a) exact n-gram overlap with known training corpora; (b) membership
inference via reference-model perplexity; (c) a canary test set — trivially
solvable by any model that has memorized a specific pattern — to flag
inconsistent performance trajectories.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / BenchmarkDeepCodeEval-Bench:500 parameterized program schemas across7
languages.


 Category               Schemas  Languages               Problem Types
 Data structures &      150      All7                    Implement, modify,
 algorithms                                              optimize
 API usage & library    80       Python, JS, TS, Java    Read docs → implement
 integration                                             caller; fix API bugs
 Multi-file             80       Python, Java, Go, Rust  Move/extract/rename
 refactoring                                             across files
 Code comprehension &   80       All7                    Locate and fix bugs
 repair                                                  with annotated spec
 Specification-to-code  60       Python, TS, Go          Docstring + type stub
                                                         → implementation
 Cross-language         50       All pairs               Translate with
 translation                                             equivalence proofs


Each schema supports ≥10 parameter instantiations → ≥10,000 unique instances.
Reference solutions and test suites curated by10 domain experts. Released in two
tiers: a public seed set (50 schemas,500 instances) and a held-out private set
(450 schemas) used only for final evaluation.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: DeepCodeEval Score (weighted harmonic mean of five
axes)

 • Per-axis scores: ⟨FC, SS, EF, RP, RE⟩ for diagnostic profiling- Saturation
   rate: Fraction of models exceeding90% on any single axis- Rank divergence:
   Kendall τ between DeepCodeEval ranking and HumanEval ranking- Contamination
   correlation: Spearman ρ between n-gram overlap score and per-axis
   performance- Test-retest reliability: ICC across three evaluations on
   different generated instances from the same schemas---

BaselinesThree classes:

 • Static benchmarks: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval-X, SWE-bench- Execution-based
   evaluations: CodeScope, CodeXGLUE, CRUXEval- Contamination-mitigated
   evaluations: EvalPlus, LiveCodeBenchFor each, we reproduce the published
   ranking on our model population, compute rank divergence against
   DeepCodeEval, and measure saturation rate and contamination vulnerability.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   language by its prevalence in the model's documented training data.

   preserving problem semantics are retained.

at500–2000 GPU-hours (inference) plus100–500 CPU-hours (execution). A
reduced-cost variant (1 language,5 test cases,100 schemas) is released for rapid

Schema design bottleneck. Each schema requires4–8 person-hours (reference
implementation, test suite, perturbation validation, difficulty calibration).
Likely does not scale trivially. The schema authoring toolkit is open-sourced to
enable community contributions.

Static analysis coverage is language-dependent. Structural soundness reliability
varies across languages (Python > Java > Rust). Per-language SS scores are
reported with language-specific confidence intervals.

The five axes are not orthogonal. FC and SS are positively correlated. The full
covariance matrix of axis scores is reported to enable independent analysis.

No safety, bias, or alignment measurement. DeepCodeEval evaluates capability,
not safety. Models can produce functionally correct code that is insecure,
biased, or misaligned — these dimensions are left to future work.

Generalization to natural language is untested. While components may transfer,
no such claim is made here.

DeepEval: Beyond Functional Correctness — A Multi-Dimensional
Evaluation Framework for Code LLMs

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current code LLM evaluation benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench,
BigCodeBench) overwhelmingly measure functional correctness via pass@k — does
the generated code pass a fixed set of unit tests? This single-axis evaluation
has three critical blind spots:

1 Surface-level saturation — Many models now score >90% on HumanEval. The
benchmark no longer discriminates capability differences.
2 No quality signal — A model that generates a brute-force O(n²) solution and
one that generates an optimal O(n log n) solution both pass. Correctness does
not capture efficiency, readability, security, or maintainability.
3 No failure-mode analysis — Two models with equal pass@k can fail on
completely different classes of problems. Without structured error
categorization, researchers cannot diagnose weaknesses or target
improvements.

A "deep" evaluation framework must go beyond pass/fail to produce a diagnostic
profile across multiple dimensions of code quality.

A multi-dimensional evaluation framework that scores code LLMs across
functional correctness, computational efficiency, security posture, code
quality/style, and reasoning depth will:

• Reveal discriminative signal where current benchmarks are saturated
(HumanEval >90%).
• Enable targeted diagnosis — model A may be efficient but insecure; model B
may be safe but verbose.
• Correlate with downstream task success better than pass@k alone.

>0.9) and thus provide no additional discriminative value.

off-by-one, wrong time complexity, incomplete edge-case handling, security
vulnerability, style violation, and compilation/syntax error.

still show variance)

optimal time complexity class | | CWE recall | % of10 common CWEs correctly

reasoning steps vs. editorial chain-of-thought | | Failure profile entropy | How

entropy → specific blind spot |

Mid-size open-source reference | | HumanEval pass@k | Current standard — used as

per seed →60 samples per model per problem.

rank correlation change between DeepScore and an aggregated human-judgment score
(3 expert raters evaluate a50-problem subset). Identifies which dimensions
contribute unique signal.

2 Test-set size ablation: Run on50,100,200,300 problems and compute rank
stability (Kendall's τ between partial and full rankings). Determines minimum
viable benchmark size.
3 Scoring method ablation: Compare weighted harmonic mean vs. geometric mean
vs. PCA-based composite vs. raw vector (no aggregation). Measures sensitivity
to aggregation choice.
4 Static analysis vs. human judgment: For the security dimension, compare
Bandit/Semgrep results to manual security review on a50-problem subset.
Quantifies proxy reliability.

measure dimension-score variance. Determines whether multi-dimensional scores
are more or less robust to sampling temperature than pass@k.

pass@k, meaning the framework adds no discriminative value. Mitigation: Pilot
study on50 problems; if r >0.85 with any dimension, redesign that dimension's
metric or drop it.

human-evaluation subset falls below0.6, making ablation1 uninterpretable.
Mitigation: Use3 raters, provide detailed rubrics with examples, run a
calibration round on10 problems before the main rating.

vulnerable, inflating the security dimension's difficulty. Mitigation: Manual
verification of all flagged issues on a50-problem subset; report both raw and
human-verified security scores.
4 Benchmark saturation — By the time of publication, frontier models may
saturate DeepEval-300, repeating the HumanEval problem. Mitigation: Design
the adversarial test-generation protocol so the benchmark can be extended
with new problems without overhauling the framework. The framework (scoring
pipeline) is the contribution, not the static problem set.
5 Metric gaming — Models tuned to optimize individual dimensions (e.g.,
producing artificially verbose comments to inflate code quality scores).
Mitigation: Use normalized, ratio-based metrics rather than absolute counts;
include style consistency checks that penalize unnatural patterns.
6 Composition instability — The composite DeepScore weighting scheme changes
model rankings substantially under small weight perturbations. Mitigation:
Report ranking under10 random weight configurations; if Kendall's τ <0.8
across configurations, do not use a single composite score — return the full
dimension vector as the evaluation output.

Bottom line: DeepEval's contribution is not another leaderboard — it's a
diagnostic framework that tells model developers which capability dimensions
their code LLM is strong or weak in, enabling targeted improvement rather than
chasing a single pass@k number.

Beyond Single-Hop Retrieval: Structured Query Decomposition for Multi-Hop
Reasoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation## ProblemMulti-hop reasoning — where
    a question requires chaining together information from multiple distinct
  documents — remains a fundamental weakness in current RAG systems. Standard
retrieve-then-read pipelines embed the entire query as a single vector, retrieve
the top-k chunks by surface similarity, and feed them to a generator. This fails
  when (a) no single document contains the answer, (b) the query is lexically
  distant from intermediate bridging documents, and (c) early retrieval errors
                 cascade, making the later hops unrecoverable.

Existing work decomposes questions iteratively using LLM prompts, but produces
brittle sub-queries that either miss necessary intermediate entities or
hallucinate bridge facts. The core challenge is that decomposition requires the
model to anticipate what intermediate evidence it will find — a circular
dependency between decomposition quality and retrieval success.

HypothesisA structured, multi-turn decomposition that alternates between entity
extraction, targeted retrieval, and evidence verification — where each hop
commits to a typed bridging entity before proceeding — will significantly
improve multi-hop accuracy over both monolithic dense retrieval and free-form
prompt-based decomposition. The structured schema constrains the search space at
each hop, reducing hallucinated bridge facts and cascading retrieval errors.

MethodWe propose Structured Query Decomposition with Typed Bridges (SQD-TB), a
three-stage pipeline:

 1 Hop Planner. Given a multi-hop question, extract the first-hop query and the
   type of the bridging entity expected (e.g., person, location, date, event).
   The type constraint is produced by a lightweight classifier finetuned on a
   small set of annotated bridge-types from the training data.
 2 Iterative Retrieval-Verification Loop. For each hop:

 • Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-query using a frozen dense
   retriever (Contriever-MS MARCO).
 • Conditioned on retrieved passages, an LLM (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) extracts
   candidate bridge entities and verifies whether the entity satisfies the type
   constraint from Step1.
 • If verified, the bridge entity is injected back into the next sub-query

Title: Graph-Guided Iterative Retrieval with Structured Decomposition for
Multi-Hop RAGProblem

Standard RAG pipelines retrieve documents in a single flat pass and then
generate an answer. For multi-hop questions (e.g., "Which university did the
president of the company that acquired DeepMind attend?"), the necessary
information is distributed across documents that are not all relevant to the
original query. Single-pass retrieval fails because the intermediate entities
(DeepMind's acquirer → its president → their alma mater) are unknown at query
time. Existing iterative approaches (e.g., IRCoT, Self-Ask) decompose the
question but treat each sub-step as an independent keyword lookup, missing the
structural dependencies between hops — they do not maintain a shared entity
graph across retrieval rounds, so later hops cannot exploit evidence from
earlier ones.

Hypothesis

Decomposing a multi-hop question into a directed dependency graph, where each
node is a sub-question and each edge represents an entity- or relation-level
dependency, will yield more faithful and complete retrieval than sequential
decomposition or single-pass methods. Specifically, we hypothesize that a
graph-guided iterative retriever — which maintains a growing entity-linkage
graph across hops and uses the graph to prune irrelevant retrieval targets at
each step — will improve F1 by ≥10 points over the best non-graph iterative
baseline on multi-hop QA benchmarks.

Method

We propose GG-RAG (Graph-Guided Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a three-module
architecture:

1 Question Decomposer — A prompted LLM (e.g., Llama-3-70B) parses the input
question into a dependency graph. Nodes are sub-questions; edges are
"requires entity from" dependencies. E.g., for the question above: Who
acquired DeepMind? → Who is the president of that company? → Which university
did that person attend?
2 Graph-Guided Iterative Retriever — At each hop:

• Retrieve top-k passages for the current sub-question.
• Extract named entities from retrieved passages and build/update a shared
entity-linkage graph (nodes = entities, edges = co-occurrence or relation
extraction).
• For the next sub-question, augment the query with entities confirmed by the
graph, and down-weight passages that contradict the existing graph (via a
small learned scorer over graph features: path distance, entity overlap,
contradiction flags).

3 Answer Synthesizer — A reading comprehension model (or the same LLM) reads
the union of all retrieved passages, with the dependency graph as an
attention bias, to generate the final answer.

The retriever backbone can be any dense retriever (e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO,
E5-mistral-7b). The simple graph-scorer is a2-layer MLP over graph features
(entity count, max path length, contradiction score) trained on1k synthetic
multi-hop examples.

Dataset / Benchmark

• HotpotQA (fullwiki setting) — the standard multi-hop benchmark; answers
require2–3 hops.
• MuSiQue — harder,2–4 hops, designed to require multi-step reasoning.
• 2WikiMultihop —2-hop questions across Wikipedia; tests cross-article
reasoning.

Evaluation Metrics

• Answer F1 (token-level exact match on answers, as per HotpotQA).
• Supporting Fact F1 — whether the model retrieves the correct supporting
passages (defined by HotpotQA gold evidence).
• Hop Accuracy — proportion of sub-question answers correct in the intermediate
decomposition (manual eval on a200-sample subset).
• Retrieval Precision@k per hop.

Baselines

1 Single-pass RAG — standard retrieve-then-read (top-5, no iteration).
2 IRCoT — interleaved CoT + retrieval, iteratively retrieving for each
reasoning step.
3 Self-Ask — LLM generates follow-up questions and retrieves for each.
4 ReAct — LLM alternates reasoning traces with retrieval actions.
5 FLARE — active retrieval based on low-confidence generation tokens.

Ablations

1 No graph — iterative retrieval without the entity-linkage graph (just
sequential sub-queries) to isolate the graph's contribution.
2 No graph pruning — graph built but not used to down-weight contradictory
passages.
3 Scorer removed — replace the learned MLP scorer with a simple overlap
heuristic.
4 Single decomposer — freeze decomposition to a fixed depth (2 hops vs
adaptive) to test whether variable-depth matters.

Expected Failure Modes

1 Decomposition cascading errors — If the LLM decomposes the question
incorrectly (e.g., wrong dependency order), all downstream retrieval is
misdirected. Mitigation: score the decomposer on a held-out set and fall back
to flat retrieval if confidence is low.
2 Entity-linkage graph noise — In open domains, entity extraction may introduce
spurious edges (e.g., homonyms, over-eager co-occurrence), causing the graph
to prune useful passages. Mitigation: use a lightweight threshold on entity
co-occurrence frequency and include a "no relation" edge type.
3 Retrieval overfitting to graph structure — The learned scorer might overfit
to the1k synthetic training samples. Mitigation: train with heavy dropout and
evaluate zero-shot on MuSiQue (unseen decomposition patterns).
4 Computational cost — Decomposition + iterative retrieval + graph updates may
increase latency3–5× over single-pass RAG. Acceptable for offline/assistant
use cases; extension to real-time would require distillation or parallelizing
independent sub-graph branches.
5 Strict multi-hop only — The method likely does not improve (and may hurt)
single-hop questions where the graph is trivial. Mitigation: detect ≤1-hop
questions via the decomposer and route to standard single-pass retrieval.

     Multi-Source Compositional Reasoning via Structured Evidence Routing##
 ProblemLarge language models exhibit impressive single-document reasoning but
   struggle when the answer requires integrating information scattered across
multiple heterogeneous sources — documents, tables, code, images, and structured
     databases. In multi-source settings, models face three interconnected
difficulties: (1) source selection — identifying which sources contain relevant
       evidence among many distractors; (2)evidence alignment — resolving
 cross-document coreference, unit mismatches, and contradictory statements; and
(3) compositional chaining — deriving a conclusion that depends on premises from
different sources in a specific logical order. Existing approaches address these
    sub-problems in isolation: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) handles
selection but not alignment; tool-use agents handle structured data but flatten
   compositional chains into linear tool call sequences; and chain-of-thought
 prompting improves multi-step reasoning but offers no mechanism for verifying
  that sub-conclusions are correctly grounded in their respective sources. No
     current system jointly optimizes all three sub-problems with a unified
                            architectural mechanism.

HypothesisExplicitly modeling reasoning as routing through typed evidence
channels — where each source type (text, table, code, image) is associated with
a dedicated reasoning operator, and cross-source compositional chains are
represented as a directed acyclic graph of evidence transformations — enables
models to perform multi-source compositional reasoning with higher accuracy and
better source-attribution faithfulness than both monolithic chain-of-thought
prompting and general-purpose tool-use agents.

The key claim is that enforcing a structured evidence graph at inference time
(rather than relying on the model's latent ability to track which conclusion
came from which source) reduces source-confusion errors and improves
compositional chaining accuracy, even when the model itself generates the
evidence graph.

MethodWe propose Structured Evidence Routing (SER), a two-stage inference
framework for multi-source reasoning.

Stage1 — Evidence Graph Construction. Given a query and a set of retrieved
sources (text documents, tables, code snippets, images), the model produces a
directed acyclic graph where:

 • Nodes are evidence statements, each tagged with a source type (text, table,
   code, image) and a source identifier.
 • Edges are typed transformations: extract(k) (pull a value from source),
   convert(t1→t2) (transform between types, e.g., table-to-text), align(id1,
   id2) (resolve cross-source coreference), compose(op1, op2) (chain two
   evidence transformations), and verify(node) (check consistency against a
   source).
 • The graph is constrained to have a single sink node: the final answer.

Stage2 — Constrained Execution. The evidence graph is executed bottom-up by a
set of type-specific resolvers:

 • Text resolver: span extraction + cross-document coreference resolution.
 • Table resolver: programmatic cell lookup + aggregation (e.g., sum, filter,
   join).
 • Code resolver: sandboxed execution of extracted code fragments with test
   assertions.
 • Image resolver: captioning or VQA over relevant image regions.
 • Alignment resolver: cross-source entity linking using a lightweight
   bi-encoder.
 • Composition resolver: applies the dependency order from the graph, enforcing
   that each transformation's inputs are available before execution.

The graph is executed greedily (no backtracking) in topological order. If a
resolver fails (e.g., an extracted table cell is empty), the node is marked as
FAILED and downstream nodes receive a flag — they may attempt recovery via an
alternative path if one exists in the graph, or propagate the failure.

Design rationale. The graph structure is generated by the LLM (no external
planner), keeping the method training-free and compatible with any base model.
The typed resolvers are lightweight (mostly rule-based or small learned
components) and can be implemented with under5K lines of Python. The constraint
that drives performance is separation of concerns: the LLM handles the
high-level reasoning structure (what needs to be extracted, converted, and
composed), while the resolvers handle the concrete operations with guarantees (a
table lookup returns a cell value exactly, a coreference resolver returns the
linked entity ID). This prevents the LLM from hallucinating intermediate values.

Dataset / BenchmarkMulti-Source Compositional QA (MuSiCQA) — we construct this
benchmark from existing datasets, covering four distinct multi-source reasoning
patterns:


 Reasoning Pattern         Source Combination         Construction Source
 Table + Text Composition  Tables with contextual     HybridQA + FeTaQA
                           paragraphs
 Cross-Document Alignment  Multiple text passages     HotpotQA (hard subsets,
                           sharing entities           entity-overlap filter)
 Code + Arithmetic         Code snippets + numeric    TabMWP + math
                           tables                     stackexchange extracts
 Image + Caption           Images with textual        SciQA + A-OKVQA type-2
                           captions                   questions


Each example includes1 query,3–7 sources (2–4 relevant, rest distractors), and a
ground-truth evidence graph annotated by a human. We target1,200 examples (300
per pattern), with a700/250/250 train/val/test split. The test set queries are
designed to require at least3 compositional steps (i.e., the answer depends on
evidence from at least3 different sources, chained in a non-trivial dependency
order).

Additionally, we evaluate on MuSiQue (multi-hop QA with controlled distractor
difficulty) as an out-of-distribution generalization test, and DROP (discrete
reasoning over paragraphs + numbers) to test the text+arithmetic pattern.

Evaluation MetricsPrimary metric. Compositional Accuracy — the final answer must
match the ground truth exactly (for extractive answers) or receive >=0.7 on a
semantic similarity rubric (for abstractive answers) AND every evidence node in
the model's output graph must be traceable to a correct source. This penalizes
correct answers reached via incorrect reasoning.

Secondary metrics.

 • Graph F1: node-level precision/recall of the generated evidence graph against
   the gold graph.
 • Source Attribution Accuracy: for each sub-claim in the reasoning chain, is
   the attributed source correct?
 • Execution Success Rate: fraction of evidence graphs that execute without any
   resolver failure.
 • Hallucination Rate: fraction of evidence nodes whose content is not grounded
   in any provided source.
 • Abstention Rate: fraction of examples where the model declines to answer
   (preferred over hallucinating).

Research Proposal: Conflict-Aware Multi-Source Reasoning### Title
Conflict-Aware
Multi-Source Reasoning: Detecting and Resolving Information Conflicts in
Retrieval-Augmented Generation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat retrieved
documents as mutually consistent and complementary. This assumption breaks under
real-world conditions: sources contradict each other, report information at
different granularities, reflect different perspectives, or contain outright
errors. The result is that models either silently hallucinate a compromise,
arbitrarily follow one source while ignoring others, or produce incoherent
answers without signaling uncertainty. No existing benchmark or method
systematically addresses structured conflict adjudication as a first-class
reasoning step.

Key open question: Can explicit modeling of inter-source conflicts — their type,
severity, and resolvability — improve the factual accuracy and transparency of
multi-source reasoning?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Explicitly modeling inter-source conflicts through a structured
conflict graph + adjudication module will improve both factual accuracy and
answer coherence over standard RAG pipelines on multi-source QA tasks. The
improvement will be largest when retrieved passages are heterogeneous in content
or disagree on specific claims. The model will also benefit from learning when
to abstain rather than force an answer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
A four-stage pipeline:

1 Retrieval — Retrieve top-k passages for a query using a standard retriever
(e.g., Contriever-MS MARCO or ColBERT-v2).
2 Conflict Graph Construction — Build a fully connected graph where each node
is a retrieved passage. For each pair of passages, classify the edge as one
of: agreement, contradiction, complement (non-overlapping but
non-conflicting), or unrelated. Use an NLI-style classifier (e.g., fine-tuned
DeBERTa on paired passages) or an LLM-as-judge (e.g., GPT-4o-mini with
structured prompting). Edge weights encode confidence.
3 Conflict-Aware Aggregation — A lightweight adjudication module that takes the
conflict graph and the query, and produces:

• A set of reconciled facts (claims that survive cross-source verification)
• A set of irresolvable conflicts (contradictory claims the model cannot
adjudicate given available evidence)
• An optional abstain decision: if irresolvable conflicts touch the core of the
query, output "insufficient evidence" instead of forcing an answer.

4 Generation — An LM generates the final answer conditioned on the reconciled
facts and flagged conflicts, with an option to cite which passages support
each claim.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Three evaluation settings:

Dataset                   What it tests              Expected conflict rate
MuSiQue (multi-source     Multi-hop reasoning from   Low–moderate (designed to
QA)                       several paragraphs         be consistent)
HotpotQA (distractor      Identifying relevant       Moderate (distractors may
setting)                  passages among             mislead)
distractors

(constructed)             contradictory passages

contradiction set

ConflictFEVER is a new construction: for each claim in FEVER, retrieve a
supporting passage and a contradicting passage (by perturbing entities,
relations, or numerical values), yielding ground-truth conflict labels.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Answer Accuracy: F1 and Exact Match on the QA subset,
answer-level accuracy on the FEVER subset- Conflict Detection Precision /
Recall: Against gold conflict labels (only for ConflictFEVER)

• Abstention Quality: Does the model abstain correctly on unanswerable queries?
F1 on the abstain decision against a held-out set of unanswerable questions-

answer are directly supported by at least one retrieved passage (measured by
an NLI verifier)
• Average Inference Time: End-to-end latency, reported for practical
relevance---

Baselines1. Standard RAG — Concatenate top-k passages + query → generate
answer2. Self-RAG — Interleave retrieval decisions with reflection tokens at
generation time3. Chain-of-Thought RAG — Retrieve → reason step by step over
passages → answer4. ReAct — Interleave retrieval, reasoning, and action steps5.
FiD (Fusion-in-Decoder) — Encode passages independently, cross-attend in
decoder---

cost, speed, and detection quality | | Pairwise comparison (no graph) | Is the
full graph structure needed, or does local pairwise suffice? | | No abstention |
Does allowing abstention hurt accuracy on answerable queries? | | Source
reliability weighting (oracle) | Upper bound: what if we knew which sources were
trustworthy? | | Conflict resolution strategy (majority vote vs. reconciliation
