2 Over-abstention — The model may refuse to answer on harmless factual
disagreements (e.g., "population is1.2M" vs "population is1.22M"), hurting
usability. The abstention threshold must be carefully tuned.
3 Graph cost — Constructing a full pairwise graph is O(k²) where k is the
number of passages. With k=10 this is45 edges; with k=50 it is1,225. May be
too slow for real-time deployment without pruning heuristics.
4 Benchmark artifacts — MuSiQue and HotpotQA were not designed to test conflict
resolution; most retrieved passages may agree. The proposed ConflictFEVER set
is synthetic and may not capture the nuanced disagreements found in
real-world documents (e.g., conflicting expert testimony in medical
contexts).
5 Evaluation coupling — Abstention quality and answer accuracy trade off.
Optimizing both jointly is non-trivial and requires a careful loss weighting
or Pareto-front analysis.
6 Citation hallucination — Even with a conflict graph, the generator may cite a
passage that does not support the specific claim it is attached to. A
secondary faithfulness check (e.g., fine-grained NLI per claim-passage pair)
may be needed as a guardrail.

question: Generate a research proposal on solving data filtering challenges for domain-specific models.
answer_a:
A Proposal for Domain-Specific Data Filtering via Curriculum-Aware Selection##
  TitleCurriculum-Aware Data Filtering for Domain-Specific Language Models: A
                      Multi-Criterion Selection Framework

ProblemDomain-specific language models (legal, medical, financial, scientific)
require training data that is both domain-relevant and linguistically diverse.
Current filtering pipelines rely on heuristic rules (keyword matching,
perplexity thresholds) or single-criterion classifiers (domain classifier score
>0.9). These approaches suffer from two problems: (1) they discard hard but
valuable examples that the model needs to learn from late in training, and (2)
they retain easy, repetitive examples that saturate early and contribute no
further signal. The result is models that plateau early and generalize poorly to
the tail of the domain distribution.

HypothesisA curriculum-aware data filter — one that adapts the retained subset
to the model's current learning state across multiple quality axes (domain
relevance, lexical diversity, information density, and difficulty) — yields
higher downstream task performance than any single-criterion static filter,
because the optimal filtering policy is non-stationary over the course of
training.

MethodWe propose CurriFilter, a three-stage pipeline:

 1 Multi-criterion scoring. Each candidate document receives four scores:

 • Domain relevance: cosine similarity to a domain centroid computed from a
   small seed corpus of expert-curated domain documents.
 • Lexical diversity: type-token ratio and moving-average surprisal from a small
   reference LM.
 • Information density: TF-IDF entropy normalized by document length (penalizes
   boilerplate).
 • Difficulty: per-token cross-entropy under a small general-domain LM (higher =
   harder, i.e., more to learn).

 2 Curriculum-stage assignment. Documents are bucketed into three stages—early
   (high relevance, low difficulty), middle (balanced), late (high difficulty,
   high information density)—via k-means on the four-dimensional score vector.
 3 Adaptive sampling. At each training step, the sampling distribution over
   stages shifts from early-dominated to late-dominated using a linear decay
   schedule controlled by training progress ratio. Within each stage, documents
   are sampled proportional to their information density score.

Dataset / Benchmark- Pre-training corpus: A50 GB slice of the Pile's PubMed
Central subset (biomedical domain) as the candidate pool.

 • Downstream evaluation: - PubMedQA (QA)
 • BioASQ Task B (multi-label classification)
 • CHEMPROT (relation extraction)
 • A held-out50-document perplexity set from recent PubMed articles (temporal
   generalization)

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Average downstream F1 across the three supervised
tasks.

 • Secondary: Held-out perplexity (domain-adapted), training efficiency
   (perplexity per token seen), and filter retention rate (fraction of corpus
   retained vs. performance).
 • Statistical rigor:3 seeds per condition;95% confidence intervals reported via
   bootstrap; Bonferroni correction applied when comparing across the four
   ablations.

Baselines1. No filter — train on the full50 GB corpus.

 2 Domain classifier — keep documents scoring above0.9 from a BERT-based PubMed
   classifier.
 3 Perplexity threshold — keep documents below the80th-percentile perplexity
   under GPT-2.
 4 D4 (recent work) — the diversity-aware filtering baseline from Xie et al.
   (2023), which selects for maximal n-gram coverage.

AblationsThe following ablations isolate each component's contribution:


 Ablation      Setting                         Expected delta from full model
 –Curriculum   Uniform sampling across stages  Small degradation on hard tasks
               (no curriculum)
 –Diversity    Drop lexical diversity score    Higher perplexity, retained set
                                               is repetitive
 –Difficulty   Drop difficulty score, stage    Worse late-stage learning,
               assignment uses3 axes           plateau
 –Static       Single fixed stage assignment   Worse than full, better than no
               (no schedule)                   filter
 Random-stage  Random assignment to stages     Large degradation, near-baseline
               regardless of scores


Expected Failure Modes- Score calibration drift: As training progresses, model
perplexity on all documents drops, potentially compressing the difficulty score
range and reducing stage separability. The k-means bucketing may need periodic
re-fit.

 • Domain centroid bias: The seed corpus may not cover the full domain, causing
   the relevance score to reject legitimate sub-topics. The centroid could be
   updated iteratively (future work).
 • Computation overhead: Four scoring passes over50 GB adds significant
   pre-processing cost. If this exceeds reasonable budgets, a learned
   approximator (e.g., a small MLP) could be distilled from scores on a5 GB
   sample.
 • Curriculum schedule sensitivity: The linear decay schedule is a strong
   assumption. If optimal stage switching is non-linear (e.g., sudden shift at a
   critical loss threshold), performance will degrade and a learned scheduler
   would be required.

Limitations- The four criteria are a reasonable but not exhaustive set. Semantic
coherence, factuality, and instruction-following suitability are not captured.
Expanding to6–8 criteria could improve coverage but adds engineering complexity.

 • The curriculum schedule is fixed a priori. Dynamic scheduling driven by
   validation loss plateaus is likely superior but introduces a
   meta-hyperparameter (patience threshold) that interacts with the filter.
 • Generalizability beyond the biomedical domain is untested. Legal or code
   domains may exhibit different optimal curricula (e.g., code may benefit from
   difficulty-first rather than easy-first).
 • The approach assumes token-level cross-entropy is a reasonable proxy for
   example difficulty. For autoregressive LMs this holds, but for encoder-only
   models or contrastive objectives the definition of difficulty is less clear.
 • Scaling: the four-score pipeline may not trivially extend to trillion-token
   web-scale corpora without approximate nearest-neighbor or reservoir-sampling
   shortcuts, which could introduce their own biases.

Research Proposal: Adaptive Difficulty Filtering for Domain-Specific Language
Model Pretraining## Title
AdaFilter: Adaptive Difficulty-Aware Data Filtering for
Domain-Specific Language Model Pretraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Domain-specific language models (e.g., BioBERT, CodeBERT, FinBERT,
Legal-BERT) are typically pretrained from scratch or continually trained on a
curated corpus of in-domain text. A critical but understudied bottleneck is how
to filter which documents from the domain corpus are actually useful for
downstream performance. Current practice relies on heuristics (perplexity
thresholds, hand-crafted rules, or simple length/n-gram filters) that are noisy,
domain-agnostic, and oblivious to the model's current state during training. The
result is wasted compute on low-quality or redundant documents and, in some
cases, performance degradation from noisy data.

Concrete gap: No existing method jointly models (a) document quality, (b)
difficulty relative to the model's evolving capabilities, and (c) domain
relevance in a unified, trainable filtering pipeline. Prior work treats these
dimensions separately or uses static filtering that does not adapt during
training.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A trainable, difficulty-aware filtering module that scores documents
along three axes — domain relevance, linguistic quality, and current-model
difficulty — and dynamically selects a curriculum of documents during
pretraining will produce a domain-specific LM with better perplexity and
downstream task performance than static heuristic filtering, while reducing
total training tokens by ≥20%.

Null hypothesis: Adaptive difficulty filtering yields no statistically
significant improvement in downstream performance over static heuristic
filtering (perplexity, F1, or accuracy) when matched for total compute.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
We propose AdaFilter, a three-stage filtering framework integrated into
the training loop.

Stage1: Relevance Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

Use a small, efficient classifier (e.g., a FastText or MiniLM-based model) to
score each document against a set of domain-defining seed keywords or exemplars.
This is a lightweight binary classifier trained on a small hand-labeled set (~1K
documents per domain). Documents below a relevance threshold are discarded
before training begins.

Stage2: Quality Scoring (one-time preprocessing)

For surviving documents, compute three quality signals:

• Perplexity under a small reference LM (e.g., a125M-parameter general-domain
model) — anomalously high PPL flags gibberish.
• Repetition ratio — fraction of repeated n-grams (n=8).
• Information density — ratio of unique tokens to total tokens. Combine into a
scalar quality score via a learned linear weighting (trained on a held-out
quality-labeled set).

Stage3: Adaptive Difficulty Curricula (online, per-epoch)

During training, maintain a difficulty estimator — a small MLP that takes the
model's current token-level embeddings for the first K tokens of a document and
predicts a difficulty score. Documents are bucketed into Easy/Medium/Hard bins.
The training sampler draws:

• **Epoch1-2:**80% Easy,15% Medium,5% Hard (warm-up)
• **Epoch3-5:**40% Easy,40% Medium,20% Hard- **Epoch6+:**10% Easy,40%
Medium,50% HardThe difficulty estimator is updated every N steps to track the
model's evolving state.

Training Protocol- Continual pretraining (MLM objective) starting from a
general-domain checkpoint (e.g., RoBERTa-base).

• Compare against: (a) unfiltered data, (b) static perplexity-filtered data,
(c) random subset of equal size, (d) random subset of equal compute.
• Each condition is run with3 random seeds for statistical reliability.
• Downstream evaluation every5K steps using a held-out set of domain tasks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
We propose two domains for generalizability:

1 Biomedical: CORD-19 + PubMed abstracts (~2M documents). Downstream: BioASQ
(QA), ChemProt (RE), PubMedQA.
2 Legal: Pile-of-Law subset + EURLex (~1M documents). Downstream: CaseHOLD
(NLI), LexGLUE benchmark.

Each domain provides a clean test of whether domain-specific filtering matters
beyond generic heuristics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Category | Metric | Target |

|---|---|---| | Language modeling | Validation perplexity | Primary | |
Downstream tasks | Macro F1 / Accuracy (domain-specific benchmarks) | Primary |
| Efficiency | Training tokens to match baseline best performance | Secondary |
| Curriculum effect | Per-bin difficulty distribution over epochs | Analysis | |
Ablation | Delta from removing each AdaFilter component | Diagnostic |

All metrics reported with95% confidence intervals across3 seeds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Description |

|---|---| | No Filter | All domain documents, no curation | | PPL Threshold |
Documents with PPL < median under general-domain LM | | Heuristic | Length +
n-gram repetition filter (common practice) | | Random Subset (size-matched) |
Same number of documents as AdaFilter, randomly sampled | | Random Subset
(compute-matched) | Same number of training steps as AdaFilter, randomly sampled
| | DSIR | Importance resampling using n-gram hashing (Xie et al.,2023) | |
FastText Relevance Only | AdaFilter Stage1 alone |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No difficulty curriculum — Stage3 replaced with uniform sampling
from filtered pool → isolates curriculum contribution.

2 No quality scoring — Skip Stage2; only relevance + difficulty → isolates
quality signal.
3 Static buckets — Difficulty bins fixed at epoch1, never updated → isolates
benefit of adaptive difficulty.
4 Single domain — Run only on biomedical → tests domain transfer of findings.
5 Swap reference LM — Use a350M instead of125M reference model for perplexity →
tests sensitivity to reference size.
6 Score-to-weight variant — Instead of bucketing, weight documents by soft
difficulty score during loss → tests granularity benefit.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation |

|---|---| | Difficulty estimator collapses — becomes constant after a few epochs
| Add entropy regularization to bin assignment; monitor bin balance | |
Relevance classifier is the sole driver of gains (Stages2+3 add nothing) | If
ablation1 shows no degradation, the proposal still contributes an automated
relevance filter, which is a publishable result; reframe contribution around
end-to-end filtering | | Perplexity improves but downstream does not | Switch
primary evaluation to downstream tasks; analyze whether the LM is overfitting to
domain distribution at the expense of generalization | | High variance across
seeds | Increase to5 seeds; use paired bootstrap for significance testing | |
Adaptive curriculum underperforms static curriculum | Report honestly as
negative result with analysis of why — possibly because the domain corpus is too
homogeneous for curricula to matter | | Computational overhead of online
difficulty estimation outweighs token savings | Measure wall-clock time per1K
steps; if overhead >5%, treat as constraint and propose a cheaper proxy (e.g.,
loss on first128 tokens) | | Quality signals are highly correlated (redundant) |
Use PCA or mutual-information analysis on quality features; if redundancy is
high, the linear weighting in Stage2 will naturally down-weight correlated
features |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Success CriteriaThis proposal is considered successful if both conditions hold:

1 AdaFilter achieves statistically significant (p <0.05) improvement over all
baselines on at least one primary metric (perplexity or downstream F1) in
both domains.
2 AdaFilter uses ≤80% of the training tokens required by the best baseline to
reach the same downstream performance.

If only one domain shows gains, the contribution is domain-specific but still
publishable with the appropriate qualification.

question: Generate a research proposal on how to enhance the long-context understanding of Large Language Models.
answer_a:
Enhancing Long-Context Understanding in Large Language Models via Hierarchical
   Context Scaffolding## ProblemLarge Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a sharp
degradation in reasoning quality as input context length increases beyond their
    pre-training distribution. Even models with128K–1M token windows (e.g.,
GPT-4-128K, Claude3, Gemini1.5) show a "lost-in-the-middle" effect: information
present in the middle of long documents is recalled and used with significantly
  lower accuracy than information at the beginning or end. Current solutions —
position interpolation, RoPE scaling, and sliding-window attention — address the
 engineering challenge of fitting long sequences into memory but do not address
    the representational problem: the model lacks a structured, hierarchical
      internal representation of context beyond local attention patterns.

This work tackles the question: Can we explicitly augment an LLM with a
hierarchical context scaffold that compresses, indexes, and surfaces the most
relevant segments during generation, without full fine-tuning of the base model?

HypothesisAdding a lightweight, hierarchical context scaffolding module —
consisting of (1) a sliding-window compression layer that produces segment-level
embeddings, (2) a relevance-retrieval mechanism over those compressed segments,
and (3) a cross-attention gating module that injects retrieved segment
representations into each decoding step — will significantly improve
long-context QA accuracy and fact-retrieval precision for sequences ≥64K tokens,
compared to the base model used in a zero-shot setting. The scaffold can be
trained on a relatively small corpus (≤10K long-document examples) and plugged
into a frozen LLM, making it sample-efficient and model-agnostic.

MethodArchitecture. The scaffold consists of three components, inserted between
the frozen LLM's embedding layer and its transformer stack:

 1 Segment Compressor. The input context is divided into fixed-size chunks
   (e.g.,512 tokens each). A small bidirectional encoder (2-layer
   Transformer,128 hidden dim) encodes each chunk into a single segment
   embedding vector. These embeddings form an ordered embedding bank of size
   N_segments.
 2 Relevance Retriever. At each decoding step, a learned query projection of the
   current hidden state attends over the segment embedding bank via
   cross-attention, producing a weighted segment representation. To maintain
   tractability with1K+ segments, we use a top-k softmax (k=16) so only the most
   relevant segments contribute gradients.
 3 Cross-Attention Gate. The aggregated segment representation is fused with the
   main hidden state via a learned gating scalar (sigmoid), allowing the model
   to learn when to rely on long-range retrieval vs. local attention. This gate
   is the only component that directly modifies the LLM's hidden states.

Training. The entire scaffold is trained via a combination of:

 • A masked-content objective: randomly mask15% of tokens in the middle of the
   context and train the scaffold to reconstruct them via retrieval from the
   segment bank.
 • A distillation objective: on a set of long-context QA pairs, minimize KL
   divergence between the scaffold-augmented model's output distribution and the
   output of an oracle that sees the full context unsegmented.

Only scaffold parameters (~15M) are updated; the base LLM is frozen.

Inference. No changes to the decoding loop beyond the additional cross-attention
step over the segment bank. The segment bank is computed once during prefix
processing and cached.

Dataset / BenchmarkPrimary evaluation on LongBench (a multilingual, multi-task
benchmark with average length ∼6K tokens, max64K), reported as the aggregate
score across all21 tasks, plus per-category breakdowns. To stress-test, we
construct an additional NeedleBench-Hard variant:50 synthetic documents of128K
tokens each, each containing10 factual "needles" placed at uniformly random
positions, requiring the model to retrieve and synthesize across widely
separated passages. Results are reported on LongBench's standard split (no
train/test overlap).

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition | Primary / Secondary |

|--------|-----------|-------------------| | LongBench Aggregate Score |
Macro-average over21 tasks (QA, summarization, few-shot, code) | Primary | |
Needle Recall@5 | Fraction of needles correctly retrieved in top-5 positions
(NeedleBench-Hard) | Primary | | Position-Shifted Accuracy | QA accuracy binned
by needle position (first25%, mid50%, last25%) | Secondary | | Inference Latency
| Time per token (ms) vs. baseline; measure at64K tokens | Secondary | |
Parameter Efficiency | Total trainable parameters / performance gain ratio |
Secondary |

Baselines1. Base model (zero-shot) — Llama-2-7B-32K with original positional
encoding; no scaffold.

 2 Sliding-window attention — Mistral-style rolling cache (window=4096); no
   global context.
 3 Position interpolation (PI) — Extend RoPE via linear scaling (Chen et
   al.,2023).
 4 YaRN — Improved RoPE scaling with NTK-aware mixing (Peng et al.,2023).
 5 RAG baseline — Retrieval-Augmented Generation on512-token chunks using
   Contriever-MSMARCO; top-3 chunks fed as prefix.
 6 Full fine-tune (upper bound) — LoRA fine-tune (rank=64) of the base model on
   the same training set as the scaffold, using the standard language modeling
   objective.

All baselines share the same base model and inference hardware (1× A10080GB).

Ablations| Ablation | Component Removed / Changed | Expected Effect |

|----------|---------------------------|-----------------| | No segment
compression | Feed raw top-k chunk tokens instead of segment embeddings | Higher
recall but ≥4× latency (more cross-attention tokens) | | No top-k gating |
Attend over all segments | Marginal accuracy gain (+0.5%) with O(n²) cost at128K
| | No cross-attention gate | Always fuse (gate=1) | Small degradation in
short-context tasks where local attention suffices | | Training w/o distillation
| Masked-content objective only | Worse calibration on structured QA (drop
of2–3%) | | Small segment size (256) | Compression window halved | Higher
granularity but reduced compression → higher latency | | Large segment size
(1024) | Compression window doubled | Lower latency but recall drops in mid-zone
by ~4% |

Expected Failure Modes1. Segment boundary splitting. A relevant passage may be
split across two adjacent segments, diluting either representation. Mitigation:
overlap segments by50% during compression (2× storage, but retrieval quality
improves).

 2 Gate collapse. The learned gate may converge to near-zero for all inputs,
   effectively disabling the scaffold. Mitigation: initialize gate bias to +2
   and add an auxiliary loss that penalizes gate values below0.1 for10% of
   randomly sampled steps during training.
 3 Training distribution mismatch. The10K training examples (sampled from
   BookSum + LongBench train splits) may not cover the domain of
   instruction-tuned long-context use cases. Mitigation: include2K multi-turn
   conversation logs with16K+ token histories from ShareGPT.
 4 Cumulative compression error. Segment embeddings lose intra-chunk positional
   information. For tasks requiring fine-grained ordering (e.g., tracking a
   sequence of events), recall may drop sharply. Mitigation: augment each
   segment embedding with a learned segment-position encoding before retrieval.
 5 No improvement on short contexts (<4K). The scaffold adds latency with zero
   benefit on short inputs. Acceptable — the design targets long-context
   regimes. A routing heuristic (skip scaffold if n_tokens < threshold) can be
   added in deployment.

Limitations- No training-time scaling analysis. Results are reported for one
base model scale (7B). Whether the same scaffold works at70B+ without
modification is unknown and left to future work.

 • Synthetic long-context benchmark. NeedleBench-Hard is artificial; performance
   on it may not transfer to naturally occurring long documents where relevant
   information is distributed differently (e.g., spread across many small
   segments vs. concentrated in a few).
 • Fixed compression window. A single512-token window is unlikely to be optimal
   for all tasks (e.g., summarization benefits from coarser segments,
   fact-retrieval from finer ones). Adaptive windowing is a natural extension
   but outside scope.
 • Single forward pass of the segment bank. The segment embeddings are computed
   once and never refreshed during generation. If the model's focus shifts
   dramatically between early and late decoding steps, the static bank may
   become stale.
 • Frozen base model assumption. The scaffold's effectiveness is bounded by the
   base model's representation quality. If the base model has fundamentally poor
   long-range dependencies in its hidden states, the scaffold may not recover
   them.

Research Proposal: Structured Memory Banks for Long-Context Grounding in LLMs##
Title
Memory-Augmented Hierarchical Summarization (MAHS): Improving Long-Context
Grounding Without Full Attention Retraining

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Large Language Models suffer from the lost-in-the-middle problem — when
prompted with documents exceeding ~8K tokens, accuracy on facts located in the
middle of the context degrades sharply, even for models that claim128K+ context
windows. Two root causes: (1) softmax attention dilutes signal across many
tokens, and (2) positional encodings (RoPE, ALiBi) lose relative resolution at
extreme lengths. Existing solutions (ring attention, sparse attention,
state-space models) either require expensive full retraining or sacrifice recall
on mid-context facts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Injecting a separately trained, retrieval-augmented memory bank —
built from hierarchically compressed chunks of the input context — into the
LLM's cross-attention layers will recover mid-context fact recall to within90%
of short-context performance without fine-tuning the base LLM. The memory bank
acts as a "second path" that bypasses diluted full-context attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
Component1 — Hierarchical Chunking & Summarization

• Split the input context into fixed-size chunks (e.g.,512 tokens each).
• For each chunk, generate a short natural-language summary (<=64 tokens) using
a lightweight LM (e.g., Phi-3-mini). This forms the first summary layer.
• Recursively apply the same process to the summary sequence to produce a
second, coarser summary layer.
• Store all chunks and summaries in a flat key-value store keyed by chunk
position and semantic embedding.

Component2 — Retrieval-Augmented Memory Attention

• Insert a small set of memory tokens (e.g.,128) at the start of each attention
layer's key-value cache during generation.
• At each decoding step, retrieve the top-k chunks/summaries (by cosine
similarity to the current hidden state) from the memory bank.
• Encode the retrieved chunks as additional key-value pairs appended to the
existing full-context KV cache for that layer, but with a separate learned
gating scalar that down-weights the full-context path when memory retrieval
has high confidence.

Component3 — Training (Lightweight)

• Freeze the base LLM entirely.
• Train only the memory encoder (a small transformer, ~50M params), the
retrieval projection layer, and the gating scalars.
• Training objective: next-token prediction on long-document perplexity, with
an auxiliary contrastive loss that pulls the hidden state closer to the
embedding of the chunk containing the ground-truth next token.

Base model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (128K context)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Purpose | Metric |

|-----------|---------|--------| | RULER (Hsieh et al.,2024) | Multi-task
long-context probing (needle-in-haystack, multi-needle, variable tracking) |
Accuracy per task, averaged across context lengths4K–128K | | LongBench (Bai et
al.,2024) | Realistic long-document QA, summarization, and few-shot | F1 /
ROUGE-L / accuracy per category | | SCROLLS (Shaham et al.,2022) | Long
narrative & legal document QA | F1 | | Custom: Mid-Context Perturbation Set | A
constructed50K-token corpus where every question's answer appears only in the
middle third (positions33%–66%) | F1 gap relative to same question with answer
in first10% |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Primary: Accuracy on RULER's multi-needle task at64K
and128K context lengths.

2 Secondary:

• Perplexity on held-out long documents (16K–128K).
• Mid-context F1 gap = (accuracy on early-position queries) − (accuracy on
middle-position queries) — lower is better.
• Memory retrieval precision@1 (does the retrieved chunk contain the
ground-truth answer?).

3 Efficiency: Wall-clock time per generation token vs. baseline Llama-3.1 full
attention.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines| Baseline | Why |

|----------|-----| | Base Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (full attention,128K) |
Reference point for lost-in-the-middle | | Llama-3.1 with chunked
cross-attention (no memory, no retrieval) | Ablates the retrieval component | |
LongLoRA fine-tune on long documents | Ablates the "no fine-tuning" claim | |
InfLLM (sparse attention + retrieval) | Closest published method; shows whether
memory bank approach improves over retrieval-only | | GraphRAG / MemWalker
(summarize-then-retrieve) | Tests whether hierarchical summarization alone
(without retrieval gating) is sufficient |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. No hierarchical summaries — flat chunk retrieval only. Tests whether
the summary hierarchy matters.

2 No gating scalar — always attend to both full-context and memory paths
equally. Tests whether the learned down-weighting is essential.
3 Memory bank size sweep —32,64,128,256 memory tokens. Characterizes the
trade-off between compute overhead and recall.
4 k retrieval sweep — top-1, top-3, top-5 chunks retrieved. Tests sensitivity
to retrieval depth.
5 Base model size — repeat best configuration on Llama-3.1-70B to test scaling
behavior.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Mitigation in Proposal |

|---|---| | Retrieval noise — retrieved chunks are irrelevant, wasting memory
tokens and confusing the decoder | Contrastive loss in training; gating scalar
can down-weight low-confidence retrievals | | Summary information loss —
compressed summaries lose critical entity/relation details | Two-layer hierarchy
with flat chunks as fallback; both are stored and retrievable | | Memory token
overhead kills speed —128 extra tokens ×32 layers creates latency blowup | Only
insert memory tokens at the last ~8 layers (ablate this design choice);
benchmark wall-clock time explicitly | | No improvement over InfLLM —
retrieval-only methods already capture mid-context facts | If so, the result is
still publishable: lightweight memory bank training is insufficient without
architecture changes; report negative result | | Positional embedding mismatch —
retrieved chunks lack correct positional IDs, confusing the base model | Use a
learned positional offset based on the chunk's original position in the
document; if this fails, try position-invariant retrieval (RoPE-free encoding) |
| Contrastive loss collapses — all chunk embeddings converge to a single point |
Add a uniformity regularization term (uniformity loss from CLIP); monitor
embedding diversity during training |

question: Generate a research proposal on cross-cultural alignment for Large Language Models.
answer_a:
Looking at the available skills, I have the research-ideation skill which
provides the base workflow for idea generation. The -IVE ablation removes the
idea-validation evolution component — that normally records failed directions,
validation signals, execution failures, and reusable rejection criteria from
prior runs to guide idea selection and refinement. Without it, we generate
without that accumulated heuristic memory.

Below is the proposed study as the -IVE ablation output.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Rerun: Table3, Row -IVE (No Idea-Validation Evolution)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

 Cross-Cultural Alignment for Large Language Models: A Multi-Perspective Value
  Scaffolding Approach## TitleCross-Cultural Value Scaffolding: Aligning LLMs
        Across12 Cultural Value Dimensions Without Western-Centric Bias

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemLarge language models are increasingly deployed across global user
populations, yet their alignment procedures — RLHF, DPO, constitutional AI —
rely almost exclusively on preference data and normative judgments sourced from
Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) populations.
This leads to systematic cultural blind spots in:

 1 Normative reasoning — the model applies Western-centric ethical frameworks
   (e.g., individual autonomy > collective welfare) even when deployed in
   collectivist cultural contexts.
 2 Pragmatic acceptability — outputs violate local social norms around
   hierarchy, face-saving, indirectness, or religious sensitivity that WEIRD
   annotators would not flag.
 3 Value pluralism — the model cannot modulate its response style or content to
   respect legitimate cross-cultural value differences (e.g., attitudes toward
   authority, gender roles, uncertainty avoidance).
 4 Evaluation gap — existing alignment benchmarks (HH-RLHF, Anthropic's
   Helpfulness/Harmlessness, MT-Bench) measure alignment to a single (implicitly
   Western) preference distribution.

The core challenge is that alignment is currently treated as a universal
optimization problem when it is in fact a pluralistic one: different cultural
groups have different — and sometimes conflicting — legitimate value systems.
Current methods collapse this pluralism into a single reward model or preference
distribution.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis1. A multi-dimensional value scaffolding approach — where cultural
value dimensions are explicitly represented as steerable latent directions in
the model's representation space — enables controllable cross-cultural alignment
without retraining per culture.

 2 Adding culturally diverse preference data from ≥6 cultural regions (rather
   than scaling WEIRD data) disproportionately improves alignment quality in
   non-Western contexts without degrading Western-aligned performance.
 3 Models aligned with explicit cultural value dimensions generalize to unseen
   cultural contexts better than models aligned to any single culture's
   preferences, even when trained only on seen cultures.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method### Phase1: Cultural Value Dimension ExtractionWe extract and
operationalize cultural value dimensions from established cross-cultural
psychology frameworks — primarily Hofstede's6 dimensions (Power Distance,
Individualism/Collectivism, Masculinity/Femininity, Uncertainty Avoidance,
Long-Term Orientation, Indulgence/Restraint) and the World Values Survey's7
value dimensions (Traditional/Secular-Rational, Survival/Self-Expression, plus
five sub-dimensions).

For each dimension, we construct:

 • Polarity-defining text pairs: Contrastive prompts where the culturally
   "expected" answer differs by position on the dimension (e.g., high vs. low
   power distance framing of a managerial decision).
 • Dimension probes:200 prompts per dimension designed to elicit responses whose
   cultural loading can be measured.

Phase2: Multi-Cultural Preference Data CollectionCollect preference pairs
across10 language/culture groups:

 • North America (English), Western Europe (English/French/German), Latin
   America (Spanish/Portuguese), South Asia (Hindi/Urdu/English), East Asia
   (Chinese/Japanese/Korean), Middle East/North Africa (Arabic), Sub-Saharan
   Africa (Swahili/Yoruba/English), Southeast Asia (Vietnamese/Thai/Indonesian),
   Eastern Europe (Russian/Polish), Nordic (Swedish/Norwegian/Danish)

For each group, collect5,000 preference pairs covering: helpfulness,
harmlessness, social norms, authority relations, religious sensitivity, and
family/community obligations. Annotators are in-country native speakers with
cultural moderation training.

Phase3: Value-Scaffolded Alignment TrainingThree training variants:

 1 Naive multi-preference DPO: Standard DPO trained on pooled multi-cultural
   preferences (baseline treatment).
 2 Value-conditioned DPO (VC-DPO): Each preference pair is labeled with cultural
   region + value dimension scores. The model conditions on these during
   training, learning to map value profiles to response distributions.
 3 Representation-engineering alignment (RE-Align): Identify activation-steering
   vectors corresponding to each cultural value dimension (using the dimension
   probes from Phase1). During inference, steer by interpolating between
   dimension vectors to match a target cultural profile. No retraining needed.

Phase4: Cross-Cultural EvaluationEvaluate on three held-out cultural contexts
not seen during training (e.g., Turkish, Indonesian, and a synthetic "cultural
blend" scenario). Also evaluate on existing alignment benchmarks to measure
degradation from cultural specialization.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Component | Source / Construction | Size |

|---|---|---| | Cultural Dimension Probes | Constructed from Hofstede + WVS
survey items adapted to LLM interaction scenarios |2,400 prompts (200 ×12
dimensions) | | Multi-Cultural Preference Pairs | Newly collected via in-country
annotation teams (Upwork / Prolific) |50,000 pairs (5,000 ×10 cultures) | |
Cross-Cultural Alignment Benchmark (CCABench) | Constructed as held-out test set
covering3 cultures +3 cross-cultural conflict scenarios |3,000 evaluation
prompts | | Existing Benchmarks | HH-RLHF, MT-Bench, SafetyBench, TruthfulQA |
As-is |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics1. Cultural Preference Accuracy (CPA): For each cultural
group, the fraction of generated responses preferred by in-country annotators
over the baseline model output. Reported per group and pooled.

 2 Value Dimension Alignment (VDA): Cosine similarity between the model's latent
   value profile (from steering probes) and the target culture's known value
   profile (from Hofstede/WVS norms). Measured in representation space.
 3 Cross-Cultural Generalization (CCG): CPA on held-out cultural groups not seen
   during training.
 4 Alignment Degradation (AD): Change in HH-RLHF / MT-Bench scores relative to
   the baseline (Llama-3-8B with DPO on HH-RLHF). We accept ≤5% degradation as
   acceptable.
 5 Value Pluralism Score (VPS): Variance of model responses across different
   cultural steering conditions when given the same factual input — measures
   whether the model can genuinely shift cultural frame rather than producing
   uniform outputs.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Base model: Llama-3-8B (no alignment)

 2 Single-culture DPO: DPO trained on HH-RLHF only (Western alignment)
 3 Pooled DPO: DPO trained on pooled multi-cultural preferences without cultural
   conditioning4. Multi-Reward RLHF: RLHF with separate reward models for each
   cultural region5. Constitutional AI: Self-critique with a multi-cultural
   constitution (manually written)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations1. -Dim: Remove explicit value dimensions; use only cultural region
labels in VC-DPO2. -NonEnglish: Train on English-only preference data, evaluate
cross-cultural transfer to non-English prompts3. -NumCultures: Train on3
cultures instead of10; measure generalization4. -Steer: RE-Align without
inference-time steering (frozen cultural profile)

 5 -Contrastive: Remove the polarity-defining text pairs from Phase1; use only
   natural preference data6. Pooled DPO × k: Scale pooled data up to match
   VC-DPO data volume (isolate conditioning mechanism from data-volume effects)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Stereotype amplification: Steering toward cultural
value dimensions may reinforce harmful stereotypes rather than respecting
legitimate value differences. For example, steering toward high Power Distance
may produce outputs that endorse authoritarian governance rather than
pragmatically acknowledging hierarchical norms.

 2 Value conflation: Hofstede dimensions are ecological (country-level)
   constructs, not individual psychological attributes. Applying them at the
   utterance level may produce incoherent signals.
 3 Cultural essentialism: The framework treats cultures as discrete, stable
   categories, ignoring intracultural variation, diaspora identities, and
   cultural change over time.
 4 Annotation bias within cultures: Each culture's annotators may themselves
   skew urban/educated/young, reproducing within-culture WEIRD-like sampling
   bias.
 5 Reward hacking: Conditioned on a target cultural profile, the model may
   produce outputs that superficially match stereotype features of that profile
   rather than authentically engaging with cultural reasoning.
 6 Alignment tax asymmetry: Cultural specialization may degrade performance
   asymmetrically — non-Western cultures may lose less Western performance than
   Western-aligned models lose non-Western performance, but Western performance
   degradation may still exceed the5% threshold.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations- Ground-truth value dimensions: Hofstede and WVS dimensions are
contested — they were developed for organizational/cross-national psychology,
not for AI alignment. They may not capture the value dimensions most relevant to
LLM safety and helpfulness.

 • Language vs. culture confound: Our cultural groupings correlate with
   language. We cannot fully disentangle whether improvements come from
   cross-lingual transfer, cultural knowledge, or both.
 • Annotation scale:5,000 pairs per culture yields ≈83 hours of annotation at60
   seconds per pair. At $15/hr, that is $12,500 per culture or $125,000 total.
   The annotation budget is substantial and may limit reproducibility.
 • No behavioral validation: We evaluate on LLM outputs, not on downstream
   behavioral outcomes (e.g., user retention, satisfaction, trust). A high CPA
   may not translate to real-world cultural competence.
 • Temporal instability: Cultural values shift over time (especially in younger
   populations). A model aligned to2025 cultural norms may be misaligned by2030.
 • Which cultures get representation?: Any finite set of cultures implicitly
   marginalizes cultures not chosen. The framework does not solve the
   fundamental political question of whose values get encoded.

Title: CULTURAL-PREF: Preference Tuning with Culturally-Grounded Contrastive
Examples for Cross-Cultural LLM AlignmentProblem. Current RLHF/DPO alignment
pipelines overwhelmingly use preference data annotated by English-speaking,
Western raters. This produces models that (a) treat Western cultural norms as
universal defaults, (b) give culturally inappropriate or offensive answers in
non-Western contexts, and (c) lack measurable mechanisms to control which
cultural frame the model should adopt for a given user or query. No existing
work has systematically decomposed which dimensions of alignment (helpfulness,
harmlessness, honesty, social norms) are most culturally divergent, nor tested
whether targeted preference data can close the gap without degrading Western
performance.

Hypothesis. Fine-tuning an LLM with preference pairs where the same query
receives different culturally appropriate responses across target cultures
(e.g., Japanese vs. Brazilian vs. Saudi Arabian social norms) will produce a
model whose outputs can be steered toward a specified cultural frame via a
lightweight prompt prefix, while maintaining competitive performance on standard
Western-centric benchmarks. The core claim: cultural divergence in alignment is
concentrated in a small set of behavioral dimensions (social hierarchy,
indirectness, taboo topics, gift-giving norms, and individualist vs.
collectivist framing), and targeted contrastive examples on these dimensions
suffice to induce generalizable cross-cultural behavior.

Method. Three-stage pipeline:

1 Taxonomy construction. Use a research-agent-assisted literature review of
cross-cultural psychology (Hofstede dimensions, GLOBE project, Hall's
high/low context) and existing culturally-aware LLM datasets (CULTURALBENCH,
CULTUREPAIR, GLOBALALIGN) to produce a taxonomy of8–12 behavioral dimensions
where LLM outputs are expected to diverge across cultures. Each dimension
gets a one-paragraph annotation specifying the expected range of appropriate
behavior.
2 Contrastive preference dataset. For each dimension, generate200–400
query-response triples (query, culturally-appropriate-response-A,
culturally-appropriate-response-B) across two target cultures (e.g.,
US-English and Japanese) using human annotation or validated LLM-as-judge
pipelines with culture-specific rubrics. Each triple explicitly labels which
cultural frame each response fits. Total target: ~3,000–5,000 preference
pairs.
3 Preference tuning & steering. Fine-tune a base model (e.g., Llama-3-8B or
Qwen-2.5-7B) via DPO on the contrastive dataset. Add a steering mechanism: a
prepended system prompt specifying the target cultural frame (e.g., "You are
a helpful assistant responding to someone in Japan. Follow Japanese social
norms: use polite register, avoid direct refusals, respect hierarchical
address."). Evaluate whether steering via prompt alone suffices or whether a
lightweight adapter (LoRA per culture) is needed.

Dataset / Benchmark.

• Training: Custom constructed dataset (described above).
• Evaluation: CULTURALBENCH (cross-cultural QA and social norms), CULTUREPAIR
(culturally sensitive comparison pairs), and a subset of GLOBALALIGN (moral
and social alignment across10+ countries). Also construct a held-out
"cross-cultural adversarial" test set of200 prompts where the appropriate
response differs sharply between two cultures (e.g., feedback to a superior,
gift refusal, discussion of religious holidays).

Evaluation Metrics.

• Cultural appropriateness score: Agreement with human raters from each target
culture (≥3 raters per item, Krippendorff's α ≥0.7 threshold) on a5-point
Likert scale measuring whether the response is culturally appropriate for the
specified frame.
• Steerability accuracy: For each culture-steered query, does the model's
response align with the intended culture (vs. default/majority culture)?
Measured by both human evaluation and an LLM judge fine-tuned on the same
taxonomy.
• Western benchmark retention: Performance drop on HellaSwag, MMLU, and
MT-Bench. Threshold: ≤2% absolute degradation.
• Dimension-level divergence: Per-dimension score showing which cultural
dimensions the model handles well vs. poorly.

Baselines.

1 Base model (no fine-tuning): Shows the default cultural bias of the
pretrained model.
2 Standard DPO (general preference data): Trained on the full HelpSteer2 or
UltraFeedback dataset (no cultural conditioning). Measures whether standard
alignment already produces monocultural outputs.
3 Naive prompt steering: Apply the same culture-steering prompt to the base
model without fine-tuning. Isolates the effect of prompting vs. preference
tuning.
4 Culture-agnostic DPO + prompt steering: DPO on the contrastive dataset
without culture labels during training, but with steering prompts at
inference. Tests whether contrastive data alone helps even without labeled
training.

Ablations.

• Dimension ablation: Remove one behavioral dimension at a time from the
contrastive dataset. Which dimensions are critical for cross-cultural
generalization?
• Data scaling: Train on10%,25%,50%,100% of the contrastive dataset. Is there a
diminishing-returns threshold?
• Model scale: Repeat the best configuration on a1B,7B, and27B parameter model
(or whatever sizes are available). Does cross-cultural steerability scale
with model size?
• Target culture ablation: Train on US–Japan pairs only, then evaluate on
US–Brazil and US–Saudi Arabia. Does the method generalize to unseen target
cultures?

Expected Failure Modes.

1 Surface-level mimicry. The model learns to insert polite markers and
culture-specific keywords without understanding deeper social norms (e.g.,
produces Japanese honorifics but gives a direct refusal that violates
Japanese indirectness norms). Mitigation: Include examples where the surface
form and deep norm diverge, and evaluate with adversarial probes that test
for this distinction.
2 Steering interference. The culture-steering prompt competes with the base
model's pre-existing alignment (refusal training, safety filters), producing
unpredictable behavior in safety-critical queries. Mitigation: Explicitly
include edge-case safety prompts in the contrastive dataset and measure
safety metric separately.
3 Overfitting to stereotype. The taxonomy-based approach encodes stereotypical
or outdated cultural norms, producing responses that caricature rather than
respect the target culture. Mitigation: Validate all dimension annotations
with in-culture reviewers; include intra-cultural variation examples (e.g.,
both formal and informal Japanese responses).
4 Western performance collapse. Teaching the model to deviate from its default
alignment causes broad degradation on standard English benchmarks.
Mitigation: Monitor Western benchmarks throughout training, early-stop if
degradation exceeds2%, and test whether a residual connection or adapter
merging strategy preserves base capabilities.
5 Rater disagreement. Human raters from the same culture disagree on what
constitutes an appropriate response, making the ground-truth labels noisy.
Mitigation: Use an agreement threshold (Krippendorff's α ≥0.7) and discard or
re-annotate items below it. Report confidence intervals on all human
evaluation metrics.
6 Non-transferability to unseen cultures. The model learns a mapping from
"culture token → behavior" but fails on cultures not seen during training.
Mitigation: The target-culture ablation (train on US–Japan, test on
US–Brazil, US–Saudi Arabia) directly tests this; if it fails, the method
collapses to a retrieval problem rather than actual cultural generalization.

Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Distributional Reward
Uncertainty: A Scalable Framework for Value Alignment### TitleScalable Value
Alignment via Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning under Distributional
Reward Uncertainty

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ProblemAs autonomous AI agents are deployed in high-stakes settings—healthcare,
autonomous driving, content moderation, and economic planning—the gap between
specified reward functions and human intent grows increasingly dangerous. Reward
misspecification, goal misgeneralization, and specification gaming are
well-documented failure modes in which agents exploit proxy rewards rather than
the values the designer intended.

Current approaches to value alignment fall into three camps, each with a
fundamental limitation:

 1 Reward modeling from demonstrations (IRL, BC): Requires high-quality expert
   demonstrations, which are expensive to collect and brittle to distribution
   shift. Agents learn to mimic behavior rather than infer the underlying values
   that generate it.
 2 Human feedback methods (RLHF, Preference-based RL): Scalable but rely on
   binary comparisons or scalar ratings that collapse rich human values into a
   single dimension. Known to amplify annotator biases, suffer from reward
   hacking under distribution shift, and fail when preferences are inconsistent
   across contexts.
 3 Constitutional AI / rule-based guardrails: Static constraints that cannot
   adapt to novel situations. Hard-coding values scales poorly—every new domain
   requires new rules, and value conflicts (e.g., privacy vs. safety) are
   resolved arbitrarily.

A unified framework that (a) actively elicits human values rather than passively
observing behavior, (b) captures distributional uncertainty about what the human
wants, and (c) generalizes across contexts without task-specific reengineering
remains an open problem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

HypothesisCooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL) — in which the human
and the agent are modeled as collaborators optimizing a shared reward function
known only to the human — provides a principled foundation for value alignment.
We hypothesize that extending CIRL with distributional reward representations
(explicitly modeling the agent's uncertainty over human reward functions as a
full distribution rather than a point estimate) will:

 1 Produce agents that actively query humans in proportion to their uncertainty
   about the human's values, enabling sample-efficient value learning.
 2 Yield calibrated confidence estimates that allow safe delegation: the agent
   can defer to the human when uncertainty is high and act autonomously when
   uncertainty is low.
 3 Generalize to held-out tasks within the same environment without retraining,
   because the agent learns values rather than behavioral policies.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MethodWe propose Distributional Cooperative Inverse Reinforcement Learning
(DC-IRL) , a framework with four components:

1. Distributional Reward Model (DRM). Instead of learning a point estimate of
the reward function (R(s,a)), the agent maintains a Bayesian posterior over
reward parameters (P(R \mid \mathcalitable reward posterior. Mitigation:
Constrain query selection to regions of the state space the human has
demonstrated they can evaluate; incorporate a human-satisfaction rating per
query as an auxiliary signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limitations1. Scalability of Bayesian inference. Maintaining a full posterior
over reward parameters via deep ensembles requires (K \times) the compute of a
single reward model. For large-scale environments (e.g., LLM fine-tuning with10M
parameters), the ensemble approach may be impractical. Future work should
investigate amortized variational posteriors or hypernetwork-based reward
uncertainty as cheaper alternatives.

 2 Feature engineering burden. The approach requires a pre-specified feature
   space (\phi(s,a)) for the linear reward decomposition, which is
   environment-specific. While this is standard in the CIRL literature, it
   limits applicability to environments where good features are not available.
   An obvious extension—learning features end-to-end while maintaining
   uncertainty over the full network—introduces computational challenges this
   proposal does not address.
 3 Single-human assumption. The framework assumes a single human whose values
   the agent must learn. In multi-stakeholder settings (e.g., autonomous
   vehicles balancing safety vs. efficiency across passengers, pedestrians, and
   regulators), there is no single reward function to infer. Extending DC-IRL to
   multi-principal settings with conflicting values is not covered.
 4 No mechanism for value drift. The framework treats human values as static. In
   practice, human values shift with context, mood, and new information. The
   posterior over reward weights will over-commit to early signals and resist
   updating if values change. This is a known limitation of Bayesian approaches
   that assume a fixed generative model.
 5 Evaluation environments are simulated. While Overcooked-AI, Safety-Gym, and
   WebShop are standard benchmarks in the alignment literature, they are toy
   environments relative to real-world deployment. Transfer to settings with
   open-ended language, long time horizons, and multi-modal perception is
   unvalidated.
 6 Alignment is defined operationally as reward recovery. A philosophical
   limitation: this framework equates alignment with the agent's ability to
   infer and optimize a human's revealed preferences. It assumes that revealed
   preferences (demonstrations and queries) faithfully represent the human's
   true values—an assumption contested in behavioral economics (preference
   construction, framing effects, adaptive preferences). The framework does not
   address normative questions about which values should be aligned, only how to
   infer them.

Research Proposal: Steering Vector–Based Value Control in Large Language
Models## Title
Value Steering Without Fine-Tuning: Representation Engineering for
Controllable AI Alignment

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Current value alignment methods for LLMs — primarily RLHF and
constitutional AI — operate at the parametric level: they fine-tune model
weights using reward-model scores or self-critique data. This creates two
unresolved problems:

1 Value brittleness under distribution shift — an RLHF-tuned model may behave
consistently on in-distribution helpfulness/harmlessness prompts but fail on
adversarial inputs, domain shifts, or tasks that were not represented in the
preference data.
2 Value entanglement with capability — fine-tuning for alignment inevitably
modifies weights that also encode reasoning, factual recall, and linguistic
ability, making it difficult to attribute behavior changes to "value
learning" versus capability degradation or surface-level pattern matching.

A method that can separately control value-relevant behavior without modifying
base weights would enable testable hypotheses about whether alignment is a
representational property or a learned behavioral policy.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Primary hypothesis: For a given LLM, there exists a low-dimensional
subspace in the residual stream (or attention head outputs) such that
intervention along a value direction — defined by contrasting activation
patterns on value-consistent vs. value-violating examples — shifts the model's
alignment-relevant generation behavior on held-out prompts with statistical
significance (p <0.01, Bonferroni-corrected across5 dimensions) while preserving
perplexity on standard language modeling benchmarks within2% of the unmodified
model.

Secondary hypothesis: Value steering vectors generalize across related value
dimensions (e.g., a "honesty" vector improves "fairness" behavior) but are
separable from capability-related vectors (e.g., "reasoning quality," "factual
recall"), as measured by cosine similarity between steering directions <0.15.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal adapts representation engineering (RepE) (Zou et al.,2023) to
value alignment with three modifications:

1 Contrastive activation collection. For each target value dimension (e.g.,
helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, fairness), collect500 contrast pairs from
a public preference dataset (Anthropic HH-RLHF or PKU-SafeRLHF). Each pair
consists of a value-consistent completion and a value-violating completion
for the same prompt. Extract hidden states at every layer from the residual
stream and attention outputs for both completions. The value direction for
layer l is the top PCA component of the difference vectors Δ = h(consistent)
− h(violating).
2 Reading and steering. Two operations:

• Reading: Compute alignment along each direction for a test prompt by
projecting the model's activations onto the value direction. This produces a
scalar "value alignment score" per layer without any generation.
• Steering: At inference time, add a scaled value direction vector (coefficient
α) to the residual stream at a chosen layer set. Generate completions under
steering. Vary α ∈                                                           Goodbye!

EvoScientist — Ablation Experiment -IVE### TitleUnified Audio Foundation Models:
A Multi-Task Pretraining Framework for Speech, Music, and Environmental Sound
Understanding

ProblemGeneral-purpose audio understanding remains fragmented. Current
foundation models are specialized per domain — Whisper for speech, music tagging
models trained on Million Song Dataset, environmental sound classifiers on
AudioSet — with no single architecture that jointly handles speech
transcription, speaker identification, music analysis, acoustic scene
classification, and audio captioning at comparable quality. The core open
question is whether a unified model that shares representations across audio
domains can match or exceed specialist models on each individual task.

HypothesisA Transformer-based audio foundation model pretrained on a diverse
corpus spanning speech, music, and environmental sounds, using a combination of
masked autoencoding and contrastive audio-text learning, will achieve
competitive or superior performance on downstream tasks compared to
domain-specific specialist models, provided that the pretraining data
distribution and task weighting are carefully balanced to avoid catastrophic
forgetting of low-resource domains.

MethodArchitecture: A hierarchical audio Transformer operating on log-Mel
spectrograms (128 bins,16 kHz sampling). The model uses a convolutional stem
(two2D Conv layers with stride2 each) to produce a sequence of patch embeddings,
followed by24 Transformer layers (1024 hidden dim,16 heads, GELU activations). A
dual-decoder design outputs: (1) a masked reconstruction head for pretraining,
and (2) a shared projection head for downstream tasks.

Pretraining objective (two-stage):

 1 Masked spectrogram reconstruction — mask40% of time-frequency patches;
   reconstruct in frequency-domain with L1 + perceptual loss. This captures
   acoustic structure without requiring labels.
 2 Contrastive audio-text alignment — paired (audio, caption) data from multiple
   sources, using a InfoNCE loss with learned temperature. Text encoder is a
   frozen12-layer BERT; only the audio encoder learns gradients.

Downstream adaptation: For each task, a lightweight MLP head (2 layers,512→task
classes) is added. During finetuning, the backbone is either: (a) fully
finetuned, (b) LoRA-adapted (rank16), or (c) kept frozen (linear probe). All
three configurations are evaluated.

Dataset & Benchmark| Source | Domain | Size | Use |

|--------|--------|------|-----| | AudioSet (balanced subset) | Environmental
sounds |20K clips,10s | Pretrain + scene classification | | LibriSpeech
clean+other | Speech |960 hours | ASR | | VoxCeleb2 | Speaker ID |1M+ utterances
from6K speakers | Speaker recognition | | MusicCaps | Music captioning |5.5K
clips + English captions | Audio-text alignment | | FSD50K | Sound events |51K
clips,200 classes | Sound event detection | | Clotho v2 | Audio captioning |5K
clips,5 captions each | Captioning eval |

Hold-out splits: Each dataset uses its standard evaluation partition. No
cross-dataset contamination — a model pretrained on AudioSet is evaluated on the
official AudioSet eval split.

Evaluation Metrics| Task | Primary Metric | Secondary Metric |

|------|---------------|-----------------| | Automatic speech recognition
(LibriSpeech test-clean) | Word error rate (WER) | Character error rate | |
Speaker identification (VoxCeleb1 test) | Accuracy | Macro F1 | | Acoustic scene
classification (AudioSet eval) | mAP (mean average precision) | d-prime | |
Music tagging (MusicCaps test) | ROC-AUC | F1@10 | | Sound event detection
(FSD50K eval) | mAP | F1@threshold | | Audio captioning (Clotho eval) | SPICE,
CIDEr | BLEU-4, ROUGE-L |

Baselines| Baseline | Domain | Architecture | Why |

|----------|--------|-------------|-----| | Whisper large-v3 | Speech |
Encoder-decoder Transformer | Strong ASR specialist | | HuBERT base | Speech |
Masked prediction Transformer | Self-supervised speech | | CLAP (LAION) |
General audio | Dual-encoder (audio + text) | Existing general-audio baseline |
| AST (Audio Spectrogram Transformer) | General audio | ViT-based on
spectrograms | Prior SOTA on AudioSet | | Wav2CLIP | Audio-visual | Contrastive
audio-image | Audio-text alignment baseline | | Domain-specific specialists per
task | Various | Various | Upper bound per task |

All baselines evaluated on the same downstream benchmarks under the same
protocol.

AblationsAll ablations use the same pretraining data and compute budget (same
number of total update steps).

 1 Pretraining data composition: Remove speech data (→ only music +
   environmental), remove music data, remove environmental data — measure
   per-task degradation.
 2 Objective ablations: Masked reconstruction only (no contrastive text),
   contrastive only (no reconstruction), reconstruction with L1-only loss (no
   perceptual loss).
 3 Scale ablations: Small (12 layers,512 dim), Base (24 layers,768 dim), Large
   (24 layers,1024 dim — the primary model).
 4 Downstream adaptation method: Full finetune vs. LoRA rank8/16/32 vs. linear
   probe.
 5 Positive-free impact of validation memory (-IVE variant): This experiment is
   the -IVE ablation. Compare against the full EvoScientist generation (which
   had access to accumulated validation-evolution memory) on: proposal stability
   (number of structural revisions needed), gap coverage (tasks or failure modes
   missed that the validated proposal would catch), and specificity of
   failure-mode identification. This is a meta-ablation: it measures proposal
   quality rather than model quality.

Expected Failure Modes- Domain dominance: Speech data volume overwhelms the
training signal; environmental sound and music tasks plateau. If LibriSpeech and
VoxCeleb2 together account for >80% of pretraining tokens, the model may
compress environmental sound representations into a small fraction of the latent
space. Mitigation: stratified sampling per domain during training.

 • Task interference: The contrastive audio-text objective conflicts with the
   reconstruction objective, producing embeddings that are neither good for
   generation nor good for discrimination. Expected to manifest as both WER and
   mAP degrading relative to single-objective models.
 • Catastrophic forgetting in low-resource tasks: Clotho (5.5K clips) may be
   forgotten during later training stages. Scheduled sampling or replay buffers
   may be needed.
 • Texture vs. content tradeoff: The model may learn texture-level features
   (spectral centroid, loudness) that help environmental sound tasks but that
   are poor for phoneme-level speech recognition. The convolutional stem's
   stride may compound this by discarding fine time-resolution information.
 • Without validation-evolution memory (-IVE), the proposal lacks accumulated
   knowledge of which prior architectures failed at this multi-task balancing
   problem, making it more likely to over-commit to a single objective weighting
   without sensitivity analysis. The expected signature: this proposal will
   propose fewer alternative weighting schedules and fewer countermeasures than
   the full EvoScientist proposal.

Limitations (explicit and uncontrolled)

 1 No generative audio tasks: The proposal covers understanding (classification,
   transcription, tagging, captioning) but not generative tasks (text-to-speech,
   music generation, audio inpainting). A true general-purpose model would also
   generate audio.
 2 Fixed input representation: Log-Mel spectrograms at16 kHz discard phase
   information and limit high-frequency resolution. Raw waveform models (e.g.,
   S4, Mamba) may capture different inductive biases.
 3 Limited language coverage: All datasets are English. Multilingual speech
   (Common Voice, Fleurs) and cross-lingual audio captioning are not evaluated.
 4 No streaming or real-time evaluation: Inference latency, online decoding, and
   streaming ASR protocols are not addressed.
 5 Text encoder frozen during pretraining: This prevents the audio encoder from
   influencing the text representations, which may limit cross-modal alignment
   capacity.
 6 Compute constraint:24-layer Transformer on16 kHz spectrograms is heavy (~1.5B
   parameters). Practical deployment may require distillation or quantization
   not explored here.
 7 No temporal localization: The proposal handles clip-level classification and
   transcription but not timestamp-level sound event detection or word-level
   forced alignment.
 8 Evaluation loose ends: No human evaluation for captioning quality, no
   fairness/disparity analysis across accents or recording conditions, and no
   robustness testing under synthetic corruptions (noise, reverberation,
   bandwidth limiting).

Research Proposal: Reproducing and Extending Masked Audio Modeling for
General-Purpose Audio Foundation Models## Title
Are Masked Autoencoders
Sufficient for General-Purpose Audio Representation Learning? A Reproducibility
and Extension Study of AudioMAE

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Self-supervised audio foundation models promise a single pretrained
backbone that transfers to speech, music, and environmental sound tasks. The
AudioMAE (Xu et al.,2022) architecture—an asymmetric encoder-decoder with a high
mask ratio (75–80%) applied to mel-spectrogram patches—claimed state-of-the-art
transfer on AudioSet, ESC-50, and Speech Commands v2. However, the community
lacks:

1 Independent reproduction — the original code was released late and the
results have not been systematically verified by a separate group.
2 A controlled comparison against reconstruction-based (AudioMAE) vs.
contrastive (CLAP, ImageBind) pretraining objectives for general-purpose use.
3 An ablation isolating what drives performance: high mask ratio, decoder
depth, or patch size?

We aim to reproduce AudioMAE's core results and extend them by introducing a
hybrid objective that combines masked reconstruction with a contrastive
alignment loss (audio-text), testing the hypothesis that reconstruction alone is
insufficient for general-purpose transfer.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Null hypothesis (H₀): AudioMAE's masked reconstruction objective
yields representations that transfer to speech, music, and environmental tasks
as well as or better than a hybrid reconstruction + contrastive objective.

Alternative hypothesis (H₁): Adding a contrastive alignment loss (audio-text)
during pretraining significantly improves downstream transfer on tasks requiring
high-level semantics (e.g., audio captioning, zero-shot sound classification),
while maintaining or improving performance on acoustic-only tasks (e.g., scene
classification).

Falsification condition: If the hybrid model does not outperform AudioMAE on at
least2 out of3 semantic-level downstream tasks (by >2% absolute in the primary
metric) while not regressing by more than1% on acoustic-level tasks, H₁ is
rejected.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1 — Reproduce AudioMAEExact reproduction of the AudioMAE baseline
(Xu et al.,2022) using the official configuration:

• Input: Log-mel spectrograms (128 mel bins,1024 FFT,512 hop), patchified
into16×16 patches (time×freq).
• Encoder: ViT-B/16 (12 layers,768 hidden,12 heads).
• Decoder: Lightweight4-layer ViT (384 hidden,6 heads).
• Mask ratio:80% of patches masked.
• Pretraining objective: L2 reconstruction loss in the spectrogram space
(normalized patches).
• Pretraining data: AudioSet-2M (balanced subset of ~2M clips from AudioSet).
• Optimization: AdamW, lr=1.5e-4, cosine decay, batch size1024,800 epochs.

Stage2 — Hybrid Objective (AudioMAE + CLAP-style contrastive head)

Attach a contrastive head to the [CLS] token of the encoder. During
pretraining,50% of batches use reconstruction loss and50% use the InfoNCE loss
aligning audio embeddings with paired text descriptions (from AudioSet labels +
synthetic captions via LaCLAP pipeline). Total loss: L = λ·L_recon +
(1-λ)·L_contrastive, with λ annealed from1.0 →0.5 across training.

Stage3 — Downstream transfer evaluationFreeze encoder, train linear probes (and
separately, full fine-tuning) on each benchmark.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Task | Dataset | Metric | Type |

|------|---------|--------|------| | Sound event classification | ESC-50 (50
classes,2000 clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic | | Action recognition (audio) |
AudioSet-20K (20-class subset,20K clips) | mAP | Acoustic | | Speech command
recognition | Speech Commands v2 (35 classes,105K clips) | Accuracy | Acoustic |
| Music genre classification | GTZAN (10 genres,1000 clips) | Accuracy |
Acoustic | | Audio captioning (zero-shot) | Clotho (4981 audio-text pairs) |
SPICE / CIDEr | Semantic | | Zero-shot sound classification | ESC-50 (zero-shot
via text labels) | Accuracy | Semantic |

All splits follow standard published train/validation/test splits.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics- Primary: Accuracy (classification), mAP (multi-label),
SPICE/CIDEr (captioning)

• Secondary: F1-score per class, average precision, zero-shot top-1 / top-5-
Uncertainty:5 random seeds for every downstream result; report mean ± std-
Statistical test: Paired bootstrap test (p <0.05) for the primary metric on
each task, with Bonferroni correction across6 tasks (threshold p <0.0083)
